## SUMMARY

Fuse the Gaussian renderer's sorted attribute gather and its backward scatter.
The existing path launches eight `index_select` operations plus packing and
their backward operations. On the tested scene, the new path reduces GPU events
per training step from 283 to 244 and gives modest measured train-step reductions
of 4.11% at 512px and 2.14% at 1024px. Numerical behavior and retained screen-space
gradients are covered by six new CUDA tests. CPU rendering keeps its existing path.

This PR is **stacked on #49**, including #48/#21: base
`ba119b2aacceabe046166fcb3a37537129769942`. The new gather change itself is
`d58ac07` + `fbb3527` + `d45b911`; the final report-only head is `229f04dfd678b999dbe711a947a4b3b3ea608d1f`.
Please account for the stack when reviewing the diff. No upstream branch is
pushed or merged by this work.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `FusedGatherFunction` packs depth-sorted means, conic parameters, opacity,
  depth and color into the rasterizer's existing ten-column attribute matrix.
  One CUDA thread handles each visible row.
- The renderer constructs unique in-range IDs from visibility `nonzero` and
  depth `argsort`, so the adjoint is an assignment scatter without atomics.
  This is an internal permutation-subset contract; metadata is checked, but
  duplicate/out-of-range ID values are not dynamically synchronized and validated.
- `means2d` stays a separate autograd input, preserving the retained gradient
  consumed by densification. Projection-gradient columns for those means stay
  zero so the view's existing backward accumulates exactly once.
- The backward saves IDs/shapes only and zeroes one allocation containing
  disjoint contiguous views for **requested** gradients. Frozen inputs allocate
  no retained gradient slice. This fixes an observed intermediate implementation
  regression (16,448 versus 2,056 retained bytes for mean-only training).
- CUDA device/current-stream handling and noncontiguous input temporaries are
  exercised explicitly. This is first-order autograd, as in the existing fused
  projection/rasterizer. The CPU and camera-pose-gradient fallback are retained.
- `--fused-gather 0/1` is a benchmark switch; the internal process-wide toggle
  should not be changed concurrently by per-request application code.

## TESTING

Native release builds used the final runtime source
`d45b9112ac664688bfefbc79d302738dd7a4aecc`. All measurements used an immutable
uninstrumented executable (SHA-256
`33922770cc2a672c231828a7f25f277a826a73d54feac5145edb598c44df43d4`).

| Full suite | CPU pass / fail / skip | CUDA pass / fail / skip |
|---|---:|---:|
| Gaussian | 47 / 0 / 5 | 68 / 0 / 0 |
| Adaptive | 119 / 0 / 1 | 123 / 0 / 0 |

Six added CUDA tests cover exact permutations/subsets/empty and strided inputs,
112 finite-difference components, metadata rejection, nondefault-stream temporary
lifetimes, frozen-input storage, and full-render gradients including retained
means. Forward render outputs are bit-identical. Isolated gradients match exactly;
full-render gradients use `1e-5 * max_abs_reference + 1e-6` because the existing
rasterizer accumulates atomically (observed maximum relative difference about
1.4e-7 in the final suite). For 257 rows, mean/projection/opacity/color-only
gradients retain exactly 2,056/10,280/1,028/3,084 bytes, matching the reference.

Compute Sanitizer memcheck, racecheck and initcheck each pass all six tests with
zero errors/hazards. The known LibTorch `indexing_backward_kernel` is excluded
from instrumentation; the new gather/scatter kernels are included. This is not
an unrestricted sanitizer pass for the excluded reference kernel.

The host lacks Docker. Runtime tests and benchmarks therefore use its existing
native environment. This PR's CUDA 12.4/13.2/13.4 Docker build CI is a separate
check and is not a claim of Docker GPU runtime testing. CI status is visible in
the checks; this description does not pre-claim its result.

<!-- gather-ci-41497415910 -->
### Docker build verification

The exact PR head `229f04dfd678b999dbe711a947a4b3b3ea608d1f` passed all three Docker build profiles in [CI run 41497415910](https://github.com/QuiteLiterallyConnor/Minkowski4CPP/actions/runs/41497415910).

| Profile | Result | Job |
|---|---|---|
| build-and-publish (124) | passed | [job](https://github.com/QuiteLiterallyConnor/Minkowski4CPP/actions/runs/41497415910/job/125455880988) |
| build-and-publish (132) | passed | [job](https://github.com/QuiteLiterallyConnor/Minkowski4CPP/actions/runs/41497415910/job/125455881076) |
| build-and-publish (134) | passed | [job](https://github.com/QuiteLiterallyConnor/Minkowski4CPP/actions/runs/41497415910/job/125455881039) |

The builder-script and PowerShell-builder checks also passed. These checks compile the modified source in Docker; they do not run GPU workloads in the container. Native CPU/CUDA correctness, sanitizer coverage and benchmark results above remain the runtime evidence. No source changes or replacement benchmark claims were made for this update.

## BENCHMARKS

Same binary, gather disabled/enabled; projection and tile fusion enabled in both.
The bundled `test.ply` contains 139,410 Gaussians. Each of ten balanced A/B rounds
has three warmups and ten synchronized measured iterations, in separate render
and train processes. All 40 subprocesses completed successfully. Entries below
are medians of process medians with min-max ranges across rounds. Throughput is
the reciprocal of latency, not an independent measurement.

| Final workload/metric | LibTorch gather | Fused gather | Change | Faster pairs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 512px render forward | 3.97 [3.67ΓÇô4.60] ms | 3.88 [3.69ΓÇô4.27] ms | -2.26% | 6/10 |
| 512px render forward+backward | 9.94 [9.06ΓÇô11.59] ms | 9.48 [8.82ΓÇô9.88] ms | -4.63% | 7/10 |
| 512px train step | 10.37 [10.06ΓÇô11.03] ms | 9.95 [9.79ΓÇô10.42] ms | -4.11% | 9/10 |
| 512px training throughput | 96.39 [90.67ΓÇô99.37] steps/s | 100.52 [96.01ΓÇô102.18] steps/s | +4.29% | 9/10 |
| 1024px render forward | 5.16 [4.76ΓÇô5.67] ms | 5.05 [4.75ΓÇô5.56] ms | -2.11% | 6/10 |
| 1024px render forward+backward | 14.85 [14.36ΓÇô15.65] ms | 14.40 [14.35ΓÇô14.94] ms | -3.01% | 6/10 |
| 1024px train step | 23.78 [23.40ΓÇô24.17] ms | 23.28 [22.96ΓÇô23.76] ms | -2.14% | 10/10 |
| 1024px training throughput | 42.04 [41.37ΓÇô42.74] steps/s | 42.96 [42.09ΓÇô43.56] steps/s | +2.18% | 10/10 |
| 512px render CUDA peak allocated (forward) | 100.15 [100.15ΓÇô100.15] MiB | 100.15 [100.15ΓÇô100.15] MiB | +0.00% | 0/10 |
| 512px render CUDA peak allocated (backward) | 195.18 [195.18ΓÇô195.18] MiB | 196.52 [196.52ΓÇô196.52] MiB | +0.69% | 0/10 |
| 512px render CUDA peak reserved | 244.00 [244.00ΓÇô244.00] MiB | 244.00 [244.00ΓÇô244.00] MiB | +0.00% | 0/10 |
| 512px render CPU peak working set | 869.53 [869.14ΓÇô871.05] MiB | 869.53 [869.32ΓÇô879.82] MiB | +0.00% | 3/10 |
| 512px training-process CPU peak working set | 964.91 [964.62ΓÇô975.00] MiB | 965.31 [965.09ΓÇô975.47] MiB | +0.04% | 1/10 |
| 1024px render CUDA peak allocated (forward) | 129.72 [129.72ΓÇô129.72] MiB | 129.72 [129.72ΓÇô129.72] MiB | +0.00% | 0/10 |
| 1024px render CUDA peak allocated (backward) | 233.73 [233.73ΓÇô233.73] MiB | 232.51 [232.51ΓÇô232.51] MiB | -0.53% | 10/10 |
| 1024px render CUDA peak reserved | 284.00 [284.00ΓÇô284.00] MiB | 284.00 [284.00ΓÇô284.00] MiB | +0.00% | 0/10 |
| 1024px render CPU peak working set | 880.58 [880.25ΓÇô882.16] MiB | 880.64 [880.43ΓÇô880.95] MiB | +0.01% | 4/10 |
| 1024px training-process CPU peak working set | 975.96 [975.71ΓÇô976.28] MiB | 976.38 [976.18ΓÇô976.54] MiB | +0.04% | 0/10 |


The CPU remained contended (20.7ΓÇô45.1% sampled utilization) despite exclusive
team benchmark locks. These modest gains need replication on a quiet system;
the mixed paired render wins are shown. Memory metrics cover the render/backward
phase before training. Training-phase VRAM is **not measured by this branch's
benchmark**. Host working set is process peak, not an allocation delta; allocator
reserved memory is not device-wide VRAM usage. The 512px backward allocation
regression (+0.69%) and small host-memory increases are not omitted.

Separate five-step 512px Kineto traces after three warmups show 283ΓåÆ244 GPU
kernel/copy/memset events per step (-13.8%), 38ΓåÆ25 memsets (-34.2%), and summed GPU
event duration 9.935ΓåÆ9.276ms (-6.6%). The fused gather and scatter kernels account
for 0.204/0.287ms per step. These are single instrumented samples, not independent
throughput measurements or wall-clock latency; no variance claim is made.

Machine-readable raw iterations, full test/sanitizer logs, rejected experiment
and summary utility are committed in `benchmarks/results/gaussian-gather/`.
The full history and measurement definitions are in
[gaussian_gather_results.md](https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP/blob/229f04dfd678b999dbe711a947a4b3b3ea608d1f/benchmarks/gaussian_gather_results.md).

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The train-step benchmark fits the fixed scene to a constant target with
densification disabled. It measures training efficiency, not classification,
F1, PSNR or long-run convergence. No new accuracy or reconstruction-quality gain
is claimed. Existing renderer/trainer coverage and new derivative tests validate
compatibility; integrated model experiments are reported separately by the team.

## TRADEOFFS

The first implementation retained all gradient arrays even when inputs were
frozen; a regression test reproduced this before `d45b911` fixed it. Earlier
benchmarks are preserved in the report, including a 1.9% 1024px render regression
on the earlier implementation. Final allocator behavior is mixed, including
the 512px backward regression above. The optimization requires unique IDs and
provides first-order differentiation only. Native GPU runtime validation covers
LibTorch 2.15.0; other versions receive Docker compile coverage. Remaining work
includes profiling sort/visibility and rasterization before further fusion.

## REPRODUCTION

Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X (6C/12T), 16GiB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8GiB (sm_75),
Windows 11, driver 610.88, MSVC 19.44, CUDA toolkit 13.4.3 / nvcc 13.4.92,
CMake 4.2.3, LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134 (CPU suite: 2.15.0+cpu).
Dataset SHA-256: `95ba6aeb2825674814543d930c1a7e1c65bbabd57a735a669ae71ca24178e1e5`.
Subset seed 0; loss-probe seed 1. The exact native suites were executed as
`gaussian_tests` and `adaptive_tests` in their respective release build directories.

```sh
git clone --branch perf/gaussian-cuda-gather https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP.git
cd Minkowski4CPP
git checkout 229f04dfd678b999dbe711a947a4b3b3ea608d1f
docker pull acaicia/minkowski4cpp:latest
docker image inspect acaicia/minkowski4cpp:latest --format '{{.Id}}'
docker run --rm --gpus all -v "$PWD:/workspace" -w /workspace acaicia/minkowski4cpp:latest bash
# Inside the existing image; rebuild the bind-mounted source:
cmake -S . -B build-gather -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/libtorch -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75
cmake --build build-gather --parallel 4 --target gaussian_tests adaptive_tests gaussian_render_bench
./build-gather/gaussian_tests
./build-gather/adaptive_tests
./build-gather/gaussian_render_bench --input tests/data/test.ply --counts 0 \
  --sizes 512,1024 --devices cuda --warmup 3 --iterations 10 --fused-gather 0 --output reference.json
./build-gather/gaussian_render_bench --input tests/data/test.ply --counts 0 \
  --sizes 512,1024 --devices cuda --warmup 3 --iterations 10 --fused-gather 1 --output fused.json
for tool in memcheck racecheck initcheck; do
  compute-sanitizer --tool "$tool" --error-exitcode 99 --show-backtrace no \
    --kernel-name-exclude kns=indexing_backward_kernel ./build-gather/gaussian_tests gaussian_fused_gather_
done
python3 benchmarks/results/gaussian-gather/summarize.py
```

Repeat the paired benchmark commands for ten rounds, reversing order on even
rounds and saving distinct output files. Repeat with `--train`. Use a separate
`-DCPU_ONLY=ON` build and CPU LibTorch prefix for CPU validation. These Docker
commands are reproduction instructions; they were not executed on the native
test host. Record the pulled image digest and rebuild the checkout so the
container cannot silently execute an older installed library.
title: perf: Fuse Gaussian CUDA attribute gathering and gradient scatter

body:
## SUMMARY

Add an independent, optional byte budget for CUDA copies retained by adaptive kernel-map part reuse. PR #47 batches uploads into shared storage; a host part byte budget alone cannot limit device retention, and dropping one tensor view does not release a slab still owned by another part. The default stays unlimited. This is a memory/throughput control, not a claim that a smaller cache always trains faster.

This branch is stacked on PR #47 (and its #41 dependencies). The new implementation starts at `d8b8e04`; the tested runtime source is `2623c56b933d7cc90d97f337778a49aa3ebb5e40`. Later reporting commits do not alter the tested implementation.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `KernelMapCache::set_part_device_bytes(size_t)` controls retained part uploads across CUDA devices. Zero disables retention; `size_t(-1)` preserves existing unlimited retention.
- Whole upload groups are evicted in least-recently-used order. Weak ownership does not retain host maps. A partially expired group remains conservatively charged at its original size until eviction; counters are not exact remaining allocator bytes in that case.
- Host kernel maps remain cached. Oversized uploads are transient. Concurrent/in-flight compositions hold their own tensor handles.
- Source allocations are recorded on the composition's current CUDA stream before kernel launch, so eviction cannot recycle cross-stream source storage prematurely.
- Repeated references to one stored part share an upload. New stats expose retained/peak group charge, groups, and unique part upload hits/misses.
- Batch benchmark adds `--part-device-mb` plus CUDA allocator peak allocated/reserved measurements.

## TESTING

Final native validation at `2623c56`:

| Backend | CTest | Adaptive cases (pass/fail/skip) | Gaussian cases |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CPU | 4/4 pass | 133/0/8 | 36/0/4 |
| CUDA | 4/4 pass | 144/0/0 | 42/0/0 |

CTest also runs the adaptive-versus-uniform benchmark smoke check and nine test-framework contract checks. The five new CUDA budget tests all pass. Compute Sanitizer: memcheck 5/5, zero errors and zero leaked bytes; racecheck cross-stream case 1/1, zero hazards; initcheck 5/5, zero errors. All sanitizer invocations use the existing `--kernel-name-exclude kns=indexing_backward_kernel` workaround for LibTorch indexing backward instrumentation; these are not unfiltered checks of every ATen kernel. Float64 forward and backward checks require exact equality against uncached maps; stream/width tests compare map indices and weights exactly.

The existing three-profile GitHub Docker build matrix (CUDA 124/132/134) is requested on this PR. Its status must be checked separately; native runtime tests are not Docker execution. The workflow compiles containers and does not run GPU tests on the hosted runner.

Five new tests exercise bounded/disabled retention with exact deterministic float64 forward/backward comparisons; whole-group eviction and live output maps; LRU order and repeated references; cross-stream eviction with allocator churn; and mixed 16/32-bit upload groups after partial host eviction. CPU execution preserves the API and skips CUDA-specific cases explicitly.

## BENCHMARKS

Results measured on 2026-11-02. Two warm-up processes per arm and mode, followed by six measured processes using all six arm-order permutations. Each process uses 64 samples, batch 16, 2048 points/sample, depth 3, four epochs, host part budget 512 MiB, CUDA device composition. Table values are medians [minimum, maximum]; lower latency/memory is better. The bounded arm uses 16 MiB. A global benchmark lock excluded team builds and other team GPU jobs, but unrelated host work remained (CPU 25.1% before/37.1% after). Treat small differences as contended-host measurements.

The timer starts after host batch/pool preparation and synchronizes at the end; without a pre-timer CUDA synchronization it can include queued preparation work. This is a synchronized batch-map phase, **not isolated kernel time**. Allocator peaks cover the whole process (batch/pool/cache/temporaries), and retained group charge is neither reserved VRAM nor exact live payload after partial expiration.

### Original versus new default unlimited mode

| Mode | Metric | Before | After | Change | Lower in paired rounds |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| center | First epoch batch phase (ms) | 127.079 [107.797, 159.233] | 121.447 [108.490, 133.207] | -4.43% | 4/6 |
| center | Warm batch phase (ms) | 9.722 [8.567, 10.896] | 10.267 [8.686, 11.079] | +5.61% | 1/6 |
| center | Reciprocal median warm phase (batches/s) | 102.86 | 97.40 | -5.31% | derived, not end-to-end throughput |
| center | Peak CPU working set (MiB) | 1059.438 [1055.078, 1060.988] | 1061.850 [1057.809, 1063.031] | +0.23% | 2/6 |
| volume | First epoch batch phase (ms) | 138.548 [125.715, 154.423] | 146.902 [126.790, 155.916] | +6.03% | 2/6 |
| volume | Warm batch phase (ms) | 11.922 [11.062, 12.188] | 11.223 [9.991, 11.846] | -5.86% | 5/6 |
| volume | Reciprocal median warm phase (batches/s) | 83.88 | 89.10 | +6.23% | derived, not end-to-end throughput |
| volume | Peak CPU working set (MiB) | 1121.668 [1119.789, 1126.715] | 1121.798 [1117.633, 1122.957] | +0.01% | 3/6 |

### New unlimited versus 16 MiB retention cap

| Mode | Metric | Before | After | Change | Lower in paired rounds |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| center | First epoch batch phase (ms) | 121.447 [108.490, 133.207] | 127.876 [119.916, 137.031] | +5.29% | 3/6 |
| center | Warm batch phase (ms) | 10.267 [8.686, 11.079] | 11.537 [10.879, 11.856] | +12.36% | 0/6 |
| center | Reciprocal median warm phase (batches/s) | 97.40 | 86.68 | -11.00% | derived, not end-to-end throughput |
| center | Peak CPU working set (MiB) | 1061.850 [1057.809, 1063.031] | 1058.756 [1055.594, 1063.555] | -0.29% | 5/6 |
| center | Peak CUDA allocated (MiB) | 784.768 [784.768, 784.768] | 781.068 [781.068, 781.068] | -0.47% | 6/6 |
| center | Peak CUDA reserved (MiB) | 818.000 [818.000, 818.000] | 818.000 [818.000, 818.000] | +0.00% | 0/6 |
| center | Final retained group charge (MiB) | 20.058 [20.058, 20.058] | 15.376 [15.376, 15.376] | -23.34% | 6/6 |
| center | Peak retained group charge (MiB) | 20.058 [20.058, 20.058] | 15.986 [15.986, 15.986] | -20.30% | 6/6 |
| center | Unique part upload misses | 96.000 [96.000, 96.000] | 190.000 [190.000, 190.000] | +97.92% | 0/6 |
| volume | First epoch batch phase (ms) | 146.902 [126.790, 155.916] | 130.306 [115.481, 145.489] | -11.30% | 5/6 |
| volume | Warm batch phase (ms) | 11.223 [9.991, 11.846] | 29.965 [24.923, 30.969] | +166.98% | 0/6 |
| volume | Reciprocal median warm phase (batches/s) | 89.10 | 33.37 | -62.54% | derived, not end-to-end throughput |
| volume | Peak CPU working set (MiB) | 1121.798 [1117.633, 1122.957] | 1151.153 [1148.145, 1152.961] | +2.62% | 0/6 |
| volume | Peak CUDA allocated (MiB) | 1319.652 [1319.652, 1319.652] | 1267.333 [1267.333, 1267.333] | -3.96% | 6/6 |
| volume | Peak CUDA reserved (MiB) | 1366.000 [1366.000, 1366.000] | 1324.000 [1324.000, 1324.000] | -3.07% | 6/6 |
| volume | Final retained group charge (MiB) | 60.175 [60.175, 60.175] | 6.942 [6.942, 6.942] | -88.46% | 6/6 |
| volume | Peak retained group charge (MiB) | 60.175 [60.175, 60.175] | 14.415 [14.415, 14.415] | -76.04% | 6/6 |
| volume | Unique part upload misses | 96.000 [96.000, 96.000] | 214.000 [214.000, 214.000] | +122.92% | 0/6 |

The 16 MiB cap cuts final retained charge 23.3% (center) /88.5% (volume), but increases warm phase latency 12.4% /167.0% in all six paired rounds. Volume peak CUDA allocation falls 3.96%; center falls 0.47%. Volume CPU working set increases 2.62%. These are explicit tradeoffs for a memory control, not an unconditional optimization. Default-unlimited overhead is mixed: center warm phase +5.61% (only 1/6 faster), volume -5.86% (5/6 faster), and opposite first-epoch movements. Retain the default unlimited budget unless memory pressure warrants the tradeoff. Baseline lacks new CUDA peak fields; no baseline GPU memory is fabricated. Kernel execution time and GPU utilization over the timed interval were not measured; endpoint GPU utilization is not representative.

Pilot exploration also tested budgets 0/8/16 before choosing 16 for the balanced experiment; those single-process pilot observations are not confirmation trials. The original test-only CUDA compilation failure (`detail` namespace ambiguity) is preserved in the local experiment history and corrected by 2623c56; final suites above were rebuilt and rerun.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The feature preserves maps and gradients in automated tests. Full-stack classification comparing unlimited/32 MiB/zero retention is running separately at integration commit `f3f74919a64bede57fab7d5f303e94ca188c931a`; no accuracy, convergence, training speed, or model-quality conclusion is claimed before those results are available. A follow-up comment will preserve the separate integration provenance.

## TRADEOFFS

The cap excludes composed batch maps, allocator reservations, and live operation temporaries; it is not an instantaneous total-VRAM cap. Lower caps may increase uploads and latency. Group eviction may discard several parts when one large group exceeds the budget. Partially expired mixed-width groups are conservatively overcharged. Default unlimited-mode overhead is measured separately. Public stats fields expand the C++ struct: source compatibility is preserved after rebuilding consumers; this is not a binary-ABI compatibility claim.

Initial CUDA compilation found an ambiguous test-only `detail` namespace; `2623c56` qualified it and the final checks above passed after rebuilding. Docker is unavailable on this Windows test host; native tests reuse the existing toolchain matching the repository's CUDA 134 profile. Do not describe these as local container execution.

## REPRODUCTION

Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X, 16 GiB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GiB (SM 75), Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134 / CPU, CMake 4.2.3. Baseline `b1a7d94`; baseline static benchmark SHA256 `41BC667DA2A2B323D0AB06F15DD5786A0969D60965F48A8C28B22D706BECEE88`.

Existing-image container recipe (provided for reproduction; not locally executed):

```sh
docker pull acaicia/minkowski4cpp:latest
docker run --rm --gpus all -v "$PWD:/workspace" -w /workspace acaicia/minkowski4cpp:latest bash -lc '
  export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=7.5
  cmake -S . -B build-budget -GNinja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/libtorch -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75
  cmake --build build-budget --parallel 4
  ctest --test-dir build-budget --output-on-failure
  ./build-budget/adaptive_kmap_bench --batch 16 --samples 64 --epochs 4 --n 2048 --depth 3 --part-reuse-mb 512 --batch-device cuda --device-compose 1 --modes center --part-device-mb 16
'
```

Use a separate build directory and execute its newly linked benchmark, ensuring the installed image library is not substituted for modified source. Record the image digest and CUDA/LibTorch profile when reproducing. Repeat with volume mode and budgets -1/0/8/16; use balanced process order and exclusive GPU access. Actual native commands, final source/binary hashes and raw results will be linked in the final report.


Actual native build/test commands (existing local toolchain, no host dependencies installed):

```powershell
pwsh -File C:\Users\User\Work\mink-lab\tools\mink-build.ps1 -Src C:\Users\User\Work\mink-wt\device-compose -Build C:\Users\User\Work\mink-build\device-compose-cpu -Cpu -Targets adaptive_tests,adaptive_vs_uniform_bench,gaussian_tests,adaptive_kmap_bench,test_framework_contract -Who adaptive-budget
pwsh -File C:\Users\User\Work\mink-lab\tools\mink-build.ps1 -Src C:\Users\User\Work\mink-wt\device-compose -Build C:\Users\User\Work\mink-build\device-compose-cuda -Targets adaptive_tests,adaptive_vs_uniform_bench,gaussian_tests,adaptive_kmap_bench,test_framework_contract -Who adaptive-budget
ctest --test-dir C:\Users\User\Work\mink-build\device-compose-cpu -V --output-on-failure
ctest --test-dir C:\Users\User\Work\mink-build\device-compose-cuda -V --output-on-failure
```

The native runs used shared GPU/build locks around these commands. Build baseline b1a7d94 in a separate directory, then use the portable stdlib runner from this branch (outside shared GPU workloads):

```sh
python benchmarks/adaptive_device_budget_ab.py --baseline /path/to/baseline/adaptive_kmap_bench --candidate /path/to/candidate/adaptive_kmap_bench --output budget-ab --budget-mib 16 --rounds 6
```

The runner reproduces the original PowerShell arm order and commands, checks process failures and required metrics, and refuses to overwrite an existing result directory. title: feat: Bound retained CUDA part uploads in adaptive map caches

body:
## SUMMARY

Fuse the eight elementwise Adam operations used by `GaussianTrainer` into one CUDA kernel per contiguous float32 parameter tensor. The original ATen path remains available for unsupported layouts/types and for same-binary comparison. This completes an unfinished implementation whose cancellation-sensitive numerical test failed: the kernel now preserves ATen's intermediate rounding and version-dependent scalar reciprocal behavior.

On the measured RTX 2080 SUPER, the 512-pixel training-step median decreased from **25.787 to 24.268 ms (-5.89%, 9/10 paired wins)**. The 1024-pixel result is inconclusive. The host was contended; these are bounded observations, not a universal speedup claim.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- Add a device-guarded, current-stream CUDA kernel with a grid-stride loop. Each element loads its parameter, gradient and two moments once, then writes the updated parameter and moments. No optimizer scratch tensors are required by the fused update.
- Preserve float32 stores between moment multiplication and accumulation, square the gradient before scaling it, and use explicit round-to-nearest multiplication/FMA to avoid compiler-dependent reassociation. Match ATen's float32 reciprocal before LibTorch 2.10 and float64 reciprocal followed by float32 conversion in newer versions. See the linked primary implementation references in [the technical note](https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP/blob/2f947ca/docs/gaussian-adam.md).
- Keep learning-rate schedules, epsilon placement, bias correction, parameter order, public API, autograd version increments, CPU execution and the existing fallback unchanged. An internal switch and `gaussian_render_bench --fused-adam 0|1` allow identical-binary comparisons.
- Measure training-phase CUDA allocation/reservation peaks after trainer construction and training, separately from the older renderer-only fields. Include the allocator `StatType` portability fix from #32; this is the only additional unmerged dependency over upstream `f4ac612`.

## TESTING

Native Release builds tested source **`977bd71e2dc87ad718e5cf323252e2347dc3d0c3`**; published head `2f947ca` adds only this report and raw evidence. The source was recompiled, and executable SHA-256 identities are retained in the [evidence](https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP/blob/2f947ca/docs/benchmarks/gaussian_adam_round9.json).

| Configuration | Adaptive pass/fail/skip | Gaussian pass/fail/skip | CTest |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU-only | 119/0/1 | 36/0/4 | 4/4 passed |
| CUDA | 123/0/0 | 47/0/0 | 4/4 passed |

Five Adam cases cover 100,003 elements over six updates (zero/tiny/ordinary/large gradients), cancellation over 16 steps with four beta2 values, invalid metadata and empty tensors, nondefault-stream execution with a partial block, and eight complete training steps comparing all six parameter groups. On the measured LibTorch 2.15 build, direct parameters **and both moments matched bit for bit at each of six steps**. This is a measured configuration result, not a cross-platform promise. Tests retain a documented scale-aware tolerance without relaxing the previous bound.

Compute Sanitizer: all five tests passed memcheck, racecheck and full initcheck with zero reported errors/hazards. Memcheck excluded the existing LibTorch `indexing_backward_kernel` issue; racecheck was restricted to `adam_kernel`; full initcheck had no kernel filter. The fused optimizer was instrumented in each relevant run. An earlier Adam-only initcheck failed after ATen initialization writes were excluded; the **same binary** passed full instrumentation. That failed experiment is preserved in the evidence.

Executed commands included native CMake builds through `mink-build.ps1`, `ctest --test-dir <build> --verbose --output-on-failure --timeout 420 --output-junit <file>`, and:

```powershell
$env:PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING = '1'
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --error-exitcode 86 --kernel-name-exclude kns=indexing_backward_kernel gaussian_tests.exe gaussian_fused_adam
compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck --error-exitcode 86 --kernel-name kns=adam_kernel gaussian_tests.exe gaussian_fused_adam
compute-sanitizer --tool initcheck --error-exitcode 86 gaussian_tests.exe gaussian_fused_adam
```

Docker was unavailable on the measurement host. PR Docker CI compilation is separate from native execution; no container GPU runtime validation or older-LibTorch runtime parity is claimed.

## BENCHMARKS

Same executable, `--fused-adam 0` versus `1`; 139,410 Gaussians from `tests/data/test.ply`; three warm-ups and ten synchronized samples per resolution per process; ten paired rounds, with arm order reversed every round. All 20 processes succeeded. Team compilation and GPU workloads were excluded by a shared benchmark lock. Host CPU utilization was **40.7–54.6% at the run boundaries**; GPU clocks were not fixed. Values are medians of round medians; brackets show the round range.

| Image | Metric | ATen Adam | Fused Adam | Change | Faster pairs |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 512 | Training step, ms | 25.787 [24.181–32.873] | 24.268 [23.310–27.006] | -5.89% | 9/10 |
| 1024 | Training step, ms | 43.438 [42.367–52.960] | 43.079 [40.860–58.813] | -0.83% | 5/10 |
| 512 | Reciprocal median throughput, steps/s | 38.78 | 41.21 | +6.26% | — |
| 1024 | Reciprocal median throughput, steps/s | 23.02 | 23.21 | +0.83% | — |
| 512 | Training CUDA allocated peak, MiB | 330.728 | 330.765 | +0.01% | — |
| 1024 | Training CUDA allocated peak, MiB | 558.366 | 558.830 | +0.08% | — |
| 512 | Training CUDA reserved peak, MiB | 408 | 400 | -1.96% | — |
| 1024 | Training CUDA reserved peak, MiB | 702 | 716 | **+1.99%** | — |
| 512 | Process CPU peak working set, MiB | 1153.535 | 1124.943 | -2.48% | — |
| 1024 | Process CPU peak working set, MiB | 1164.625 | 1136.033 | -2.46% | — |

Training allocation includes model cloning, optimizer construction and persistent scene/probe tensors. Reserved memory can include earlier render-phase allocator caches. CPU memory is a process-lifetime high-water mark. These are not optimizer-only or whole-device VRAM metrics. Throughput is the reciprocal of latency, not a separate run. Kernel-only and cold-start times were not measured. Whole-run GPU telemetry covers both arms and initialization (75 samples, utilization median 64%, range 1–92%); it cannot establish an arm-specific utilization gain.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The eight-step 3,000-Gaussian trainer regression compares reconstruction loss and all six learned parameter groups. Both arms displayed final loss 0.491019; maximum relative parameter-group difference was about 1.86e-7 in ordinary execution and 2.08e-7 under sanitizer instrumentation, within the unchanged parameter/loss tolerances of 1e-4/1e-5. This is short-run optimizer integration validation, not a new dataset-accuracy or long-run convergence experiment. Classification, segmentation, F1 and independent-scene accuracy are not applicable to this isolated optimizer change and were not measured here.

## TRADEOFFS

- The 1024-pixel result has only 5/10 paired wins and is **inconclusive**; its +1.99% reserved-memory peak is a regression. No GPU-memory reduction is claimed.
- Unchanged renderer control medians also moved about -4%, with mixed pair counts. Shared-host variability limits attribution of small timing differences, including the observed 512-pixel result.
- The original failure was not a tiny-gradient problem: an ordinary gradient near parameter/update cancellation exposed a reciprocal precision mismatch. Correcting only the reciprocal still left 506 differing parameter elements after six steps; fixing the moment rounding boundaries removed those differences on this configuration. Historical diagnostics remain recorded.
- Unsupported dtypes/layouts retain ATen. Runtime parity on older supported LibTorch builds, long training runs and other GPU architectures remains future work. This standalone branch does not contain projection, tile-list or SSIM fusions from #48–#50; combined-stack measurements will be added separately, without replacing these results.

## REPRODUCTION

Source: `977bd71e2dc87ad718e5cf323252e2347dc3d0c3`; documentation/evidence head: `2f947ca`. Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X (6C/12T), 16 GiB-class RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GiB / sm_75, NVIDIA driver 610.88, Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, MSVC 19.44, LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134, CUDA profile 13.4.3 (nvcc 13.4.92), Release. Benchmark binary SHA-256: `489624E1492BD5C0DC133815D15A76CDE333FBD492448C3FB7115AE2311C0547`; scene SHA-256: `95BA6AEB2825674814543D930C1A7E1C65BBABD57A735A669AE71CA24178E1E5`.

On a Docker GPU host, reuse the existing image and explicitly compile/run the mounted changed source. These commands are reproduction instructions, **not evidence of a local Docker run**:

```sh
git clone --branch perf/gaussian-cuda-adam https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP.git
cd Minkowski4CPP
git checkout 2f947ca
docker pull acaicia/minkowski4cpp
docker image inspect acaicia/minkowski4cpp --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'
docker run --rm --gpus all -v "$PWD:/src" -w /src acaicia/minkowski4cpp \
  bash -lc 'export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=7.5; \
    cmake -S . -B build-adam -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/libtorch -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75 && \
    cmake --build build-adam -j4 && \
    ctest --test-dir build-adam --output-on-failure && \
    build-adam/gaussian_tests gaussian_fused_adam'
```

Use the GPU's architecture and image's LibTorch prefix. Record the actual pulled digest; none was available on this native host. Use a separate build directory with `-DCPU_ONLY=ON` for CPU tests. Run both benchmark settings in balanced alternating order for ten rounds inside the same mounted build:

```sh
build-adam/gaussian_render_bench --input tests/data/test.ply --counts 0 \
  --sizes 512,1024 --devices cuda --warmup 3 --iterations 10 --train \
  --fused-adam 0 --output aten-r1.json
build-adam/gaussian_render_bench --input tests/data/test.ply --counts 0 \
  --sizes 512,1024 --devices cuda --warmup 3 --iterations 10 --train \
  --fused-adam 1 --output fused-r1.json
```

The [machine-readable evidence](https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP/blob/2f947ca/docs/benchmarks/gaussian_adam_round9.json) preserves every timing sample, arm/round identity, hardware and executable identities, test summaries, memory measurements and failed-experiment history. [The technical note](https://github.com/itsSio/Minkowski4CPP/blob/2f947ca/docs/gaussian-adam.md) explains tolerances and measurement scope.

title: perf(gaussian): fuse CUDA Adam updates with ATen-compatible rounding

body:
## SUMMARY

`ssim()` in `GaussianTrainer`'s loss now runs as two fused CUDA kernels, one forward and one backward. Before, it was five 11×11 depthwise convolutions plus about 25 element-wise kernels each way.

**Why this was next:** a Kineto trace of one 512 px training step on the 139k-splat test scene (on #49's branch) showed SSIM's depthwise convolutions alone took ~1.7 ms of 9.4 ms GPU time. Only the rasterizer backward was larger.

**Accuracy:** against a float64 dense reference, the fused SSIM matches LibTorch's float32 accuracy or beats it:
- gradient error 0.5–1.5e-6 (LibTorch 1.0–2.8e-6);
- values within 2e-7.

It is deterministic: there are no atomics, and two runs give bit-identical gradients.

Training step on the test scene (same binary, switch only, 10 alternating rounds): **-8.6 %** at 512 px (25.07 -> 22.91 ms) and **-22.2 %** at 1024 px (42.99 -> 33.46 ms), faster in 10/10 rounds at both sizes.

**Stacked on #42** (separable, batched SSIM on CPU). It edits the same function and keeps #42's CPU path unchanged.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

New `MinkowskiEngine/gaussian/gaussian_ssim_cuda.cu`:
- **Forward**, one block per 16×16 tile and channel:
  - loads x and y with a `window/2` halo into shared memory, reading zeros outside the image like `conv2d`'s padding;
  - runs a horizontal pass of the five moments (x, y, x², y², xy), then a vertical pass per pixel;
  - writes the SSIM map and three per-pixel partials: A = ∂S/∂μx (including the dependence of σxx and σxy on μx), B = ∂S/∂σxx and C = ∂S/∂σxy.
  - `ssim()` returns `map.mean()`.
- **Backward:** filters A, B and C the same way and writes `dL/dx = g/N · (G*A + 2x·G*B + y·G*C)`. The Gaussian window is symmetric, so correlation equals convolution. It reads the incoming gradient from device memory, so there is no host sync.
- **Taps:** computed on the host with the same formula, so the step never waits for the device. Windows up to 15 are supported.
- **Fallbacks:** the LibTorch filters still run for CPU tensors, a target that requires grad (the fused node returns no target gradient), windows above 15, and when `detail::cuda_fused_ssim()` is off. The benchmark gets `--fused-ssim 0|1`.
- **Memory:** the forward saves x and y (3·H·W floats each, contiguous copies only if the input was a view) and the partials (9·H·W floats). I did not measure LibTorch's saved intermediates for comparison.

## TESTING

New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_ssim_cuda.cpp` (CUDA builds):

| test | result |
|---|---|
| fused vs LibTorch vs float64 dense reference: 8 shapes, including 6×5 (smaller than the window), 17×300 and 128×96, with windows 1/3/7/11/15; loss `0.2 · (1 − SSIM)` so the incoming gradient ≠ 1 | values ≤ 1.8e-7 apart; gradients ≤ 3.2e-6 relative to LibTorch (window 1: 2.8e-5) and ≤ 1.5e-6 relative to float64, where LibTorch's own error is ≤ 2.8e-6 |
| non-contiguous prediction (the renderer's `[H,W,3]` slice of `[H,W,5]`) | same value; gradient into the slice only |
| determinism | two runs give bit-identical value and gradient |
| fallbacks: target requiring grad, window 17 | LibTorch path, target gradient present |

compute-sanitizer 13.4 on the 4 `gaussian_fused_ssim_*` tests: memcheck 0 errors, racecheck 0 hazards, initcheck 0 errors.

#42's existing `gaussian_ssim_matches_dense_reference_cuda` now runs the fused path: 9.5e-7 and 5.8e-7 relative gradient error vs float64.

Suites: `gaussian_tests` CUDA 50 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped. CPU: 39 passed, 0 failed, 5 skipped (the fused path is CUDA-only; CPU is #42 unchanged).

## BENCHMARKS

`gaussian_render_bench --train`, `tests/data/test.ply` (139,410 splats), CUDA, on this branch (#42's base, so the projection, culling and tile lists are still the LibTorch versions; #48/#49 make the rest of the step faster, which makes this saving a larger share). Both arms ran the **same binary**, switched only by `--fused-ssim 0|1`. There were 10 alternating rounds, each with 3 warm-ups and 10 timed steps; the table shows the median over rounds of each round's median, with [min-max]. The host was moderately loaded (32-40 % CPU from background processes plus another build), so the run counts as contended.

| workload | LibTorch SSIM | fused SSIM | change | fused better |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| training step 512 px | 25.07 ms [24.54-51.35] | 22.91 ms [22.11-24.18] | **-8.6 %** | 10/10 |
| training step 1024 px | 42.99 ms [41.81-129.88] | 33.46 ms [32.77-65.94] | **-22.2 %** | 10/10 |
| host peak working set (512 / 1024 px runs) | 1153 / 1164 MB | 1097 / 1108 MB | -4.9 / -4.8 % | 10/10 |

The saving is about 2.2 ms per step at 512 px and 9.5 ms at 1024 px; LibTorch's 11x11 depthwise convolution scales badly with image size.

The same runs also time the plain render (no SSIM involved), and those rows moved within noise in both directions:
- forward +5.0 % (4/10) and -0.3 % (4/10);
- backward +1.1 % (2/10) and +0.2 % (5/10);
- forward+backward +0.4 % and -1.7 %.

The 50+ ms maxima are isolated single-round outliers in a contended run (a build was compiling during part of it); the medians and the 10/10 counts do not depend on them.

The bench's CUDA peak-memory counters cover only the plain render, not the training step, so the SSIM memory change is not measured here. The fused forward keeps up to 15·H·W floats for backward (x, y and the partials).

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The loss and its gradient are the same function to within float32 rounding, and closer to float64 than before, so training behaviour is unchanged. The training-step times are under BENCHMARKS. I did not run a separate convergence study.

## TRADEOFFS

- **No target gradient.** The fused node returns none; when the target requires grad, the LibTorch path runs, so results stay correct.
- **Window limit.** Windows above 15 use LibTorch; the default is 11.
- **One kernel per tile and channel.** It recomputes nothing across channels. At these image sizes the kernels are memory- and launch-bound, so fusing the three channels into one block was not tried.

## REPRODUCTION

- Branch `perf/gaussian-cuda-ssim`: #42 (`28b172e`) plus one commit.
- Tests: `gaussian_tests.exe gaussian_fused_ssim` and `gaussian_tests.exe gaussian_ssim`.
- Benchmark:
  ```
  gaussian_render_bench --input tests/data/test.ply --counts 0 --sizes 512,1024 --devices cuda --warmup 3 --iterations 10 --train --fused-ssim 0|1
  ```
- Hardware and software:
  - Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88;
  - Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0.
  - Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors `docker/cuda-profile.sh`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)


## Round 9 combined-stack follow-up

Additional measurements on `integrate/round8b` (`5215e9c`, #48/#49/#21 + this PR):
ten order-balanced same-binary pairs, 3 warm-ups and 10 timed samples, 139,410 splats.
**Host contended: CPU load 38.8–97.7%.** All 9 CPU and all 9 CUDA CTest suites passed.

| Training resolution | LibTorch SSIM median [range] | Fused SSIM median [range] | Change | Faster pairs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 | 11.26 ms [10.18–15.70] | 8.75 ms [7.90–12.90] | -22.3% | 9/10 |
| 1024 | 25.10 ms [23.56–35.08] | 15.77 ms [15.09–24.47] | -37.2% | 10/10 |

Peak process working set fell 6.3%/6.2%. Training-phase CUDA memory and isolated kernel
time were not measured by this binary; its CUDA peak fields precede training and must
not be presented as training VRAM. The unchanged render-only 1024 forward median rose
6.2% with only 5/10 favorable pairs; no renderer speedup is claimed for SSIM.
Prior standalone results above remain historical measurements of a different stack.

[Full technical update, test counts, caveats and reproduction](https://github.com/QuiteLiterallyConnor/Minkowski4CPP/pull/50#issuecomment-6583967117).
PR-head Docker compilation passed all three profiles; combined-stack execution was
verified natively, with no claim of Docker GPU runtime testing.

body:
## SUMMARY

On CUDA, Gaussian culling, tile bounds and tile lists now run as three small kernels, replacing about 60 small LibTorch ops and one host synchronisation (`repeat_interleave`). With the fused projection from #48, these steps had become most of the forward pass.

On the 139k-splat test scene, same binary, switch only, 10 alternating rounds:
- forward: −34.5 % at 512 px, −36.4 % at 1024 px;
- training step at 512 px: −16.1 %, better in 10 of 10 rounds;
- peak CUDA allocation: −11 % (512 px forward) to −37 % (1024 px forward);
- host working set: −16 %.

The output is **bit-identical**: same visibility, radii, tile bounds, pair counts, ids and ranges, so the forward image, depth and alpha are equal bit for bit.

**Stacked on #48 (fused projection) and #21 (opacity-aware tile bounds).** The culling kernel reads #48's projection output and uses #21's tight-extent math. Merge #21 and #48 first, or review only the last commit.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

New `MinkowskiEngine/gaussian/gaussian_cull_cuda.cu`:
- `cull_kernel` works per Gaussian. It reads the `[N,10]` projection and the opacity and writes:
  - `visible`;
  - `radius` (0 when culled), which is `RenderOutput::radii`;
  - tile bounds `[N,4]` and the tile count per Gaussian.

  It uses the same float32 operations in the same order as the LibTorch code it replaces: extent `sqrt(max(2 ln(255 max(o, 1/255)), 0) + 0.01)`, `ceil(extent * sqrt(a|c))`, the same visibility predicate including the `isfinite` checks, and `floor((m ± r) / 16)` clamped. NaN propagates the same way, and nothing is compiled with fast math.
- `render_gaussians` keeps `visible.nonzero()` and the stable depth argsort. It gathers the bounds in depth order, and `tile_pairs = counts.sum()`.
- `build_tile_lists` (CUDA):
  - `tile_counts_kernel` computes the counts, and an exclusive cumsum gives each Gaussian's offset.
  - `tile_keys_kernel` writes `tile * M + row` for every tile a Gaussian touches, starting at its offset. These replace `repeat_interleave`, which synchronises on its own, and eight gathers and arithmetic ops over all pairs.
  - The keys are sorted with `torch::sort` as before.
  - `finish_lists_kernel` splits the sorted keys into `ids` and tile `ranges`. Thread `i` sees tiles `t[i-1]` and `t[i]`; every tile in `(t[i-1], t[i]]` starts at pair `i`, and the tile before it ends there. This gives exactly the `(end - count, end)` ranges of the old `bincount` + `cumsum`, including empty tiles, without atomics.
- The fused path runs when #48's fused projection is active and `detail::cuda_fused_tiles()` is on (the default). The LibTorch code is unchanged and stays in use for CPU, for camera-pose gradients and when the switch is off. The benchmark gets a `--fused-tiles 0|1` flag.
- The int32 range check on the pair count is unchanged and runs before any kernel.

## TESTING

New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_cull.cpp` (CUDA builds only):

| test | result |
|---|---|
| `cull_cuda` vs the LibTorch culling on 20,000 random projections, with NaN/inf means, covariance and opacity, `det` = 1e-12 and 0, opacity at 1/255 and one ulp below, means on tile and image borders, z at the near plane (13,266 visible) | visible, radius, bounds and counts identical |
| tile lists vs the LibTorch formulation (`repeat_interleave` / `bincount`) for 1 Gaussian on 1 tile, small odd grids, 3,000 Gaussians, mostly empty grids with empty first and last tiles, and Gaussians covering the whole image | ids and ranges identical |
| whole render with fused cull and tiles on vs off: 4,000 splats, 96×64 and 131×77 with an off-centre principal point, splats behind the camera, off-screen, needles, at and below the alpha cut | visible, radii and `tile_pairs` identical; image, depth and alpha **bit-identical**; gradients within 3.6e-7 relative (the rasterizer backward accumulates with atomics) |
| empty scene and all Gaussians culled | 0 pairs, empty image |

Suites on this branch:
- `gaussian_tests` CUDA: 62 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped.
- `gaussian_tests` CPU: 47 passed, 0 failed, 5 skipped. The new tests are CUDA-only; the CPU path is unchanged.

compute-sanitizer 13.4 on the 8 `gaussian_fused_*` tests (new tests plus #48's): memcheck 0 errors, racecheck 0 hazards, initcheck 0 errors (LibTorch's own `indexing_backward_kernel` excluded, see #39).

## BENCHMARKS

`gaussian_render_bench`, `tests/data/test.ply` (139,410 splats), CUDA. Both arms ran the **same binary**, switched only by `--fused-tiles 0|1`, with the fused projection on in both. There were 10 alternating rounds, each with 3 warm-ups and 10 timed iterations; the table shows the median over rounds of each round's median, with [min–max]. The host was moderately loaded (32–35 % CPU from background processes, GPU idle).

I read the backward differences as noise, but I am reporting them as measured.

The training step on the test scene is 16 % faster with mathematically and bitwise identical forward results. Gradients differ only by atomic accumulation order (≤3.6e-7 relative), so convergence behaviour is unchanged by construction. I did not run a separate convergence study.

## TRADEOFFS

- **Load imbalance.** `tile_keys_kernel` uses one thread per Gaussian and loops over its tiles, so a warp waits for its largest splat. On the test scene it is not visible in the totals; a per-pair binary-search variant would balance it if a scene had very large splats.
- **Remaining host synchronisations.** There are still two: `visible.nonzero()` and the pair total, which allocates the key buffer. Removing them would need upper-bound allocation or CUB directly.
- **Kept paths.** The LibTorch path stays for CPU, for pose gradients and for the switch. Both paths are tested against each other.
- **Fused projection required.** Culling only takes the fused path when #48's projection is fused, because it reads that kernel's packed output. With the projection switch off, the whole LibTorch path runs as before.

> **Stacked on #27** (principal-point-aware frustum clamp and the Lagrange-identity determinant). This PR fuses exactly that projection math. The diff against `main` includes #27's commits; this PR alone is `253c966..HEAD` on `perf/gaussian-cuda-projection`.

## SUMMARY

`render_gaussians` on CUDA spends most of its time *outside* the rasterizer kernels. I profiled one render of the 139,410-splat test scene (`tests/data/test.ply`) at 1024 px with synchronised phase timers in a throwaway build:

| phase (ms per call) | forward | backward |
|---|---|---|
| projection to screen space: ~60 small LibTorch ops forward, their autograd graph backward | 4.4 | ~9 (backward total 14.5 minus raster) |
| culling, depth sort, tile bounds | 5.1 | |
| tile lists | 4.7 | |
| rasterizer kernel | 1.1 | 5.5 |

The projection, from 3D mean, quaternion and scale to 2D mean, conic and depth, is per-Gaussian arithmetic. LibTorch runs it as dozens of element-wise kernels over `[N]`, `[N, 2, 3]` and `[N, 3, 3]` tensors, each one a launch plus a temporary, and autograd then replays about twice as many in backward.

This PR computes it in **one CUDA kernel** and its gradient in **one analytic backward kernel** (`gaussian_project_cuda.cu`). That is the same split as the reference 3DGS implementation's preprocess, with this repository's exact math:
- camera transform, near-plane clamp, the principal-point-aware frustum clamp of the Jacobian (#27);
- `J W R(q) S` with the 0.3 px low-pass;
- determinant by the Lagrange identity (#27), the conic.

The LibTorch path is unchanged and is still used:
- for CPU tensors and the LibTorch reference rasterizer;
- when the camera pose requires grad (pose optimisation needs the camera gradient, which the fused kernel does not produce);
- when `detail::cuda_fused_projection() = false`.

Result on the 139k-splat scene (same binary, switch only, 6 alternating rounds, quiet host): the **training step at 512 px is -37.3 %** (19.3 -> 12.1 ms), forward+backward -40 % (512 px) / -29 % (1024 px), and peak CUDA memory -10..-11 %.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `MinkowskiEngine/gaussian/gaussian_project_cuda.cu` (new):
  - `project_forward_cuda`: one thread per Gaussian writes `[N, 10]`: x2, y2, conic a/b/c and camera z (differentiable), plus a, b, c and det (used under `NoGradGuard` for culling and radii, as before).
  - `project_backward_cuda` recomputes the forward values in registers and applies the chain rule. The order is: conic -> clamped det -> cross product / dot products of the two covariance rows -> `T = J W` and `B = R(q) diag(s)` -> quaternion normalisation (the `|q| < 1e-12` branch matches `clamp_min`) and scales -> Jacobian entries -> frustum clamp (no gradient where clamped, as `clamp`'s backward) -> `x/z`, `y/z`, near-plane `clamp_min` -> camera point -> positions.
  - No atomics: every Gaussian writes only its own gradient rows.
- `gaussian_render.cpp`:
  - `FusedProjectFunction` is one autograd node.
  - `means2d` is a view of its output, so `means2d.retain_grad()` and the trainer's densification statistics work unchanged; the test checks `means2d.grad` against the LibTorch path.
  - The frustum-clamp limits are computed once and shared by both paths.
- `gaussian_cuda.hpp`: `ProjectParams`, the two entry points, and the `cuda_fused_projection()` switch.
- `benchmarks/gaussian_render_bench.cpp`: `--fused-projection 0|1`.

## TESTING

New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_project.cpp` (CUDA builds):
- `gaussian_fused_projection_matches_libtorch_render`: 3,000 Gaussians. 5 % are behind the camera, 5 % are far outside the image (frustum clamp active), and the set includes near-degenerate quaternions and needles. The test uses a centred and an off-centre principal point.
  - Fused vs LibTorch projection must agree on image, depth and alpha, and on the gradients of positions, rotations, scales, opacities and colors and `means2d.grad`, under a random loss on all three outputs.
  - Culling may flip for at most 3 splats sitting exactly on a float32 boundary.
- `gaussian_fused_projection_matches_float64_reference`: the 10 kernel columns and the backward kernel's gradients against a float64 LibTorch implementation of the same math, on 4,000 Gaussians with an off-centre principal point.
- `gaussian_fused_projection_falls_back_when_the_camera_needs_grad`: a camera with `requires_grad` still gets its pose gradient.
- `gaussian_fused_projection_empty_scene`.

Measured agreement (relative to each quantity's scale; the test bounds are 1e-4 for outputs and 2e-3 for gradients):

| comparison | outputs | gradients |
|---|---|---|
| fused vs LibTorch projection, whole render (2 cameras) | image / depth / alpha <= 1.1e-6 | positions <= 2.0e-5, rotations <= 4.6e-6, scales <= 6.2e-6, opacities <= 3.3e-6, colors <= 3.1e-6, `means2d.grad` <= 4.0e-6 |
| fused kernels vs float64 reference | 10 columns <= 4.6e-7 | positions 2.0e-6, rotations 3.8e-7, scales 3.0e-7 |

Culling flips between the two paths: 0 of 3,000 in both camera setups.

`gaussian_tests`:

| build | CUDA | CPU |
|---|---|---|
| this branch | **53 / 0 / 0** (4 new) | 43 / 0 / 4 (the new file is CUDA-only) |
| integration of all open PRs + this branch | **95 / 0 / 0** (91 before) | |

The existing render, gradcheck (#14), CUDA-backward (#22) and tile-bounds (#21) tests pass with the fused path on, since it is the default.

## BENCHMARKS

`gaussian_render_bench --input tests/data/test.ply --counts 0 --devices cuda --warmup 3 --iterations 10`, with `--sizes 512,1024` (render) and `--train --sizes 512` (training step). **Same binary**, switch only (`--fused-projection 0` = the LibTorch projection, `1` = this PR). 6 rounds alternate the order; each value is the median of 10 timed iterations, and the table gives the median over rounds with min-max in brackets. 139,410 splats, 91.5k visible; 0.50M / 1.24M (tile, Gaussian) pairs, identical in both arms. The host was quiet (8-14 % background CPU), so these numbers are **not contended**. Integration build of all open PRs (the projection code is identical to this branch).

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

All timings improved in 6/6 rounds. Peak memory drops because the ~60 projection temporaries and the autograd graph saved for them are gone.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The Gaussian training step (`GaussianTrainer::step`, `gaussian_render_bench --train`, 512 px, 139k splats) is in the table above: **19.32 -> 12.12 ms (-37.3 %)**. The image and gradients agree with the LibTorch projection within float32 rounding (see TESTING), so training curves are unchanged up to that rounding. The repository's ML study (#31) uses Gaussian *features*, not rendering, so it is n/a here.

## TRADEOFFS

- Float32 results differ from the LibTorch projection in the last bits: different evaluation order, and fused multiply-adds. A splat exactly on a culling boundary (radius ceil, near plane, image edge) can therefore flip; the test allows 3 out of 3,000 and saw 0 of 3,000 in both camera setups.
- The camera pose gradient is only available through the LibTorch path, which is selected automatically when `world_to_camera.requires_grad()`.
- More code to maintain: the analytic backward duplicates the math of the LibTorch path. Both stay in the tree, and the tests compare them.
- Not done: the culling / sort / tile-list phases (about 10 ms of the 1024 px forward in the profile) are still LibTorch ops. They are the next target.


body:
> **Stacked on #41** (kernel-map part reuse). The diff against `main` includes #41's commits. The diff of this PR alone is `9831857..HEAD` on `perf/adaptive-device-part-compose`.

## SUMMARY

**Update 1 (b1a7d94):** 16-bit device part indices cut the extra GPU memory roughly in half (peak CUDA +72 % -> +37.5 % vs #41) and removed the first-epoch slowdown. Against the same build without this PR: 3-epoch training -8.3 %, epoch 3 -19 %, evaluation +32 %; see the Update 1 comments.

With part reuse (#41) on, a new training batch's kernel map is put together from stored per-sample part maps. Before this PR that happened **on the host**: four `[P]` arrays (int64 in/out/kernel slot, float64 weight, 32 B per pair) were written, then the in/out arrays (16 B per pair) were uploaded on the first CUDA convolution. In a GPU profile of the repository's ML study this was the largest library cost of a training step: about 4.6 ms of host composition plus 1.5 ms of uploads per step (4 new maps per step).

For CUDA tensors the batch map is now **composed on the device**:
- Each stored part keeps a device copy of its int32 pair arrays (uploaded once, on first use, and freed with the part).
- A new batch map uploads only a small table: one row per (kernel slot, level, part) segment, plus the parts' leaf numbering. That is O(segments + leaves) instead of O(pairs).
- One kernel then writes the int64 in/out index arrays (and float64 weights for weighted modes) straight into the entry's device cache.

The map's **host arrays are not built at all** unless someone asks for them:
- `KernelMapCache::get_or_build(input, config, host_arrays = true)` gains a defaulted flag. Called as before, it fills the host arrays from the device on request, so existing callers and `build_adaptive_kernel_map` see the same full host map as before.
- `adaptive_convolution` / `adaptive_convolution_transpose` pass `false` and use the device arrays only.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `kernel_map_cuda.cu` (new): `cuda_compose_parts`. Each block takes one segment and copies pairs `q0 .. q0+n` of part `p` to `dst ..`, mapping local leaf indices through the uploaded leaf lists (`leaves_in[base_in[p] + local]`, the same for outputs). The kernel writes no atomics and makes no ordering decisions: the result is bitwise identical to the host composition, pair for pair, every run.
- `kernel_map.cpp`:
  - `PartMap::device_copies` holds the device copies, guarded by a mutex and not counted in the host byte budget.
  - `compose_parts_device` computes the segment table on the host: the same binary searches as `compose_parts`, over the parts' host arrays. It uploads one packed int64 table, launches the kernel and installs the arrays with `KernelMapDeviceCache::put`.
  - `fill_host_arrays` builds the host map from the device slot (in/out downloaded, `kernel_index` filled per slot, weights downloaded or 1).
  - `KernelMapDeviceCache::get` copies from the composing device's slot when a map with no host arrays is used on another device (e.g. the same topology on the CPU), and casts the float64 device weights to the requested dtype.
- `detail::cuda_part_compose()` (default on) switches back to host composition, for A/B runs and tests.
- `bench_adaptive_kmap --batch` gains `--batch-device cuda` (time what a CUDA convolution needs: `get_or_build(..., false)` plus the map's device arrays, synchronized) and `--device-compose 0|1`.
- Not changed: the first time a part is seen (the full build, cut into parts) and CPU tensors (host composition). Map contents are identical in every mode.

## TESTING

New tests in `tests/adaptive/test_part_reuse.cpp` (CUDA):
- `part_reuse_device_compose_matches_full_build`:
  - covers CenterSampled and VolumeWeighted, kernels 3 and 5, output shifts 0 and -1, with mixed stored and new parts over 4 batches;
  - checks the device slot (in/out, float64 and float32 weights) and the lazily filled host arrays against a full build, **exactly**;
  - runs with device composition on, and again off to confirm the switch.
- `part_reuse_device_compose_then_cpu_convolution`: a device-composed map then used for a CPU convolution of the same topology is copied from the device slot. The result equals the convolution without part reuse bitwise, and CUDA within 1e-12 (float64).

The existing `part_reuse_convolution_cuda_forward_backward_identical` (deterministic mode, bitwise) now runs through device composition, since it is on by default.

Results (`adaptive_tests`, full suite):

| build | CPU (LibTorch 2.15.0+cpu) | CUDA (LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134) |
|---|---|---|
| #41 (9831857) | 133 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped | all pass |
| this branch (61720fd) | 133 / 0 / 3 (the 2 new CUDA-only tests skip) | **139 / 0 / 0** |
| integration of all open PRs + this branch | | 181 / 0 / 0 |

## BENCHMARKS

**Kernel-map time per training batch, same binary** (`adaptive_kmap_bench --batch 16 --samples 64 --epochs 4 --n 2048 --depth 3 --part-reuse-mb 512 --batch-device cuda --modes center`, alternating `--device-compose 0` / `1`, 6 rounds). Each batch is 16 samples of about 6.9k leaves placed along x; the batch map is timed together with the maps of its pooled versions (4 maps), each including what a CUDA convolution needs (`get_or_build(..., false)` plus the device arrays), synchronized. `--device-compose 0` is exactly #41: host composition plus upload on first use. Host busy with other programs (10-35 % CPU): **contended**.

| metric | #41 (host compose + upload) | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| later epochs (all parts stored), per batch | 25.85 ms [23.76-26.68] | 9.68 ms [8.87-10.18] | **-62.6 %** (6/6 rounds) |
| first epoch (full builds, unchanged path), per batch | 121.2 ms [105.4-144.9] | 122.6 ms [106.7-130.4] | +1.1 % (2/6; noise) |
| peak host working set | 2258 MB | 1061 MB | **-53.0 %** (6/6) |
| pairs in the first batch's 4 maps | 3,413,571 | 3,413,571 | identical maps |

An earlier head of this branch (dd79d81, before the packed part upload) measured 23.01 -> 8.79 ms (-61.8 %), first epoch -8 %, peak working set -53 %.

The host working set drops because composed maps no longer allocate four `[P]` host arrays (32 B per pair). GPU memory goes up, see ML below and TRADEOFFS.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The repository's ML study (`benchmarks/ml_representations`, #31) on the integration build of all open PRs (CUDA, fused apply #43, part reuse at 512 MB, plus #45/#46). Adaptive representation, 300 train / 200 test samples, batch 16, 3 epochs, seed 1, data seed 2026. 6 alternating rounds, one exe each, same build dir, host 11-35 % busy (contended). The only difference between the arms is this PR (at 61720fd).

| metric | without | with this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| epoch 1 time | 1.044 s [1.003-1.148] | 1.176 s [1.130-1.265] | **+12.6 %** |
| epoch 2 time | 0.453 s [0.428-0.492] | 0.472 s [0.441-0.532] | +4.1 % |
| epoch 3 time (steady state) | 0.422 s [0.404-0.480] | 0.342 s [0.322-0.372] | **-19.0 %** (disjoint ranges) |
| total training time, 3 epochs | 1.944 s | 2.019 s | +3.8 % |
| test-set throughput (eval reuses stored parts) | 1094 samples/s | 1610 samples/s | **+47.2 %** |
| conv apply per training step | 4.00 ms | 2.63 ms | -34.2 % (index upload 1.43 ms -> 0) |
| peak CUDA allocated (training) | 226.8 MB | 389.5 MB | **+71.7 %** |
| accuracy | 0.280 | 0.290 | CUDA run-to-run noise (see #41: maps are identical) |

The first epochs pay for creating the device copies of every part: 160 MB of new device memory, so caching-allocator growth, plus the uploads. From then on every epoch is faster, so break-even is at about the 4th epoch of this small study. Longer training and repeated evaluation gain about 19 % per epoch and 47 % in evaluation throughput.

## TRADEOFFS

- **GPU memory (regression):** each stored part keeps a copy of its pairs on the device. Since **Update 1 (b1a7d94)** that is 16-bit indices for parts with at most 65,536 leaves (4 B per pair; int32 above that), plus 8 B per pair for weighted modes. In the ML study peak CUDA allocation is 227 MB without this PR, 390 MB at 61720fd (int32 copies, +72 %) and **312 MB with Update 1 (+37.5 %)**. The copies of one batch's new parts share one buffer, freed when all of them are evicted, and they are not counted in `set_part_reuse_bytes` (that budget is host memory; the part store held 171 MB of host data there).
- **Short runs:** at 61720fd the first epochs paid for creating the device copies (+12.6 % epoch 1, +4.1 % epoch 2; +3.8 % over 3 epochs). With Update 1 (16-bit copies) that is gone: epoch 1 -7.0 %, epoch 2 -3.5 %, epoch 3 -19 %, 3-epoch training time -8.3 % (see the "head to head" comment).
- First attempt (recorded): uploading each new part's arrays separately cost epoch 1 +16.6 % and epoch 2 +10.9 %. Packing a batch's new parts into one transfer (61720fd) brought that to +12.6 % / +4.1 %.
- Host arrays of device-composed maps are filled only on request, through a device-to-host copy; callers asking for host maps of CUDA tensors pay that copy instead of the host composition.
- Only maps that are *composed* from stored parts move to the device; full builds (e.g. the first epoch) are unchanged.
- Off switch: `minkowski::adaptive::detail::cuda_part_compose() = false`.

## REPRODUCTION

```
# tests (CUDA build)
build/adaptive_tests part_reuse
# same-binary A/B
build/adaptive_kmap_bench --batch 16 --samples 64 --epochs 4 --n 2048 --depth 3 --part-reuse-mb 512 --batch-device cuda --modes center --device-compose 0
```

body:
## SUMMARY

`adaptive_pool` / `coarsen` used to rebuild the whole tensor at every level step. Each step:
- created an entry for **every** leaf (40-byte key + index + scale);
- ran `stable_sort` over all of them;
- gathered **every** feature row (`index_select`);
- scatter-added every row into a zero tensor (`index_add_`).

Only two runs of the sorted topology actually change: the leaves at `level` that merge, and the parents they join at `level - 1`. This PR rebuilds just those two runs:

- **No sort.** The merged leaves of one parity class (`coordinate & 1` on every axis) already have strictly increasing parents in key order: `c -> c >> 1` is monotone and one-to-one within a parity, and that holds for negative coordinates too. So the parents in (key, index) order are a merge of 2^D sorted lists, done in D rounds of `std::merge`, with O(n·D) comparisons instead of O(n log n).
- **Merge, not re-sort.** The new parents are merged into the existing `level - 1` run. Every other run keeps its keys and order.
- **Slice, not gather.** Features of untouched runs are `slice`d. Only the merged leaves are reduced (`remap_features` on the merged subset), and only the `level - 1` run is permuted when parents interleave with existing leaves.

The result is the same as before: identical keys, and identical features with the reduction applied in the same order (children of a parent in index order). On the CPU the new path is bit-identical to the old one (`torch::equal`). The only bit-level difference: an untouched leaf holding `-0.0` keeps it, where `0 + x` used to give `+0.0`. These compare equal.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `MinkowskiEngine/adaptive/adaptive_tensor.cpp`, `coarsen_step`:
  - Level runs come from `Topology::counts`, since keys are sorted by level first.
  - Merged leaves are bucketed by parity class, then merged pairwise. Ties (same parent) are ordered by leaf index, as `stable_sort` did.
  - New key list: `[levels < L-1] + merge([L-1 run], parents) + [kept leaves at L] + [levels > L]`.
  - Features: `cat` of slices, the pooled parents, and one `index_select` over the `L-1` run only when parents interleave with existing leaves. Kept leaves at `L` are a slice when contiguous.
- `Topology::make` still validates the result (sortedness, overlap), exactly as before.
- `finish()` and the full-sort path are unchanged for `refine`.
- `tests/adaptive/bench_adaptive_kmap.cpp`: new `--pool cpu|cuda` mode. It times `adaptive_pool` (Mean) to every coarser level, a chained pool (depth-1, ..., 0, as in a network) forward, and the same chain with backward.

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_coarsen_merge.cpp`. Its oracle is the original algorithm: map every merged leaf to its parent, `stable_sort` all entries, merge equal keys, and reduce with `index_add_` / `scatter_reduce`.
- `coarsen_merge_matches_full_sort_oracle_bitwise_cpu`: 288 cases (24 random multi-level trees with negative coordinates and 1-7 channels, float32 and float64, Mean/Sum/Max, targets 0-3, the whole space or random sub-regions). Keys must be identical and features `torch::equal`. Each tree also contains a `-0.0` row.
- `coarsen_merge_adaptive_pool_matches_oracle_and_keeps_input`: `adaptive_pool` to every level, and the input tensor is left untouched.
- `coarsen_merge_edge_cases`: empty tensor; only level-0 leaves (same feature tensor returned); a region holding no complete parent; all leaves merging into one parent; parents interleaved with existing level-0 leaves on both sides.
- `coarsen_merge_gradients_match_oracle`: backward of `sum(out * probe)` equals the oracle's, for every reduction and region.
- `coarsen_merge_cuda_matches_cpu`: CUDA keys identical; features and gradients within 1e-5 (float32) / 1e-12 (float64).

Results (`adaptive_tests`, full suite):

| build | CPU (LibTorch 2.15.0+cpu) | CUDA (LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134) |
|---|---|---|
| main f4ac612 | 119 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped | 123 / 0 / 0 |
| this branch (5200ee5) | 123 / 0 / 2 (4 new pass; the CUDA-only test skips) | 128 / 0 / 0 (5 new pass) |

The existing coarsen/pool tests (`topology_coarsen_*`, `numeric_local_pool_matches_coarsen_to_target_level`, `gradient_*coarsen*`, `coverage_large_topology_refine_and_coarsen_roundtrip`, the Max tie test) pass unchanged.

## BENCHMARKS

`adaptive_kmap_bench --pool cpu|cuda --warmup 2 --reps 7` (new mode). Workload: the bench's default 20,000 points, half spread over [0, 256)^3 and half in [0, 16)^3, refined to depth 4 in [0, 16)^3, so **41,376 leaves**, most of them at level 4. Mean pooling, float32, 8 channels.

Both binaries were built in the **same build dir**: the branch, and the branch with main's `adaptive_tensor.cpp` swapped in (same bench source). 6 rounds alternate which binary runs first; each value is the median of 7 timed repetitions, and the table gives the median over rounds with min-max in brackets. The host was busy with other programs (10-35 % CPU), so the numbers are **contended**.

**CPU build** (6/6 rounds faster in every metric):

| metric | main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| pool to level 3 (12,704 leaves out), fwd | 7.53 ms [7.39-7.94] | 4.05 ms [3.79-4.52] | **-46.3 %** |
| pool to level 2, fwd | 9.24 ms [8.55-10.11] | 4.84 ms [4.39-5.11] | **-47.7 %** |
| pool to level 1, fwd | 10.36 ms [9.67-10.59] | 5.08 ms [4.74-5.25] | **-51.0 %** |
| pool to level 0 (8,616 leaves out), fwd | 11.48 ms [11.06-13.40] | 5.09 ms [4.03-5.52] | **-55.6 %** |
| chained pool 3 -> 0, fwd | 12.10 ms [11.80-15.26] | 5.06 ms [4.28-5.63] | **-58.2 %** |
| chained pool 3 -> 0, fwd + bwd | 13.06 ms [12.47-17.68] | 6.07 ms [4.94-6.94] | **-53.5 %** |
| peak working set | 110.7 MB | 110.1 MB | -0.5 % |

**CUDA build, features on the GPU** (6/6 rounds faster in every timing):

| metric | main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| pool to level 3, fwd | 6.18 ms [5.23-6.82] | 2.56 ms [2.42-3.22] | **-58.6 %** |
| pool to level 2, fwd | 7.67 ms [6.32-9.99] | 3.40 ms [3.08-3.78] | **-55.7 %** |
| pool to level 1, fwd | 8.08 ms [7.21-11.66] | 3.78 ms [3.39-4.43] | **-53.3 %** |
| pool to level 0, fwd | 9.56 ms [8.85-12.53] | 4.25 ms [3.83-4.91] | **-55.6 %** |
| chained pool 3 -> 0, fwd | 9.66 ms [8.87-12.20] | 4.24 ms [3.83-5.21] | **-56.0 %** |

| peak working set (host) | 495.5 MB | 523.6 MB | **+5.7 %** (6/6) |

Pooling is host-bound on both builds: the sort, entry building and `Topology::make` run on the host. CUDA kernel time is a small part of it. Throughput follows from the latency (e.g. chained forward: 82.7 -> 197.6 pools of 41k leaves per second on the CPU).

**GPU memory.** The bench does not record allocator peaks for this mode. In the ML study below, peak CUDA allocation is 228.0 -> 226.8 MB (-0.5 %) with this PR and #45 together. The `cat` of slices allocates the same output tensor as before. The `index_select` / `index_add_` temporaries now cover only the merged rows instead of every row.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The repository's ML study (`benchmarks/ml_representations`, #31) on the integration build of all open PRs (CUDA, fused apply #43, part reuse #41 at 512 MB). Adaptive representation, 300 train / 200 test samples, batch 16, 3 epochs, seed 1, data seed 2026. 4 alternating rounds, one exe each in the same build dir, host 35 % busy (contended). The B arm adds **this PR and #45** (O(n) `from_voxels` for batches); their effects are separated by phase:

| metric | integration | + this PR + #45 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fwd_pool` per training step (3 pools) | 5.25 ms | 3.27 ms | -37.6 % (4/4) |
| `make_batch` per step (#45) | 4.82 ms | 1.79 ms | -62.9 % (4/4) |
| epoch 3 time (not profiled) | 0.578 s [0.561-0.631] | 0.486 s [0.426-0.570] | **-15.9 %** |
| epoch 1 time | 1.170 s | 1.144 s | -2.2 % |
| test-set throughput | 791 samples/s | 1022 samples/s | +29.2 % |
| accuracy / macro F1 | 0.2875 / 0.261 | 0.2875 / 0.266 | same (CUDA run-to-run noise) |
| peak CUDA allocated / reserved | 228.0 / 260 MB | 226.8 / 258 MB | -0.5 % / -0.8 % |
| peak RSS | 1473 MB | 1476 MB | +0.2 % |

Caveat on `fwd_pool`: the baseline binary had extra synchronising phase timers inside pooling (a profiling build). The per-step pool numbers therefore overstate the gain slightly. The epoch-3 time comes from unprofiled steps and is not affected.

## TRADEOFFS

- The `-0.0` vs `+0.0` difference above (numerically equal).
- Exact zeros in a Max gradient test: the oracle, like the old code, halves the gradient of a maximum that is exactly 0 at every step (a PyTorch `scatter_reduce` `amax` backward quirk; fixed separately in #44). The new path no longer sends unchanged rows through that reduction, so for unchanged leaves holding exactly 0 it is already correct. The gradient test therefore uses features without exact zeros.
- Unsuccessful first version (recorded): replacing only the full sort with `std::sort` over the merged leaves was not faster. In the benchmark workload the merged level holds most leaves, and the 40-byte key comparisons dominated (CPU profile: 8.7 ms per chain for the sort vs 3.2 ms for the parity merge).

## REPRODUCTION

```
build/adaptive_tests coarsen          # the new tests + every coarsen/pool test
# benchmark (the A/B swaps in main's adaptive_tensor.cpp for the base binary, same build dir)
build/adaptive_kmap_bench --pool cpu  --warmup 2 --reps 7
build/adaptive_kmap_bench --pool cuda --warmup 2 --reps 7
```
