## SUMMARY

`AdaptiveSparseTensor::from_voxels` sorts the leaf keys (`detail::sort_keys`): a parallel comparison sort on the host, or above 16384 keys on CUDA builds, an upload, a device sort and a download. The most common way to build a training batch is to place each sample's leaves side by side along the first axis and call `from_voxels` on the concatenation. That input is **already sorted within every level**: each sample's keys are sorted, and samples are disjoint and increasing along x. Only the levels are interleaved between samples.

For such input, a stable counting sort by level *is* the full sort. This PR checks for that case in one O(n) pass and then places the keys by level, so it does no comparison sort and no device round trip. Keys are distinct, so the resulting keys and permutation are exactly what the full sort produces. Every other input takes the old path.

The `sort_keys` order also changes slightly: the cheap parallel "already sorted" check now runs before the CUDA branch. Already-sorted inputs with 16384 or more keys no longer go to the device just to come back unchanged; the permutation is then empty ("nothing moved") instead of the identity.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

`MinkowskiEngine/adaptive/adaptive_topology.cpp`:
- `sort_by_level_if_levels_sorted`, new:
  - One sequential pass checks that every level's keys are strictly increasing and counts keys per level. Levels are bounded by `kMaxSupportedDepth`.
  - Prefix offsets, then `order[pos[level]++] = i` and a parallel gather of the keys.
  - Returns false, with nothing changed, on the first out-of-order or repeated key within a level. Duplicates are therefore still rejected by `Topology::make`, exactly as before.
- `sort_keys` now runs: parallel sorted check, then per-level counting sort, then (CUDA, n >= 16384) device sort, then host parallel sort.

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_sort_keys.cpp`:
- `sort_keys_batches_sorted_within_levels_match_full_sort`: 20 random batches (1-9 samples, mixed levels 0-3) compared with a reference `stable_sort` of (key, index). Keys and permutation must be identical, and the permutation empty when the input was already sorted.
- `sort_keys_large_batch_matches_full_sort`: more than 16384 keys, the size at which CUDA builds sorted on the device.
- `sort_keys_unsorted_levels_sorted_and_empty_inputs`: already sorted, shuffled (general path), one swap, empty, and one key.
- `sort_keys_from_voxels_batch_matches_presorted_input`: `from_voxels` on a batch gives the same coordinates, levels and features (bitwise) as on the presorted input.
- `sort_keys_duplicates_still_rejected`.

Results (`adaptive_tests`, full suite, CPU build with LibTorch 2.15.0+cpu): main f4ac612 **119 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped**; this branch **124 / 0 / 1** (5 new tests pass). The CUDA build, where large inputs used to take the device sort, runs in the integration build of all open PRs; I'll post that result as a comment.

## BENCHMARKS

`adaptive_kmap_bench --concat S` (new mode). S samples are built like a training batch and concatenated along x, then `from_voxels` is timed. Each sample is `--n` points on a random ellipsoid surface over 4 level-0 cells, half of it refined to depth 3, giving about 8k leaves per sample.

Both binaries were built in the same build dir: the branch, and the branch with main's `adaptive_topology.cpp` swapped in. 6 rounds alternate the order; each value is the median of 9-15 timed repetitions (after 2-3 warm-ups), and the table gives the median over rounds with min-max in brackets. CPU build. The host was busy with other programs (5-35 % CPU): **contended**.

| batch | leaves | main | this PR | change | faster rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 samples, `--n 2048` | 128,760 | 14.83 ms [11.80-16.44] | 7.86 ms [7.41-8.58] | **-47.0 %** | 6/6 |
| 16 samples, `--n 256` | 100,548 | 12.63 ms [10.39-14.80] | 6.85 ms [5.68-11.08] | **-45.7 %** | 6/6 |
| 64 samples, `--n 512` | 429,394 | 39.40 ms [37.46-51.12] | 19.94 ms [18.24-21.08] | **-49.4 %** | 6/6 |

| batch | peak working set, main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 x 2048 | 122.5 MB | 121.9 MB | -0.5 % |
| 64 x 512 | 200.0 MB | 196.3 MB | -1.8 % |

What remains (about 7 ms at 129k leaves) is building the keys, `Topology::make` (validation, coordinate/level/volume tensors) and the feature gather. GPU memory: n/a, since `from_voxels` runs on the host.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

The ML study (`benchmarks/ml_representations`, #31) builds every training batch with `from_voxels`, with samples 6 level-0 cells apart along x: exactly the case handled here. On the integration build of all open PRs (CUDA, 300 train / 200 test samples, batch 16, about 13k leaves per batch, 3 epochs), 4 alternating rounds, host 35 % busy. The B arm adds this PR and #46 (coarsen); the two touch different phases:

| metric | integration | + this PR + #46 | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `from_voxels` per training step (library timer) | 3.99 ms | 1.10 ms | **-72.5 %** (4/4) |
| `make_batch` per step | 4.82 ms | 1.79 ms | **-62.9 %** (4/4) |
| epoch 3 time (not profiled, both PRs) | 0.578 s | 0.486 s | -15.9 % |
| accuracy | 0.2875 | 0.2875 | same |

A batch of about 13k keys is below the 16384-key threshold, so it was sorted on the host before as well. The gain here is from skipping the comparison sort, not from avoiding a device round trip.

## TRADEOFFS

- Inputs that are not sorted within levels pay one extra sequential O(n) pass before the old sort. It stops at the first out-of-order key, and the comparison sort that follows costs O(n log n).
- Already-sorted inputs with 16384 or more keys on CUDA builds now return an empty permutation instead of the identity. `from_voxels` treats both the same way: no feature gather.

## REPRODUCTION

```
cmake --build build --target adaptive_tests adaptive_kmap_bench
build/adaptive_tests sort_keys
build/adaptive_kmap_bench --concat 16 --n 2048 --depth 3 --warmup 2 --reps 9
build/adaptive_kmap_bench --concat 64 --n 512  --depth 3 --warmup 2 --reps 9
```

The base binary for the A/B is the branch with `git show origin/main:MinkowskiEngine/adaptive/adaptive_topology.cpp` swapped in, built in the same build dir. Timing ran under an exclusive machine lock (no builds and no other GPU work).

## SUMMARY

`Reduction::Max` (used by `adaptive_pool`, `coarsen` and `resample_to`) lost gradient whenever a maximum was **exactly 0**: half of it at every pooling step the value passed through. ReLU outputs make exact zeros common in networks.

The cause is in `remap_features`. It computes Max as `scatter_reduce(zeros, ..., "amax", include_self=false)`. PyTorch's backward for `amax` divides the gradient among all entries equal to the result, and it counts the initial `self` value in that tie count even when `include_self=false`; only `self`'s own share is masked afterwards. With a zero-initialised output and a maximum of 0, the true maximum receives 1/2 of the gradient instead of 1. Because `coarsen` passes every leaf through `remap_features` at every level step, an unchanged leaf holding 0 gets 1/2^k after k steps. The existing test `coverage_gradient_max_with_ties_splits_evenly` states the intended contract: the tied entries share the unit gradient. That holds for every value except 0.

The fix initialises the Max output with `-inf`, so the initial value can never tie a finite maximum, and then sets rows that received no entry back to 0 (the previous output for empty rows, e.g. reference cells without inputs in `resample_to`). Forward values are unchanged.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

**Update 1** (485a166): the sparse engine's `MAX_POOL` quantization (`sparse_tensor.cpp`, `tensor_field.cpp`) used the same zero-initialised `amax` and now starts from `-inf` as well. Every quantized row has a point, so no masking is needed there.

- `MinkowskiEngine/adaptive/adaptive_tensor.cpp`, `remap_features`, `case Reduction::Max`:
  - Floating-point features: `scatter_reduce(full(-inf), ..., "amax", include_self=false)`.
  - Rows without entries are found on the host from `dst` (already host-side) and zeroed with one `masked_fill`. That step is skipped when every row has an entry, which is always the case for `coarsen`.
  - Integer features keep the old path (no gradients, no `-inf`).
- Not changed: Mean and Sum, forward results, and the documented subgradient for real ties (it is still split evenly).
- Limitation: if inputs contain `-inf` and a row's maximum is `-inf`, the initial value ties again and gradients split as before. That case is documented in the code comment.

## TESTING

New tests in `tests/adaptive/test_gradients.cpp`:
- `gradient_max_pool_at_zero_keeps_unit_gradient` (CPU, and CUDA when available) checks that each of these receives a gradient of exactly 1:
  - a merged child whose parent's maximum is 0;
  - an unmerged leaf holding 0;
  - a positive leaf.
  
  The gradient sum must equal the number of outputs. It also checks that `resample_to(..., Max)` gives the same values and the same unit gradient.
- `gradient_max_pool_rows_without_entries_stay_zero` checks that a `resample_to` reference cell with no inputs is 0, not `-inf`.

Results (CPU build, LibTorch 2.15.0+cpu, `adaptive_tests`):

| build | adaptive_tests | `gradient_max_pool_at_zero_keeps_unit_gradient` |
|---|---|---|
| main f4ac612 | 119 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped | n/a |
| main's `adaptive_tensor.cpp` + the new tests (same build dir) | | **FAIL**: gradient 0.5, expected 1 |
| this branch (5984162) | 121 / 0 / 1 | pass |
| this branch, Update 1 (2b87082; + `gradient_sparse_max_pool_quantization_at_zero_keeps_unit_gradient`, which fails on main with gradient 0.5) | 122 / 0 / 1 | pass |

Command: `adaptive_tests.exe` (full suite) and `adaptive_tests.exe gradient_max`. The existing tie test `coverage_gradient_max_with_ties_splits_evenly` passes unchanged. The CUDA half of the new test runs in the integration build of all open PRs; I'll post that result in a comment.

## BENCHMARKS

n/a. This is a correctness fix with no measurable cost. What changes per Max reduction: the output is filled with `-inf` instead of zeros (same allocation), plus one host pass over the destination indices. A `masked_fill` runs only when an output row has no entry, which never happens for pooling. CPU and GPU memory are unchanged apart from a temporary `nnew`-byte mask in that case.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a. The ML study uses Mean pooling. Networks that Max-pool ReLU features are the ones affected.

## TRADEOFFS

- One extra `masked_fill`, only when some output row has no entry (never for pooling).
- One host pass over `dst` (already a host vector) per Max reduction.
- Bit-level forward results are unchanged. Gradients change only where a maximum is exactly 0, which is the fix.

## REPRODUCTION

```
git checkout fix/adaptive-max-zero-gradient   
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCPU_ONLY=ON -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<libtorch-cpu>
cmake --build build --target adaptive_tests
build/adaptive_tests gradient_max
```
To see the bug: build the same tests with `git show origin/main:MinkowskiEngine/adaptive/adaptive_tensor.cpp` in place of the fixed file.

Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB (sm_75), driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors `docker/cuda-profile.sh`.

> **Stacked PR.** This branch is #28 (`perf/adaptive-device-kmap`, ec3abba) plus commits 02df9d8, 99ecb43, 4ea50ef and d84e61e (Update 1), with merge 8030675 of #32 for the CUDA 12.4 CI build. Review the diff against #28. Once #28 (and #32) are merged, this diff reduces to those commits. It is independent of #40 and #41 and merges cleanly with them (see the integration check below).

## SUMMARY

On CUDA, adaptive convolution was the largest remaining adaptive cost. In the ML study with #41 the training step is ~74 ms, with ~33 ms in backward. #28 runs a gather, one cuBLAS GEMM per kernel slot (27 for a 3³ kernel), concatenations and a scatter per call, and roughly three times as many kernels in backward. At small channel counts the time is set by the number of launches and autograd ops, not by arithmetic. The round-5 conv probe was flat at 6.5–7.9 ms forward+backward from 16 to 128 channels.

This PR replaces that path, for float and double CUDA inputs, with **fused gather-GEMM-scatter kernels**. One launch covers every kernel slot in each direction: forward, input gradient and weight gradient. Nothing of size `[pairs, C]` is allocated or kept for backward.

Results against #28, from the same benchmark run with arms in rotating order (6 rounds, host contended):
- **Forward + backward: −49 % to −92 %**. That is −71 % at 20k points / 8→16 channels, −49 % to −56 % at 200k points / 32→64, −50 % at 64→64, −67 % for OverlapWeighted and −92 % in float64.
- **Forward: −45 % to −81 %.**
- **Peak CUDA memory (caching allocator max allocated): −77 % to −89 %.** For example 665 → 80 MB at 200k points.
- The first call after a map is built is 58–85 % faster, since fewer large allocations are needed.
- Results agree with the per-slot path within float tolerance; the tests are listed below. Deterministic mode keeps #28's exact path and is bit-identical to it.

**Update 1 (d84e61e):** the tile tables are now expanded on the device. Before, a new map spent ~4 ms building them on the host. In the ML study, forward conv time per step drops a further 33 % and the step 18 %. Details and numbers are in the PR comment "Update 1". The tables below are from 4ea50ef and remain the baseline.

The first version, with one output per thread, was **slower than #28 at 32→64 channels**: forward +42 %, forward+backward +77 %. The second commit adds register-blocked kernels for wider channels, which fixed that (details under TRADEOFFS).

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

**Before (#28).** The CUDA `apply_map` gathers all pairs once (`index_select`, `[P, C_in]`), multiplies the pair weights, splits the rows per kernel slot, runs one GEMM per slot, concatenates each group's products and scatter-adds them. Forward is ~27 GEMMs plus ~6 other kernels. Backward is about three times that: a GEMM pair per slot, the `cat`/`split` backward and the input-gradient `index_add_`. Autograd keeps the `[P, C_in]` gather alive until backward.

**After.** The pairs are already sorted by kernel slot. A per-map **tile table** (`[T, 3]` int64: begin, end, slot) cuts every slot's pair range into row blocks. It is built once per device and row count and cached in `KernelMapDeviceCache` next to the index arrays (`KernelMapDeviceCache::tiles`). The kernels in `MinkowskiEngine/adaptive/fused_apply_cuda.cu` each cover **all slots in one launch**:

| kernel | computes | block |
|---|---|---|
| `gather_gemm_scatter` (forward) | `y[to[p]] += w_p · x[from[p]] @ W[k(p)]` | one tile of pairs × a block of output channels |
| same, `trans_w` (input gradient) | `gx[from[p]] += w_p · gy[to[p]] @ W[k(p)]ᵀ` | as above, `from`/`to` swapped, W read transposed |
| `weight_grad` | `gW[k] += Σ_{p∈chunk} w_p · x[from[p]]ᵀ gy[to[p]]` | one 256-pair chunk of one slot × a tile of `[C_in, C_out]` |

- **Narrow channels** (tile edge 8 or 16, from the engine's shared-memory rule, made symmetric in C_in/C_out). These use the tile structure of the engine's `matmul` kernel in `src/convolution_kernel.cu`: BS×BS threads with shared-memory A/B tiles and one output per thread. The changes are a slot taken from the tile table, `int64_t` indices, the pair weight applied on the A load, channel counts that need not be multiples of BS, and `atomicAdd` into the output rows.
- **Wider channels** (the engine's 32 case) use register-blocked variants. Each thread computes a 4×4 micro-tile of a 64×64 output tile. A side with at most 32 channels gets a 32-wide tile, so no lanes idle, for example the 32-channel input gradient of a 32→64 layer. The K steps are 16 wide and shared memory is padded. Loads are coalesced along the contiguous dimension of each operand, including the transposed weights of the input gradient.
- **Grid layout.** Tiles go on `gridDim.x` (limit 2³¹−1). Maps with more than 65,535 tiles therefore need no grid-stride loop; the test `fused_apply_cuda_more_tiles_than_one_grid_row` runs about 113k tiles.
- **Weight gradient.** It is split-K by chunk. Each block keeps its partial in registers and adds it once, so there are `P/256 × C_in × C_out` atomics. Within a chunk each 16-row (or BS-row) step is summed on its own before it is added. This keeps float32 rounding close to cuBLAS's: the first version was 3× worse (below).
- **`FusedApplyMap`** (a `torch::autograd::Function` in `adaptive/ops.cpp`):
  - It saves only `x`, the weight and the non-differentiable index, pair-weight and tile tensors.
  - The weight is cast to `x`'s dtype outside the Function, so a float64 weight with float32 features still gets a float64 gradient.
  - With `create_graph=true`, backward switches to a differentiable formulation of the same math, so higher-order gradients keep working. The input gradient goes through the Function again, and the weight gradient uses gather plus per-slot `mm`.
  - An empty map has no tiles. Its output is zeros that stay in the graph, with zero gradients.
- **Dispatch.** The fused path is used when `x` is CUDA, the dtype is float or double, `at::globalContext().deterministicAlgorithms()` is off, and `detail::cuda_apply_map_fused()` is true. That switch defaults to true and is a process-wide hook like `cuda_apply_map_group_bytes`. Everything else takes #28's path unchanged: CPU, half/bfloat16 and deterministic mode.
- **`adaptive_kmap_bench`** gains `--fused 0|1` and `--grad-split 1`. The second times forward+backward with only the features, or only the weight, requiring a gradient.
- `docs/adaptive.md` describes the fused path.

## TESTING

New: `tests/adaptive/test_fused_apply.cpp`, 8 cases in `adaptive_tests`. The CUDA cases skip on CPU builds.

| test | checks |
|---|---|
| `fused_apply_cuda_matches_per_slot_reference` | forward, grad x and grad W vs the per-slot reference. Covers 3 modes × shift {0, −1} × forward/transposed × channels {4→5, 3→70, 8→16, 24→32, 32→64, 40→70}, so every kernel variant and non-multiple channel counts run, in float64 (1e-10) and float32 |
| `fused_apply_cuda_matches_unfused_path_and_cpu` | fused vs `cuda_apply_map_fused()=false` vs CPU, float64, 1e-10 |
| `fused_apply_cuda_finite_difference_gradients` | float64 central differences (ε = 1e-6, tol 1e-6) for x and W in all 3 modes |
| `fused_apply_cuda_second_order_gradients_match_unfused` | `create_graph` double backward vs the unfused path, 1e-9 |
| `fused_apply_cuda_edge_cases` | empty map (zero rows and zero gradients), kernel size 1 (one slot), non-contiguous features, float64 weight with float32 features |
| `fused_apply_cuda_more_tiles_than_one_grid_row` | more than 65,535 tiles, vs the unfused path, float64 |
| `fused_apply_tile_table_covers_each_slot_once` | tile table covers each slot exactly once and is cached (also runs on CPU) |
| `fused_apply_cuda_deterministic_mode_uses_unfused_path` | deterministic mode is bit-identical to the unfused path |

**Float32 tolerance.** Fused and per-slot results are both compared with float64 on the same float32-rounded inputs. The fused error must be at most twice the per-slot path's own error, or at most 1e-6 of the largest value. The first fused weight gradient summed 256 rows into one float sequentially and failed this check: 1.16e-4 vs 3.8e-5, with max |value| 87. Per-step partial sums fixed it.

`device_kmap_cuda_slot_groups_match_reference` now turns the fused path off, because the slot groups exist only on the unfused path.

The merge had textual conflicts only in the CMake test list and the bench option list (both unions). Results:

- CUDA: adaptive **179/0/0**, gaussian 91/0/0, core 51/0/1, ctest 9/9.

`coverage_large_topology_cpu_cuda_agreement` (1 failure in 22 runs in round 5) passed in every run here.

## BENCHMARKS

Each round runs all three in a fresh process, and the order rotates per round (6 rounds, each arm first twice). Each run does 3 warm-ups and 10 timed reps. ## TRADEOFFS

- **First version slower at wider channels (recorded failure).** The initial fused kernels (02df9d8) used one output per thread. - **Nondeterminism.** As with #28's `index_add_`, float sums use atomics, so the last bits vary between runs. Deterministic mode takes #28's path (bit-identical, slower).
- **Accuracy.** Float32 results are not bitwise equal to #28's. The tests bound the error at twice the per-slot path's error against float64.
- **Coverage.** Half and bfloat16 inputs, and the CPU, keep the existing path. Channel counts above 32 always use the 64×64 kernels; no autotuning is done.
- **Atomic contention.** It grows with the number of pairs per output row. In these benchmarks OverlapWeighted (more pairs per output) still gains 67 %.
- **More code.** One new `.cu` file (435 lines: four kernel templates and their launchers); the whole diff against #28 is +1,054 / −14 lines, about half of it tests. The fused path can be switched off at runtime (`detail::cuda_apply_map_fused() = false`) and is covered by its own tests.
- **Rejected alternative.** A padded batched GEMM was tried again in round 5. It was dropped before measurement because it repeats round 4's failed experiment (see #28's comments). This PR keeps the split-K weight gradient that experiment lacked.

body:
## SUMMARY

The Gaussian trainer's loss uses `ssim()`. On the CPU, `ssim()` filtered five moment images (μx, μy, E[x²], E[y²], E[xy]) with **five dense 11×11 depthwise `conv2d` calls**. After #30 made the CPU rasterizer fast, these convolutions **dominate the CPU train step at 256–512 px** (a probe showed ~110 ms of a step at 256 px, scaling with pixels, not with Gaussians).

The 11×11 Gaussian window is the outer product of a 1-D kernel, and zero padding separates as well. So on the CPU the five moments are now stacked as **15 planes** (5 moments × 3 channels) and filtered by **one vertical and one horizontal 1-D depthwise convolution**:
- 22 instead of 121 taps per pixel;
- 2 instead of 5 convolutions, in both forward and backward.

The math is the same; only float32 rounding differs. CUDA keeps the dense cuDNN path unchanged, because a probe showed the separable form is not faster there.

Result (CPU, 5000 splats, 6 order-alternated rounds): **train step −42 % / −59 % / −68 % at 128 / 256 / 512 px**, with 256 and 512 px faster in every round.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `MinkowskiEngine/gaussian/gaussian_trainer.cpp`, `ssim()`:
  - CPU branch: `planes = cat({x, y, x*x, y*y, x*y}, 1)` → `conv2d(planes, k_vertical[15,1,w,1], pad (w/2, 0), groups 15)` → `conv2d(·, k_horizontal[15,1,1,w], pad (0, w/2), groups 15)` → `split(3, 1)` into the five moments.
  - CUDA branch: unchanged (dense `window × window` depthwise filter per moment).
  - The SSIM map and its mean are computed as before from the moments.
- Numerics against the dense float64 reference: value |Δ| < 3e-8, gradient relative error ~2e-6 (float32 rounding of a different summation order).
- Memory: the 15-plane intermediate raises the peak working set at 512 px (see BENCHMARKS).
- No API change.

## TESTING

New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_ssim.cpp` (registered in `gaussian_tests`):
- `gaussian_ssim_identical_images_is_one`.
- `gaussian_ssim_matches_dense_reference_cpu`: value and gradient against a dense float64 reference, for windows 11/7/3/1, non-square images, and an image smaller than the window.
- `gaussian_ssim_matches_dense_reference_cuda`: the same checks on CUDA.
- `gaussian_ssim_rejects_bad_arguments`.

body:
> **Stacked PR.** This branch contains #28 (`perf/adaptive-device-kmap`, ec3abba) and #40 (`fix/adaptive-integer-taps`, bbd4cff). The new commits are b3555b1, 9547439, d103663, 472e1d1 and 5d9c49e, after the merge 650ab7d. Review the diff against #28 merged with #40. Once both are merged, this diff reduces to those commits.

## SUMMARY

Training batches of adaptive tensors are formed by placing samples side by side along the first axis. The ML study (#31) does this, and it is the natural way to batch without a batch coordinate. As a result every batch is a **new topology**, so the kernel-map cache (keyed by topology id) misses on every layer of every step, although each sample's share of the map is the same in every epoch.

Profiling #31 on top of #28 showed the map build at **26–32 ms of a ~100 ms adaptive training step**: 4 cache misses per step, one for the input level and three for the pooled levels.

This PR adds **opt-in part reuse** to `KernelMapCache`. A batch topology is split into its samples, each sample's map is reused from earlier batches, and the batch map is assembled from those maps instead of being searched again. The result is **identical to a full build, pair for pair**: same pairs, order, weights and output topology. Outputs and gradients are therefore bit-identical, which the tests verify on CPU and on CUDA in deterministic mode. A topology that does not split is matched as one part, so a validation set evaluated every epoch, or a repeated single sample, is reused too.

```cpp
KernelMapCache::instance().set_part_reuse_bytes(size_t(512) << 20); // 0 = off (default)
```

Headline numbers (contended host, details below):
- Kernel-map time per training batch after the first epoch: **−80 to −82 %** (`adaptive_kmap_bench --batch`).
- ML study on CUDA: **−17 % epoch time** after epoch 1 and −22 % step time, eval throughput **+55 %**, b1 inference **−20 %**.
- ML study on CPU: −16 % total train time.
- Accuracy is identical, verified with deterministic runs on CPU and CUDA.
- Cost: +7 to +13 % peak RSS (171 MB part store for 500 samples × 4 levels), a slower first epoch, and no VRAM change.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- **Split.** A topology splits into parts: runs of occupied level-0 x cells separated by at least `r = (kernel_size - 1) / 2` empty level-0 cells. A tap lands at most `r` level-0 cells from its output leaf's level-0 cell (outputs are never coarser than level 0), so no tap crosses between parts. A topology without such gaps is one part. Reuse covers `CenterSampled` and `VolumeWeighted`; `OverlapWeighted` (and #19's `CenterAveraged`) keep the normal path, as does everything while reuse is off.
- **Content match.** Each part's keys are moved to level-0 x = 0 by whole level-0 cells (`x - first_x * 2^level`). They are hashed together with D, `max_depth`, the base voxel size bits and the kernel config, and a hit also requires full key equality. A part's map does not depend on its position because of #40, which resolves taps on the integer grid; that is what makes reuse exact.
- **Paths**, all producing the full-build result:
  1. All parts stored: compose. Per slot, pairs are copied level by level and part by part with local-to-batch index remaps, which reproduces `build_pairs` order (slot, then output by level and then x, then input).
  2. Few new parts (at most 1/4 of the leaves): build those parts alone (as translated topologies), store them, then compose.
  3. Otherwise, e.g. the first epoch: one normal full build, cut into the new parts' maps in parallel, one part per thread. A part's outputs at a level form one run of the batch outputs, so its pairs per slot are found by binary search; the run assumption is checked, and nothing is stored if it fails.
- **Store.** An LRU of `PartMap`s holding int32 local indices, weights only for `VolumeWeighted`, and the keys used for matching. Its size is bounded by `set_part_reuse_bytes`. `Stats` gains `part_hits`, `part_misses` and `part_bytes`. `clear()` also clears the store, and `set_part_reuse_bytes(0)` frees it.
- **Pooled levels benefit too.** `adaptive_pool` output keeps the samples apart, because coarsening never leaves a level-0 cell, so every encoder level reuses.
- **Benchmark tool.** `adaptive_kmap_bench --batch B --samples S --epochs E --part-reuse-mb M` runs a training-style loop: shuffled epochs, B samples per batch placed 6 cells apart, and the batch plus each pooled level timed per batch.
- Docs: `docs/adaptive.md` ("CUDA and caching").

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_part_reuse.cpp` (part of `adaptive_tests`):
- `part_reuse_matches_full_build_modes_shifts_kernels`. Four batches cover every path (all new, many new, all stored, few new). Each map and output topology is compared with `torch::equal` against a full build with reuse off. The grid is D = 1/2/3 × {CenterSampled, VolumeWeighted} × kernel 1/3/5 × output shift 0/-1/-3. Hit and miss counters are checked against a content-aware expectation: in 1–2 D some random samples coincide and correctly hit.
- `part_reuse_needs_a_gap_wider_than_the_kernel_radius`: a gap of `r - 1` cells gives one part, and a moved single sample hits.
- `part_reuse_skips_overlap_weighted`.
- `part_reuse_budget_and_eviction`: a half-size budget is respected, results stay exact after evictions, and budget 0 frees the store.
- `part_reuse_convolution_{cpu,cuda}_forward_backward_identical`: `adaptive_convolution` output, input gradient and weight gradient are `torch::equal` with reuse off vs on. On CUDA this runs with deterministic algorithms, because the scatter's float atomics otherwise vary run to run.

Every A/B uses the same binary with reuse off (A) vs 512 MB (B), each process fresh, the order swapping every round (A B, B A, ...), in one benchmark lock. The host was contended at 30–50 % background CPU from other processes (the 25 % load gate timed out), so the numbers are labelled contended.

**Kernel-map time per training batch** (CPU, 5d9c49e): `adaptive_kmap_bench --batch 16 --samples 64 --epochs 4 --depth 3 --modes center`. Each timing is one batch of 16 samples plus its 3 pooled levels, about 110k leaves and ~3M pairs; 6 rounds.

| `--n 2048` (6,917 leaves/sample) | per batch, epochs 2–4 | 111.2 ms [96.9–133.7] | 20.2 ms [18.8–23.8] | **−81.8 %** |

| `--n 256` (6,829 leaves/sample) | per batch, epochs 2–4 | 104.1 ms [94.8–118.8] | 20.8 ms [19.5–24.6] | **−80.1 %** |

Peak memory goes down, most likely because a composed map does not need `build_pairs`' per-thread pair lists. The earlier commit 9547439 (5 rounds) measured −81 % / −84 % later and +5 % / +10 % in the first epoch, with ranges overlapping.

**ML study** (#31 on this branch, integration 460b28d). Adaptive method, 300 train / 200 test samples, 3 epochs, batch 16, 2048 points, seed 1. RTX 2080 SUPER, 4 rounds:

| step time, profiled (12 steps, epoch 2) | 95.4 ms [85.5–106.8] | 74.1 ms [70.0–76.2] | **−22.3 %** |
| kernel map per step | 25.9 ms [21.7–33.6] | 7.8 ms [7.1–9.1] | **−70.0 %** |

| eval throughput (batched test set) | 296 samples/s | 457 samples/s | **+54.8 %** |
| inference latency, batch 1 (median) | 16.1 ms | 13.0 ms | −19.5 % (stored single samples) |
| peak RSS | 1,299 MB | 1,468 MB | +13.0 % |
| peak CUDA allocated / reserved | 459 / 526 MB | 459 / 526 MB | 0 % |
| part store | — | 171.5 MB (5,086 hits / 1,944 misses) | |

The same study on CPU (2 rounds, 9547439, before the one-part and threshold commits): total train time **−15.9 %** (19.4 → 16.3 s), step −24.6 %, kernel map per step −72.5 %, peak RSS +16.4 %, accuracy identical (0.325).

History (kept for the record, CUDA):
- 9cac48b, serial extraction, 3 rounds: epochs 2–3 −20.7 %, epoch 1 +3.6 %.
- 5f84024, parallel extraction, 4 rounds: epochs 2–3 −16.8 %, but **epoch 1 +40.6 %**. In the first epoch a few coarse pooled parts already matched, which sent whole batches down the build-alone path. 5d9c49e fixed this by building parts alone only when they are a small share; epoch 1 is now +12.6 % with overlapping ranges.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

Model results are unchanged by construction, and the deterministic runs above show identical losses and accuracy on CPU and CUDA. In the non-deterministic CUDA A/Bs, accuracy varies between rounds of the *same* arm (0.245–0.29 off, 0.25–0.355 on across series) because of float atomics in the scatters. The only effect on ML is training and evaluation speed (tables above).

## TRADEOFFS

- **Memory.** The store keeps every part seen, up to the budget. In the ML study (500 samples × 4 levels) that is 171 MB and +13 % peak RSS. A smaller budget evicts the least recently used parts, which are then rebuilt, still exactly.
- **First epoch.** It is slower (+13 % in the ML study, +18–33 % kernel-map time in the batch benchmark) because new parts are cut out of the full map and stored. The gain starts with the second time a sample is seen.
- **Opt-in.** Off by default, because workloads that never repeat a sample only pay the first-epoch cost and the memory.
- **Layout.** Samples must be moved by whole level-0 cells along the *first* axis and separated by at least `r` empty cells. Other placements simply find fewer or bigger parts and fall back to normal builds.
- **Modes.** `OverlapWeighted` and `CenterAveraged` are not reused, because their weights come from floating-point overlap volumes.
- Not attempted here: a cheaper build of small new parts (shared node-table scratch), and keeping the composed batch map on the device.
- An idea dropped this round: a padded batched-GEMM CUDA apply_map would have repeated round 4's failed experiment (see #28's comments).

body:
## SUMMARY

`CenterSampled` and `VolumeWeighted` adaptive convolutions read, for every output leaf and kernel offset, the leaf that contains the tap point: the centre of the neighbouring output-level cell. `build_pairs` located that point in floating point (`lo + 0.5 s + offset * s`, then `floor((p - origin) / s)` per level). When the neighbouring cell is split into finer leaves, its centre is **exactly the corner those leaves share**, so the floor sits on a tie. With a voxel size or origin that is not a binary fraction (0.05, 0.1, 0.3 ...), rounding then decides which of the touching leaves the tap reads.

The test suite's own randomized trees (random voxel sizes `0.5 + u` and origins) show how often this happens: **3–16 % of all CenterSampled/VolumeWeighted taps** (table below). In practice:
- which leaf is read depends on rounding noise, not on geometry;
- the same leaves moved by whole cells can get a **different kernel map**. Verified on main f4ac612 with only the new test added: for voxel sizes 0.1 and 0.05 (origin 0.3), 32 of 36 translated copies get a different map. With voxel size 2.0 none do.
- a tap can even land on an empty sibling and drop the pair, while the "upper" sibling would have matched.

This PR resolves those taps on the integer grid. It also makes a kernel map depend only on the leaf keys. A follow-up PR uses that property to reuse kernel maps across training batches.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `kernel_map.cpp`: new `find_containing_center(topology, node_table, cell)`. It walks the present levels coarse to fine with integer keys, the same way `Topology::find_containing` does, but with exact coordinates:
  - at a level `l <= cell.level`, the cell's ancestor (`c >> m`, floor for negatives);
  - at a finer level `l = cell.level + m`, the child whose lower corner is the centre: `c * 2^m + 2^(m-1)`. This is the half-open-cell convention the float code already followed whenever its arithmetic was exact.
  - It stops at the first leaf or empty cell, like `find_containing`. Coordinates are bounded by `Topology::make` (|c| < 2^52 at the finest level), so `c * 2^m` cannot overflow.
- `build_pairs` uses it for `CenterSampled` and `VolumeWeighted`. The tap cell is `output key + offset`, and the float tap point is no longer computed for these modes. `OverlapWeighted` is unchanged: it integrates overlap volumes, with no point location.
- **Behaviour change.** The result is identical whenever the float arithmetic was exact: binary-fraction voxel sizes and origins such as 1, 0.5, 2, 0.0625. It differs only on non-binary grids, and only for taps that sit exactly on a shared corner of finer leaves. There the tap now always reads the leaf whose lower corner is the tap point, instead of whichever leaf rounding picked. Existing models on such grids see a slightly different (now consistent) neighbourhood at those taps.
- Docs: `docs/adaptive.md` describes the tap rule.

| randomized oracle tree (`test_parallel_kmap`) | pairs | taps that change | share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| D=3, shift 0 | 296,316 | 8,153 | 2.8 % |
| D=3, shift -1 / -2 | 20,953 | 2,677 | 12.8 % |
| D=2 (kernel 5), shift 0 | 325,665 | 8,829 | 2.7 % |
| D=2 (kernel 5), shift -1 | 28,173 | 4,623 | 16.4 % |
| D=4, shift 0 | 542,166 | 10,704 | 2.0 % |
| D=4, shift -1 / -2 | 34,144 | 5,675 | 16.6 % |

The same counts hold for `CenterSampled` and `VolumeWeighted`, and `OverlapWeighted` has 0 changes. Every change was audited as a tie: both the old and the new leaf touch the tap point (closed box), or the old answer was an empty sibling. There is no case where either answer is a leaf away from the point.

## TESTING

Tests added or changed:
- `test_parallel_kmap.cpp`, `parallel_kmap_matches_serial_oracle`. The serial oracle now locates CenterSampled/VolumeWeighted taps on the integer grid, with its own `std::map` key lookup, independent of the node table. It also runs the old float location next to it and checks that every difference is a tie (`bad == 0`). It prints the per-case counts in the table above.
- New `test_integer_taps.cpp`:
  - `integer_taps_translation_invariant`: a topology moved by 1, 37 and -1,000,003 level-0 cells gets the identical map. Covers voxel sizes 2.0 (origin 0), 0.1 and 0.05 (origin 0.3), CenterSampled and VolumeWeighted, shifts 0/-1/-2.
  - `integer_taps_coarse_to_fine_reads_upper_child`: a level-0 leaf next to a refined cell. The +x tap reads child (3,1,1) at level 1, on grids 1.0/0 and 0.1/0.3, at x offsets 0, 5 and 123457.

Commands (Windows, native toolchain, see REPRODUCTION):
```
pwsh -File tools\mink-build.ps1 -Src <worktree> -Build <dir> -Cpu -Targets adaptive_tests,adaptive_kmap_bench
<dir>\adaptive_tests.exe
```

| suite | main f4ac612 | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| adaptive_tests CPU | 119 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped | **121 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped** |
| adaptive_tests CUDA | — | the stacked part-reuse branch (#28 + this commit + part reuse, b3555b1): `parallel_kmap_matches_serial_oracle`, `find_containing_matches_level_probe_oracle`, both `integer_taps_*` and every `device_kmap_*` test PASS. 136 passed; the 1 failure was that branch's own new CUDA test, fixed there in d103663 |
| new tests on **main** (f4ac612 + `test_integer_taps.cpp` only) | **2 FAIL** (translation: 32/36 non-binary cases differ, 0 binary; coarse-to-fine read leaf 1 instead of 8) | 2 PASS |
| integration: main + all 22 open itsSio PRs + this PR + part reuse, CPU | — | adaptive 162/0/6, gaussian 75/0/10, core 37/0/15, ctest 9/9 |

## BENCHMARKS

Kernel-map build time: the integer walk replaces per-level floating-point division and floor. The A/B used `ab_compare.py` from #36 (3787b94): each process is fresh, the order inside a pair swaps every pair (A B, B A, ...), and there are 8 timed rounds (4 per order) plus 1 warm-up pair, all in one benchmark lock (09:15–09:17). CPU build, workload `adaptive_kmap_bench --n 20000 --depth 4 --modes center,volume --interp 0 --warmup 2 --reps 7`: 41,376 leaves and 905,482 pairs, **identical on both sides** because the grid is binary. Values are medians of the per-process medians, [min–max] over rounds.

| metric | main f4ac612 | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| kmap CenterSampled, cold (fresh topology) | 37.6 ms [30.0–54.7] | 34.5 ms [29.5–42.1] | −8.5 % |
| kmap CenterSampled, warm (lookup table built) | 35.7 ms [23.7–58.0] | 24.0 ms [19.2–38.9] | **−32.7 %** |
| kmap VolumeWeighted, cold | 34.6 ms [31.9–45.6] | 27.3 ms [21.3–34.0] | **−20.9 %** |
| kmap VolumeWeighted, warm | 28.0 ms [22.2–48.4] | 22.9 ms [17.4–25.1] | −18.2 % |
| process CPU time | 7.04 s [6.78–7.20] | 5.76 s [5.14–6.14] | **−18.2 %** (ranges disjoint) |
| process wall time | 1.88 s [1.54–2.38] | 1.52 s [1.39–1.71] | −18.8 % |
| peak working set | 175.7 MB | 175.5 MB | −0.1 % (noise) |
| GPU memory / kernel time | n/a | n/a | kernel maps are built on the host; CUDA apply is unchanged |

The host was contended: the 25 % load gate timed out at about 40–48 % background CPU from other processes, so absolute times are pessimistic and most ranges overlap. All medians moved in the same direction, and the process CPU-time ranges do not overlap.

*History.* The first A/B (08:40, 6 rounds) accidentally used a harness copy that always ran main first. It gave center cold −29.1 %, center warm −15.8 %, volume cold −8.4 %, volume warm −19.8 % and CPU time −22.7 %. Those numbers were in the first version of this description. They are superseded by the order-balanced run above, and kept here for the record.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a. The ML study's grid (voxel size 0.5, origin -1) is a binary fraction, where maps are unchanged.

## TRADEOFFS

- This is a behaviour change on non-binary grids, as described above. It is limited to ties, but it is visible: a model trained on main with voxel size 0.05 gets a slightly different neighbourhood at those taps after this change. Binary-fraction grids are bit-identical.
- `OverlapWeighted`, `Topology::find_containing` (used by interpolation and the CenterAveraged proposal #19) and interpolation are untouched.
- PR #19 (CenterAveraged) conflicts textually in the same `else` branch. In our integration branch it resolves by doing CenterAveraged's first lookup with the integer tap too. Its averaging branch triggers in the same cases, because a tie always resolves to a finer leaf or nothing.

## REPRODUCTION

## SUMMARY

Memory-safety and memory-leak testing for the native suites:

- `memory_growth_tests` (new CTest target, label `memory`): repeated forward + backward of sparse convolution,
  adaptive convolution / interpolation / pooling and Gaussian rendering, on CPU and CUDA, checking that process
  memory and CUDA allocated memory stop growing after a warm-up, plus self-checks that a planted per-iteration
  leak is detected.
- `tests/run_sanitizers.ps1`: one runner for NVIDIA compute-sanitizer (memcheck with leak check, racecheck,
  initcheck, synccheck), MSVC AddressSanitizer builds, and plain/uncached CUDA runs, with a per-job summary CSV.
- The test framework flushes each result line and the summary, so a suite that hangs or is killed (CTest timeout,
  sanitizer wrapper) still shows how far it got.

Result of the round: no ASan report and no CUDA device fault in the suites, no memory growth on any workload;
two real bugs found and fixed separately (#37 CMake source filter, #38 CUDA prune of an empty tensor) and the
`core_tests` exit hang root-caused (fix pushed to #12). compute-sanitizer itself could not run on the test host
(details below). **Stacked on #37** (the worktree path contains "test", which #37 fixes); the diff of this PR
alone is the `tests/` files and the `memory_growth_tests` block in `CMakeLists.txt`.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

`tests/memory/test_memory_growth.cpp` (12 cases):
- Each case runs `MINK_MEMORY_WARMUP` (30) warm-up and `MINK_MEMORY_ITERS` (120) measured iterations, sampling
  after every iteration (CUDA synchronized): process private bytes and working set (`GetProcessMemoryInfo`;
  `/proc/self/statm` elsewhere) and the c10 caching allocator's current allocated bytes (`allocated_bytes[0]`, index
  literal so it compiles with older LibTorch where `StatType` moved).
- Growth = median of the last 10 samples minus median of the first 10. Tolerances: CUDA allocated <= 16 KiB (steady
  state is exact; one leaked tensor per iteration is >= ~50 KiB), CPU private bytes <= 4 MiB, working set <= 16 MiB.
- Workloads: `sparse_conv` (new `SparseTensor` / coordinate manager each iteration, stride-1 + stride-2 conv,
  backward), `adaptive_conv` (fresh voxelize + refine each iteration, kernel-map cache capacity 4 so LRU eviction is
  exercised and full after warm-up), `adaptive_interp` (nearest + multilinear), `adaptive_pool` (mean, max, global),
  `gaussian_render` (2000 splats, 77x45, fused CPU / CUDA rasterizer, backward to all inputs).
- `memory_growth_detects_planted_{cpu,cuda}_leak` retain 128 KiB (CPU) / 1 KiB (CUDA) per iteration and require the
  detector to flag it. Cases skip under AddressSanitizer (its quarantine grows memory by design).

`tests/run_sanitizers.ps1 -BuildDir <dir> -OutDir <dir> -Jobs <tool>:<suite>[:<filter>],...`:
- tools `memcheck|racecheck|initcheck|synccheck` (compute-sanitizer; `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1` so each tensor
  is its own allocation), `plain` (`CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` + uncached allocator), `run`, `asan`.
- Statuses: `done`, `TIMEOUT`, `EXIT-HANG` (summary printed, process did not exit within `-ExitGraceSec`),
  `SANITIZER-UNAVAILABLE` (Windows/WDDM without the GPU debugger interface: the suite would otherwise run unchecked
  and look clean), `NO-SUMMARY`. Timed-out jobs are killed through the runner's own process handle.

## TESTING

Memory growth, CUDA build (CUDA 13.4.3, sm_75), 30 warm-up + 120 iterations:

| case | device | private bytes growth (MB) | working set growth (MB) | CUDA allocated at start (KiB) | CUDA allocated growth (B) | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sparse_conv | cpu | 0.09 | 0.01 | - | - | PASS |
| sparse_conv | cuda | -28.37 | 0.00 | 90 | 0 | PASS |
| adaptive_conv | cpu | 0.57 | -1.38 | - | - | PASS |
| adaptive_conv | cuda | 0.10 | -1.80 | 6 | 0 | PASS |
| adaptive_interp | cpu | 0.06 | -0.47 | - | - | PASS |
| adaptive_interp | cuda | 0.00 | -0.35 | 164 | 0 | PASS |
| adaptive_pool | cpu | 0.00 | -0.04 | - | - | PASS |
| adaptive_pool | cuda | -0.69 | -0.75 | 70 | 0 | PASS |
| gaussian_render | cpu | 0.00 | 0.49 | - | - | PASS |
| gaussian_render | cuda | -0.11 | -0.88 | 110 | 0 | PASS |
| planted leak 128 KiB/iter | cpu | 35.07 | 13.79 | - | - | detected (PASS) |
| planted leak 1 KiB/iter | cuda | 0.03 | 0.04 | 36 | 112,640 | detected (PASS) |

An earlier run (64 KiB planted CPU leak) measured `adaptive_conv` cpu at +3.4 MB private (+0.57 MB in the run
above) and the planted leak at only +5.0 MB, which is why the planted leak was raised to 128 KiB; CPU growth below
~40 KiB per iteration is within the tolerance at the default count (raise `MINK_MEMORY_ITERS` for a finer check).

Suites (this branch + #37 + #38's fix in the same build directory):

| suite | CUDA build | CPU_ONLY + MSVC ASan (RelWithDebInfo, /fsanitize=address) |
|---|---|---|
| adaptive_tests | 111 / 0 / 0 (127 s) | 106 / 0 / 2 skipped (CUDA-only), **0 ASan reports**, EXIT-HANG |
| gaussian_tests | 42 / 0 / 0 (42 s) | 36 / 0 / 4 skipped, **0 ASan reports**, EXIT-HANG |
| memory_growth_tests | 12 / 0 / 0 (73 s) | growth cases skipped under ASan by this PR (before the skip: quarantine growth, e.g. sparse_conv +269 MB) |
| cmake_source_filter (#37) | Passed | - |

Snapshot of the integration head e1af851 (main 3524eff + 18 PRs), CUDA, "plain" mode
(`CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`, uncached allocator): adaptive 147/0/0, gaussian 81/0/0, core 44/0/0, 0 device faults.

compute-sanitizer 2026.3.0 (CUDA 13.4.3) on the test host: every tool prints `Failed to initialize WDDM debugger
interface. Please run EnableDebuggerInterface.bat as an administrator` + `Device not supported` and runs the
target unchecked (the 2 "errors" in each ERROR SUMMARY are these; racecheck additionally crashed the target). The
account is not an administrator, so **no compute-sanitizer coverage was obtained**; the runner now reports this as
`SANITIZER-UNAVAILABLE`. A static review of the project's CUDA code (raster forward/backward, gaussian kernels,
adaptive topology, thrust policy, the #28 device kernel-map path) found no confirmed out-of-bounds or race; it led
to #38.

ASan notes: built with `/D_DISABLE_VECTOR_ANNOTATION /D_DISABLE_STRING_ANNOTATION` (LibTorch is not instrumented;
avoids container-overflow false positives) and `/Z7` (sccache cannot cache `/Zi`). Every ASan suite process hangs
after printing its summary, also with zero tests selected (`adaptive_tests zzz`), one thread spinning; unaffected by
`ASAN_OPTIONS` (detect_leaks, windows_hook_rtl_allocators, alloc_dealloc_mismatch, detect_stack_use_after_return,
quarantine_size_mb) or `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`. Treated as an ASan + LibTorch teardown artifact (`EXIT-HANG`), not a
library bug.

Commands:
```
memory_growth_tests                                   # or: ctest -L memory
pwsh -File tests/run_sanitizers.ps1 -BuildDir <cuda build> -OutDir out -KeepCachingAllocator -Jobs run:memory_growth_tests
pwsh -File tests/run_sanitizers.ps1 -BuildDir <cuda build> -OutDir out -Jobs memcheck:core_tests,plain:adaptive_tests
pwsh -File tests/run_sanitizers.ps1 -BuildDir <asan cpu build> -OutDir out -TimeoutMin 40 -Jobs asan:adaptive_tests,asan:gaussian_tests
```

## BENCHMARKS

n/a: tests only. Cost: `memory_growth_tests` takes 73-80 s on the CUDA build (CPU + CUDA cases).

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a.

## TRADEOFFS

- CPU growth is measured from process counters, so small CPU leaks (< ~40 KiB per iteration at the default count)
  are below the tolerance; CUDA allocated bytes are exact. MSVC ASan has no LeakSanitizer.
- The growth test runs ~75 s in the default CTest run; set `MINK_MEMORY_ITERS` lower for quick runs (the planted CPU
  leak check needs the default count to clear its tolerance).
- No compute-sanitizer results on this host (needs an administrator to enable the debugger interface once); on
  Linux/Docker the runner's compute-sanitizer jobs work unchanged.
- Flushing each result line costs nothing measurable.

## REPRODUCTION

- Branch `test/memory-sanitizers` (on #37), commits fe36db7, fb47356, 00ca387, 7b9899e, c52a3d4, 7dbbcc0.
- Raw outputs: `mink-lab/results/testing-r4/` (cuda/run2, asan/main4, cs/e1af851, core-hang).
- Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44,
  CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors
  `docker/cuda-profile.sh`. Host load: other agents' builds and benchmarks ran concurrently.

## SUMMARY

`MinkowskiPruning` on CUDA failed on an empty sparse tensor (for example pruning again after an earlier pruning
removed every row): `CoordinateMapGPU::prune` read `d_inclusive_scan[N - 1]` with `N == 0`, i.e. one element before
a zero-size buffer, and `cudaMemcpy` threw `invalid argument at .../coordinate_map_gpu.cu:1089`. The CPU path
already handled it. An empty map now prunes to an empty map on CUDA too. Found by the memory-safety testing round
(static review of out-of-bounds index arithmetic, then confirmed by a regression test).

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `MinkowskiEngine/src/coordinate_map_gpu.cu`, `CoordinateMapGPU::prune`: early return for `N == 0` with an empty
  map that reserves one hash slot (`reserve(0)` would leave `m_map` null, which later `*m_map` uses would
  dereference) and `m_size = 0` (`m_size` is not initialised by the constructor).
- Before the fix the pointer `d_inclusive_scan + N - 1` was formed from the allocator's zero-size result; with the
  caching allocator that is a null pointer minus 4 bytes, so the copy errored instead of silently reading memory,
  but it is an out-of-bounds access either way.
- Pre-existing upstream code (unchanged since the original MinkowskiEngine port); no other caller changes.

## TESTING

New tests in `tests/adaptive/test_regression.cpp` (run with `adaptive_tests`):
`regression_pruning_to_empty_and_again` (CPU) and `regression_pruning_to_empty_and_again_cuda`: prune all 50 rows,
prune the empty result again, check 0 rows / 3 channels, backprop through both prunes (gradient defined and zero).

| test / suite (CUDA build, RTX 2080 SUPER) | before (af118a4) | after (a79a3b0) |
|---|---|---|
| regression_pruning_to_empty_and_again (CPU) | PASS | PASS |
| regression_pruning_to_empty_and_again_cuda | FAIL: `invalid argument at coordinate_map_gpu.cu:1089` | PASS |
| adaptive_tests (full, CUDA build) | not run on the unfixed build | 111 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped |
| gaussian_tests (CUDA build) | not run on the unfixed build | 42 / 0 / 0 |
| memory_growth_tests (CUDA build, from the companion test PR) | 12 / 0 / 0 | 12 / 0 / 0 |

Commands: `adaptive_tests regression_pruning`, `adaptive_tests`, `gaussian_tests` from the build directory.
The verification build also carried PR #37 (CMake source filter, needed because the checkout path contains
"test") and the memory-test branch (test infrastructure only). CPU_ONLY: the change is in a `.cu` file that a
CPU_ONLY build does not compile; the CPU regression test passes in the CUDA build's CPU path.

## BENCHMARKS

n/a: the change only adds an early return for an input size that previously threw; the N > 0 path is unchanged.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a.

## TRADEOFFS

- The empty result reserves one hash slot (a few bytes of device memory) so that later kernel-map code sees a
  valid hash table, matching how an emptied map (N > 0, nothing kept) already looks.
- compute-sanitizer could not be used to confirm the access on this host (Windows WDDM needs the GPU debugger
  interface, which requires an administrator), so the evidence is the CUDA error plus the index arithmetic.

## REPRODUCTION

- Branch `fix/prune-empty-cuda`, commit a79a3b0 on af118a4.
- `cmake --build <build> --target adaptive_tests` then `adaptive_tests regression_pruning`.
- Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44,
  CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors
  `docker/cuda-profile.sh`.

## SUMMARY

The library globs in `CMakeLists.txt` return absolute paths, and the test/example exclusions
(`list(FILTER ... EXCLUDE REGEX ".*test.*")` / `".*example.*"`) were applied to the whole path. Any checkout whose
path contains `test` or `example` (for example `~/latest/Minkowski4CPP`, `C:/tests/...`, `/srv/examples/...`)
therefore built a `minkowski_cpp` that contained only the Gaussian sources (they are appended after the filter),
and every executable failed to link. This PR matches the exclusions against the file name only and adds a CTest
check for the regex.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- One `MINK_SOURCE_EXCLUDE_REGEX` = `/[^/]*(test|example)[^/]*$` drives both the CPU and the GPU source filters
  (same intent as before: drop `*test*` / `*example*` files; no file under `MinkowskiEngine/` matches today).
- New CTest case `cmake_source_filter` runs `tests/cmake/check_source_filter.cmake` with that regex: paths whose
  directories contain `test`/`latest`/`examples`/`tests` must be kept, `test_*.cpp`, `*_test.cu`, `example_*.cpp`,
  `*tests.cpp` file names must be dropped. The old pattern fails it (drops 3 library sources, keeps

## SUMMARY

Adds `benchmarks/ab_compare.py`, a one-command A/B harness that runs the **same benchmark executable from two build
directories** alternately (A B A B ...) and reports original vs candidate side by side, with the cold start (whole
process) separated from the benchmark's own warm timings, plus peak working set, CPU time and GPU utilization /
memory sampled during every run. The benchmarks merged so far (`adaptive_vs_uniform_bench` #17,
`gaussian_render_bench` #25, `gaussian_bench`, `gaussian_ply_bench`) each time one build; comparing two builds fairly
on a shared machine needed ad-hoc scripts. Standard-library Python only; no library code changes.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `python benchmarks/ab_compare.py --a base=BUILD_A --b new=BUILD_B --out DIR --name NAME [--rounds 5]
  [--warmup-rounds 1] [--budget-s S] [--load-gate PCT] [--extract key=REGEX] -- EXE [args...]`
- One fresh process per run, interleaved, so slow drift in machine load hits both sides equally. Per process:
  - `wall_ms`: whole-process elapsed time = cold start (DLL load, CUDA context, first calls) + run.
  - `peak_ws_mb`, `cpu_s`, `cpu_cores`: `GetProcessMemoryInfo` / `GetProcessTimes` on the exited process (Windows).
  - `gpu_util_mean`, `gpu_util_max`, `gpu_mem_max_mb`: `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used -lms 200`
    during the process (device-wide; other GPU processes are included and are logged per block).
  - every `key   value` stdout line (the existing benches' format), every number of the JSON file the benchmark
    writes when an argument contains `{json}` (list items keyed by name/device/count), and `--extract` regexes for
    free-form output such as `train`'s epoch time. `{tmp}` gives each process its own scratch directory.
- Resumable: `NAME.json` keeps every run; calling again appends rounds until `--rounds` timed rounds exist.
  `--budget-s` stops before a pair that would not fit and exits 3, so long comparisons can be split into short
  exclusive-benchmark windows; it never stops between A and B. `--load-gate` waits (bounded, 3 x 30 s) for total
  CPU load to fall under a threshold and records the samples.
- Output: `NAME.md` (median [min-max] per side, % change, constants that must match listed once, keys present on one
  side only), raw stdout per run, `nvidia-smi` samples per run, GPU process snapshots before/after each block.
- `EXE` ending in `.py` runs with the current interpreter (used by the self-test; also handy for script benches).

## TESTING

- New `tests/tools/test_ab_compare.py` (unittest, 6 cases: interleaving + warm-up exclusion + stdout/JSON/regex
  parsing + Markdown row; resume adds only missing rounds; budget stop exits 3 and never splits a pair; a failing
  candidate exits 1; a changed command is rejected; stdout parser). Registered in CTest as `ab_compare_selftest` when
  CMake finds a Python 3 interpreter (`find_package(Python3 COMPONENTS Interpreter QUIET)`), otherwise skipped.

| check | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `python -I tests/tools/test_ab_compare.py` | n/a (new) | 6 passed / 0 failed |
| `ctest -N` (CPU_ONLY configure of this branch) | 4 tests | 5 tests (`ab_compare_selftest` added) |
| `ctest -R ab_compare_selftest` | n/a | Passed (14.2 s) |

No C++ source changed, so the existing suites are unaffected (configure-only check; nothing rebuilt).

## BENCHMARKS

The harness itself changes no runtime. Measured with it (Windows host below, `-Kind bench` exclusive lock, 5 timed
interleaved rounds, contended host: CPU load 45-69 % from other services) — upstream `f93b7bc` vs the lab integration
head `e1af851` (main `3524eff` + open PRs incl. #28), `adaptive_kmap_bench --conv cuda --n 20000 --depth 4
--channels 8 --cout 16 --modes center,volume --warmup 3 --reps 10`:

| metric | f93b7bc median [min-max] | e1af851 median [min-max] | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| process wall (cold start + run) | 2176 [1829-2275] ms | 1218 [1080-1503] ms | -44.1 % |
| first conv after map build (cold), CenterSampled | 38.70 [37.72-43.83] ms | 45.59 [36.24-50.93] ms | +17.8 % |
| conv fwd CenterSampled (warm) | 4.84 [4.58-5.94] ms | 1.75 [1.49-1.79] ms | -63.7 % |
| conv fwd+bwd CenterSampled (warm) | 15.69 [11.89-16.49] ms | 5.30 [4.75-6.06] ms | -66.2 % |
| CUDA max reserved | 128 MB | 302 MB | +135.9 % |
| process peak working set | 620.1 MB | 583.7 MB | -5.9 % |

Validation: the externally measured peak working set equals the benches' own `peak_working_set_mb` /
`peak_rss_mib` to 0.01 MB in all three workloads checked (adaptive CUDA conv, adaptive CPU kmap, core CPU conv).
Harness overhead: one `nvidia-smi` sampler process per run (disable with `--gpu-sample-ms 0`).

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a (tooling only).

## TRADEOFFS

- GPU utilization and memory are device-wide (`nvidia-smi` cannot attribute per process on Windows/WDDM); on a
  shared GPU use the benchmark's CUDA-event timings and allocator peaks for your own cost. Documented in the README.
- Peak working set / CPU time are Windows-only (the keys are absent elsewhere); everything else is portable.
- Process-level warm-up rounds only warm file caches; steady state is the benchmark's own in-process warm-up.
- The load gate uses `typeperf` (Windows); elsewhere it is skipped.

## REPRODUCTION

```powershell
python -I tests/tools/test_ab_compare.py
cmake -S . -B build-cpu -G Ninja -DCPU_ONLY=ON -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<libtorch> ; ctest --test-dir build-cpu -R ab_compare_selftest
python benchmarks/ab_compare.py --a base=<build-f93b7bc> --b new=<build-e1af851> --out ab --name conv20k --rounds 5 -- `
  adaptive_kmap_bench --conv cuda --n 20000 --depth 4 --channels 8 --cout 16 --modes center,volume --warmup 3 --reps 10
```

Commits: this branch `perf/ab-compare-harness` off main `af118a4`. Benchmarked builds: `f93b7bc` (`adaptive_kmap_bench`
from `f93b7bc` + the bench file only) and `e1af851`. Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB
sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test
host; the native toolchain mirrors `docker/cuda-profile.sh`. Upstream CI builds `docker/Dockerfile` for this PR.

> **Stacked on #20** (`feat/adaptive-drop-empty`, head `036eadd`). This branch contains #20's commits. Until #20 merges, the diff below includes #20. The fallback-only diff is `036eadd..4b99f95`: `ops.{hpp,cpp}`, `adaptive_tensor.hpp` (1 doc line), `docs/adaptive.md`, `tests/adaptive/test_interp_fallback.cpp`, `tests/adaptive/bench_adaptive_kmap.cpp`, and `CMakeLists.txt` (+1 line).

## SUMMARY

`drop_empty` refinement (#20) removes point-free children, and `interpolate()` returns zeros for every point in that removed space. This PR adds an opt-in `InterpFallback::CoarserAncestor`. With it, a point that no leaf contains gets the volume-weighted mean of the leaves inside its **finest occupied ancestor cell** instead of 0. It was proposed in the #20 TRADEOFFS / findings.

On the 25 dataset x method cases of the adaptive vs uniform benchmark (CPU, depth 4, 100k points, `--drop-empty`):
* Held-out **coverage returns exactly to the default (no `drop_empty`) value in all 25 cases.** Example: variance refinement on `ply` goes 0.601 -> **0.991**, and the default is 0.991.
* Nearest held-out nRMSE with `drop_empty` + fallback is back to within -12.9 % / +2.5 % of the default. Without the fallback it is up to +73 % worse. It is often *better* than the default, e.g. `clustered a_dens4` 0.473 default, 0.571 drop, **0.419** drop+fallback.
* Covered points are unchanged in both modes, and the default `InterpFallback::Zero` is unchanged.
* Cost: only uncovered points pay. See BENCHMARKS for the interleaved Zero vs CoarserAncestor latency.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

* API: `enum class InterpFallback { Zero, CoarserAncestor }` and `interpolate(input, points, mode = Nearest, fallback = Zero)`. Feature-test macro `MINK_ADAPTIVE_HAS_INTERP_FALLBACK`. Works with both `Nearest` and `Multilinear`.
* Definitions:
  * A cell "holds data" when at least one active leaf lies strictly inside it.
  * Below the coarsest present level, `AncestorIndex` answers that with the topology node table (#15, `kInternal`).
  * Above it, it answers with a small hash set of leaf ancestors (at most one entry per occupied coarse cell).
  * For an uncovered point, the walk goes from level 0 down until a cell no longer holds data. The last cell that did is the point's ancestor.
  * Points whose level-0 cell holds no leaf still get zeros.
* Aggregation:
  * Uncovered points are collected per worker block.
  * Cells get rows in first-use (serial point) order, and leaves contribute in index order. The result therefore does not depend on the number of blocks.
  * One pass over the leaves walks each leaf's ancestors between the lowest and highest fallback level and accumulates volume weights.
  * Output = sparse weights x features, so it is differentiable w.r.t. the features. CUDA features are supported (weights on CPU).
* `adaptive_kmap_bench --drop-empty 1` refines with `drop_empty` and reports the covered fraction with and without the fallback. It also reports `interp_<mode>_{zero,ancestor}_il_ms`: Zero and CoarserAncestor timed **interleaved**, alternating order every repetition.
* The adaptive vs uniform bench reports `coverage_fallback`, `nrmse_nearest_all_fallback` and `rmse_multilinear_all_fallback` once this macro exists: separate PR `test/adaptive-bench-fallback-metrics`.
* History:
  * `9ede74f` feature;
  * `1a6a977` fixes two test fixtures (a query that was inside a leaf; gradient rows looked up by key);
  * `84e1dfc` bench timing;
  * `4b99f95` merges #20 `036eadd` (contains main `af118a4`). Conflicts: CMake test list, and the `docs/adaptive.md` interpolation paragraph (kept #9's Multilinear note + the fallback sentence).

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_interp_fallback.cpp`, 7 tests:
* `interp_fallback_default_is_zero_and_unchanged`
* `interp_fallback_hand_computed_values`
* `interp_fallback_gradients`
* `interp_fallback_matches_brute_force_after_drop_empty` (brute-force oracle)

## SUMMARY

Test-only follow-up to the merged #17 (adaptive vs uniform benchmark). When the library provides them, the benchmark also reports:
* **`--sphere`**: every target accuracy with both `SphereErrorMetric::SignedVolume` and `::Geometric` (#29, merged). Each row gets a `"metric"` field. Unreachable targets are reported as an `"error"` row instead of aborting the run.
* **accuracy**: `coverage_fallback`, `nrmse_nearest_all_fallback`, `rmse_multilinear_all_fallback` and `interp_nearest_fallback_ms` with `InterpFallback::CoarserAncestor`, from the interp-fallback PR (stacked on #20).

Both are behind the libraries' feature-test macros (`MINK_SPHERE_HAS_ERROR_METRIC`, `MINK_ADAPTIVE_HAS_INTERP_FALLBACK`), so the bench builds on main today. The fallback keys appear once that PR lands. No library change.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

One file: `tests/adaptive/bench_adaptive_vs_uniform.cpp` (+47 / -1).
* `accuracy()`: `#ifdef MINK_ADAPTIVE_HAS_INTERP_FALLBACK` re-runs Nearest (all held-out points) and Multilinear (first `ml_queries`) with `CoarserAncestor` on the same queries. Coverage uses a ones-feature tensor.
* `sphere_analysis()`: loops over the metric list (`signed_volume` only without the macro). It catches `std::runtime_error` from `voxelize_sphere`, which is "target accuracy not reachable within limits".
* Commit `d017b15` = `d6998cd` (written on #17's `e633b9b`) cherry-picked onto main `af118a4`. The fallback path was compiled and run in an integration build (`2c3e406`, with the fallback branch). On this branch alone only the sphere path is active.

body:
## SUMMARY

Adds an opt-in interpolation mode `InterpMode::ContinuousMultilinear` for `adaptive::interpolate()`. Its result is **continuous across leaf-level changes**. `Multilinear` jumps there: its averaging box takes the containing leaf's size, so the box size jumps when the level does (documented in #9, e.g. 1/6 -> 0 in 2-D).

* Continuity: 8 adaptive trees (2-D/3-D, up to 209k leaves), 7,725 level-change face crossings. With `Multilinear` the largest jump is 0.055-0.28 (field range = 1). With `ContinuousMultilinear` it is **<= 5.4e-9** (float64 evaluation noise) and no crossing jumps more than 1e-6.
* It is identical to `Multilinear` on single-level neighbourhoods. Against smooth analytic fields on mixed-level trees its error is **higher**: nRMSE +8 % to +267 %, still below Nearest. On the held-out points of the 5 adaptive-vs-uniform benchmark datasets it is within -3.2 % / +3.1 % of `Multilinear`. See TRADEOFFS.
* Latency: about the same as `Multilinear`. Over 14 interleaved runs the median per-run ratio is +16 %, with a spread of -44 % to +57 %, measured on a contended host. Peak working set +3.1 % (229.5 -> 236.7 MB at 200k queries).
* `Nearest` / `Multilinear` code and defaults are unchanged. The new enum value is appended.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

* `ops.hpp`: `enum class InterpMode { Nearest, Multilinear, ContinuousMultilinear }`, and the `interpolate()` doc comment describes the new mode. `ops.cpp` dispatches to a separate `interpolate_tent` at the top of `interpolate()`. The existing paths are not touched.
* Weights: leaf i (centre `c_i`, edge `s_i`) gets the tensor-product tent `phi_i(x) = prod_d max(0, 1 - |x_d - c_id| / s_id)`. The result is `sum_i phi_i(x) v_i / sum_i phi_i(x)` for points inside an active leaf. Every `phi_i` is continuous, and the containing leaf has `phi >= 2^-D`, so the denominator never vanishes inside the leaves. Consequences:
  * continuous everywhere inside the union of leaves;
  * constants are reproduced exactly;
  * equal to `Multilinear` wherever every leaf that reaches the point has the containing leaf's level.
* Candidates per level l: the cells `floor(a)` and `floor(a)+1` per axis, with `a = (x - o)/s_l - 1/2` (at most 2^D per level), looked up in the topology node table (#15). The descent starts at the coarsest present level. It stops below the first level whose candidates contain no internal node, because finer candidates lie inside coarser ones.
* Parallel deterministic blocks (as in #23). Empty input, or no hit, returns zeros that stay connected to autograd (as in #8). Linear in the features, so differentiable. The weights are computed on the CPU; features may live on CUDA.
* Docs: `docs/adaptive.md` (formula and properties, next to #9's note on the Multilinear jump) and the `docs/api.md` table. `adaptive_kmap_bench` also prints `interp_continuous_ms`.
* History:
  * `b0629c3` feature, on main 3524eff;
  * `88b165c` merges main 1ace388;
  * `8c5c125` merges main af118a4.
  
  Merge conflicts were only the CMake test list and the test-target `foreach`. The PR diff to `CMakeLists.txt` is only the new lines: main's three LF-only lines are kept byte-identical.

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_continuous_interp.cpp`, 10 tests registered in `adaptive_tests`:
* level-change example and brute-force oracle;
* parallel determinism;
* reproduces constants;
* equals Multilinear (single level, and uniform neighbourhoods);
* continuity across levels;
* gradcheck;
* empty / outside points;
* CPU vs CUDA agreement.

New eval tool `adaptive_interp_eval` (`tests/adaptive/bench_adaptive_interp.cpp`; not a test): continuity / accuracy / latency / peak working set.

| suite | main af118a4 (before) | this PR 8c5c125 (after) |
|---|---|---|
| CPU `adaptive_tests` | 102 / 0 / 1 | **111 / 0 / 2** (+9 pass; `continuous_interp_cpu_cuda_agreement` skips without CUDA) |
| CPU `gaussian_tests` | 36 / 0 / 4 | 36 / 0 / 4 (CUDA-only skips) |

"Before" is main af118a4 as measured on `test/adaptive-bench-fallback-metrics` (main + a bench-only change): 102/0/1. The CUDA run of this exact merged head comes with the lead's round-4 integration, and the lead will comment the result here.

## BENCHMARKS

## TRADEOFFS

* **Accuracy vs continuity.** Across level changes the tent partition is a Shepard-type weighted average and does not reproduce linear fields. `Multilinear` is closer to exact inside a level.
  * On mixed-level trees with smooth analytic fields, nRMSE is +8 % to +267 % higher than `Multilinear`. The worst case is 3-D gauss refined: 0.0043 vs 0.0012 (Nearest 0.0056).
  * It is equal to `Multilinear` on single-level trees.
  * The max error is sometimes much lower, because there is no jump error: front refined 0.015 vs 0.051 (2-D) and 0.022 vs 0.049 (3-D).
  
  This is why the mode is opt-in. Use it when continuity matters (smooth fields across resolution changes, gradients w.r.t. the query position), not as a drop-in accuracy upgrade.
* Latency is roughly that of `Multilinear` (median +16 %; contended measurements with a wide spread). It looks up up to 2^D candidates per present level.
* Defined only for points inside active leaves; points outside get zeros, as in the other modes. The stacked interp-fallback PR handles uncovered points and also changes `ops.hpp` / `interpolate()`. Both PRs touch the same `interpolate()` dispatch (enum, signature, `ops.cpp` entry, `adaptive_kmap_bench`), so whichever lands second needs the other merged in. A tested combined resolution is on the fork as `scratch/interp-both` (`9e9d339`, CPU adaptive_tests 129/0/2, ctest 4/4). There, `ContinuousMultilinear` also honours `InterpFallback::CoarserAncestor`, covered by the new test `interp_fallback_continuous_mode`.
* Both bench rounds ran on a contended host and both are reported. No failed method attempts.

* Commands: see TESTING. Seeds are deterministic (default `--seed 1`).

body:
## SUMMARY
`build-and-publish (124)` fails on every open PR, and on any branch that contains main since #15/#25. Two benchmark sources on main use `c10::CachingAllocator::StatType`. That name does not exist in LibTorch 2.5.1, which the CUDA 12.4 Docker profile uses:

```
tests/adaptive/bench_adaptive_kmap.cpp:213:20: error: 'c10::CachingAllocator' has not been declared
tests/adaptive/bench_adaptive_kmap.cpp:214:46: error: 'StatType' has not been declared
```

(from https://github.com/QuiteLiterallyConnor/Minkowski4CPP/actions/runs/41348424341/job/124973160956). `benchmarks/gaussian_render_bench.cpp:118` has the same spelling. This PR switches both files to `c10::CachingDeviceAllocator::StatType::AGGREGATE`, which resolves in both LibTorch versions. 2 files, +6/-3 lines, no behaviour change.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS
- LibTorch **2.5.1** (`docker/cuda-profile.sh`, profile 124): `c10/core/CachingDeviceAllocator.h` defines `namespace c10::CachingDeviceAllocator { enum struct StatType : uint64_t { AGGREGATE = 0, ... } }`. There is no `c10::CachingAllocator::StatType`.
- LibTorch **2.15.0** (profiles 132/134): `StatType` moved to `c10::CachingAllocator`, and `c10::CachingDeviceAllocator` re-exports it with `using namespace c10::CachingAllocator;`. Qualified lookup through that using-directive finds `c10::CachingDeviceAllocator::StatType`.
- `getDeviceStats` already returns `c10::CachingDeviceAllocator::DeviceStats` in both versions, so the new spelling is the one that matches the stats type.

## TESTING
- Compile check with LibTorch 2.15.0 + CUDA 13.4.3 (MSVC 19.44): both changed translation units compile with the exact compiler command lines of a CUDA build tree (`ninja -t commands`), exit 0.
- LibTorch 2.5.1 is not installed on our test host. Its header layout was checked against the v2.5.1 sources (`c10/core/CachingDeviceAllocator.h`, `c10/cuda/CUDACachingAllocator.h`). The `build-and-publish (124)` job of this PR is the end-to-end check.
- No test sources change. The two files only print peak-memory fields.

| check | before (main 1ace388) | after |
|---|---|---|
| CI `build-and-publish (124)` | fails (`c10::CachingAllocator` not declared) | see this PR's CI run |
| CI `build-and-publish (132)` / `(134)` | pass | expected pass (same code path compiled locally with 2.15) |
| local compile, LibTorch 2.15 cu134 | ok | ok (both TUs) |

## BENCHMARKS
n/a: this is a compile fix. The printed peak-memory values are the same array element (`AGGREGATE = 0`) as before.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS
n/a.

## TRADEOFFS
None known. If a future LibTorch drops the `c10::CachingDeviceAllocator` re-export, these lines would need `c10::CachingAllocator::StatType` again. Open PRs that add new benchmark files with the old spelling need the same one-line change: #26 `gaussian_adaptive_bench.cpp` and the ML study PR `ml_representations.cpp` already have it.

## REPRODUCTION
- Commit 4bb14b7 on top of upstream main 1ace388.
- `docker/docker-build.sh` with profile 124 (CI), or natively with LibTorch 2.15: `cmake --build build --target adaptive_kmap_bench gaussian_render_bench`.
- Hardware for the local compile check: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors docker/cuda-profile.sh.
