body:
> **Stacked on #26** (`feat/gaussian-adaptive-bridge`). The base is `main`, so until #26 merges this diff also contains #26's bridge code. The ML-only part is 5 files (+1508 lines): `benchmarks/ml_representations.cpp`, `benchmarks/ml_representations_smoke.cmake`, `benchmarks/ml_representations_summary.py`, `benchmarks/test_ml_representations_summary.py` and a CMake block. To review only that part, diff `fc913cb..171689d`.

## SUMMARY
This PR adds a reproducible experiment that compares four input representations on the same 3-D shape classification task. All four use the same data, training budget and evaluation:

| method | representation | network |
|---|---|---|
| `uniform` | points -> uniform sparse voxels 32^3 (cell 0.0625) | `MinkowskiConvolution` net (8 convs, 3 stride-2 stages) |
| `adaptive` | points -> `AdaptiveSparseTensor` (levels 0..3, `refine_by_density(12)`) | `adaptive_convolution` net (8 convs, 3 `adaptive_pool` stages) |
| `gaussian` | points -> adaptive Gaussian mixture (PCA split fit) | PointNet-style set MLP over the Gaussian parameters |
| `adaptive_gaussian` | the same Gaussians -> `gaussians_to_adaptive` (#26 bridge) | the same adaptive conv net as `adaptive` |

Findings (3 model seeds, one fixed data seed, CUDA):
- **Gaussian features give the best accuracy per parameter.** The `gaussian` set network reaches 81.2 ± 1.6 % accuracy with 110 k parameters and 276 Gaussians per sample. `uniform` reaches 79.0 ± 0.6 % with 678 k parameters and 1004 voxels per sample. The 2.2-point gap is within about 1.5 standard deviations at 3 seeds, so it is not a significant difference. The `gaussian` method also has the lowest inference latency (1.3 ms at batch 1) and the highest throughput (about 9100 samples/s).
- **`adaptive` on its own is worse and much slower here.** It reaches 72.3 ± 1.9 % (-6.7 points against `uniform`). Training is 6-10x slower per sample, batch-1 latency is 4.4x higher, and peak VRAM is 9x higher (316-333 MB against 36-37 MB).
- **The bridge recovers the accuracy.** `adaptive_gaussian` feeds the Gaussians through #26 into the same adaptive network and reaches 80.8 ± 0.4 % (+8.5 points over `adaptive`, with the lowest seed variance). It converges fastest early on: 52.8 % after epoch 1, against 17-29 % for the others. It still pays the adaptive-conv cost (training about 5x `uniform`) and the Gaussian-fit conversion cost (about 15 ms per sample on the CPU).

## TECHNICAL DETAILS
**Dataset generator** (`make_split`, deterministic from `--data-seed` only, so every method and model seed sees the same samples):
- 10 procedural classes: sphere, cube, cylinder, cone, torus, pyramid, capsule, annulus, helix, dumbbell.
- Area-weighted surface samples (2048 points per sample) in about [-1, 1]^3.
- Random rotation, anisotropic scale, translation, jitter and outliers.
- Train and test splits come from different split streams.
- `--seed` sets only the model initialization and the shuffle order.

**Representations** are precomputed once per sample on the CPU, and the conversion time per sample is recorded:
- `uniform`: per-voxel features `[1, log1p(count)/2]`.
- `adaptive`: per-leaf features `[log1p(count)/2, log1p(count / leaf volume), level/depth]`, from `find_leaves` (#26) counts.
- `gaussian`: the fit starts from 0.25 cells and splits a cell (down to 0.0625) while its points are not planar (smallest eigenvalue share > 0.015) and it holds at least 16 points. Each Gaussian gets 11 features: mean, normal, sigmas, log count and fit cell.
- `adaptive_gaussian`: the same Gaussians go through `gaussians_to_adaptive` (Center splat, `cell_per_sigma = sqrt(12)`). Leaf features are `[mass, normal (as colour), sigma, log count, level/depth]`.

**Models.** All models use widths 16/32/64/128, BatchNorm + ReLU, and global mean+max pooling into a linear head.
- Batches of adaptive tensors put each sample `kSampleStrideCells` level-0 cells apart along x. Sample ids are recovered from leaf centres.
- Training: Adam, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 16, cross-entropy, 12 epochs.

**Metrics.** Each run writes one JSON record with these fields:
- per-epoch train loss, train accuracy and test accuracy, plus epoch time
- final accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1, per-class P/R/F1 and the confusion matrix
- train time (excludes the per-epoch evaluation)
- batch-1 inference latency (median/min/max; includes batch assembly, excludes conversion) and batched throughput
- CUDA allocator peak allocated/reserved
- process peak working set
- active elements per sample (min/mean/max) and the level histogram
- conversion ms per sample

`ml_representations_summary.py` aggregates matched-seed runs (mean ± std). It rejects mixed controls, mismatched seed cohorts, duplicate seeds or keys, malformed or incomplete curves, and invalid metrics, so a partial study cannot produce a table.

**Device.** `--device cuda` is the default and fails if CUDA is missing. `auto` falls back to the CPU only when asked (the smoke test uses it). Real runs train on CUDA because the CPU `MinkowskiConvolution` on upstream main has the GEMM layout bug fixed in #10.

## TESTING
Tests added:
- CTest `ml_representations_smoke` runs all 4 methods for 1 epoch on a tiny dataset (3/2 samples per class, 512 points) and validates every JSON field (finite numbers, curve length, types).
- `benchmarks/test_ml_representations_summary.py` has 16 unittest fixtures for the summary guards.

No library code changes beyond #26.

| suite | build | before (#26 head fc913cb) | after (this branch 171689d) |
|---|---|---|---|
| gaussian_tests | CPU (LibTorch cpu, CPU_ONLY, + PR #5 CMake fix) | 44 passed, 0 failed, 5 skipped (CUDA-only) | 44 passed, 0 failed, 5 skipped |
| adaptive_tests | CPU | 77 passed, 0 failed | 77 passed, 0 failed |
| gaussian_tests | CUDA sm_75 | 51 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped | 51 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped |
| adaptive_tests | CUDA sm_75 | 79 passed, 0 failed | 79 passed, 0 failed |
| ctest `ml_representations_smoke` | CPU | n/a (new) | 1/1 passed (749 s on a heavily loaded host; the CPU adaptive conv is slow) |
| ctest `ml_representations_smoke` | CUDA | n/a (new) | 1/1 passed (20 s) |
| `python -m unittest benchmarks/test_ml_representations_summary.py` | - | n/a (new) | 16/16 OK |

Commands (from each build dir; CUDA runs hold the shared GPU lock):
- `gaussian_tests.exe`
- `adaptive_tests.exe`
- `ctest -R ml_representations_smoke --output-on-failure`
- `python -m unittest benchmarks.test_ml_representations_summary`

Merge check against the current upstream main 1ace388 (after #29 and #30): `git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main 171689d` is clean, and so is #26's fc913cb. Those two upstream PRs touch `gaussian_render.cpp` and `utils/sphere*`, which this branch does not use.

## BENCHMARKS
This is a new experiment, so there is no before/after for library code (n/a). The cost of each representation is part of the ML results below. Two timing sources:
1. **Quality runs**: under the GPU lock only, 12 epochs, mean ± std over 3 seeds. The host was busy (see the note under the tables).
2. **Bench-lock timing**: exclusive `bench` lock (no concurrent compiles), the 4 methods **interleaved** (U A G AG) for 3 rounds, 300 train / 200 test, 2 epochs, seed 1. Values are median (min-max) over the rounds.

| method | train ms / sample / epoch (2 ep) | train ms / sample, steady-state epoch | conversion ms / sample | latency b1 ms | throughput samples/s | peak VRAM alloc MB | peak RSS MB |

Notes:
- Every model reaches near-zero training loss (`gaussian` 0.057, the others ≤ 0.003), so with 600 training samples the gaps come from generalization, not from fitting capacity.
- `gaussian` beats `uniform` on the hard cone/pyramid classes (+17/+7 F1 points) but loses on cylinder (-23). Its epoch-to-epoch test accuracy is the noisiest (76.4-85.2 % over epochs 8-12).
- `adaptive` loses about 5-13 F1 points on most classes.

## TRADEOFFS
- **Small study.** It uses 1 data seed, 3 model seeds, 600 training samples, synthetic shapes and no augmentation. The `gaussian` vs `uniform` gap is not significant at this size; the `adaptive` deficit is (more than 3 std).
- **Adaptive cost.** The adaptive conv path dominates `adaptive` and `adaptive_gaussian` time and memory:
  - Every training batch has a new topology, so its kernel maps are built on the host each step. `KernelMapCache` only hits within a step.
  - `apply_map` loops over the 27 kernel slots, with gather, GEMM and scatter per slot, and copies the host index tensors to the device on every conv.
  - Adaptive leaves have more kernel-map neighbours than uniform voxels (#17).

- **Conversion cost.** The Gaussian fit is a serial CPU reference (per-cell `linalg_eigh`). Converting costs 13-15 ms per sample against 0.3 ms for uniform voxelization. It runs once per sample here (static dataset), but would be paid per sample in an online pipeline.
- **Timing under contention.** The host was shared with the owner's GPU/CPU processes (numbers and load are above). Ratios come from interleaved runs; absolute ms are pessimistic.
- **CPU runs.** CPU training is not a valid comparison until #10 (CPU conv GEMM layout) lands. On the CPU only the smoke test runs.
- **Failed attempts, kept for the record.** The first CUDA build failed because `json.hpp` was not on the include path (fixed in 171689d). A first evidence draft accepted mixed controls and partial seed cohorts; the summary guards (17c4c41) now reject them.

## SUMMARY

CPU inputs were rendered by the LibTorch reference rasterizer: per tile it materializes `[pixels, chunk]` tensors for the Gaussian falloff, alpha, transmittance (cumprod) and weights, and its backward goes through autograd over all of them. This PR adds a fused, multi-threaded C++ rasterizer for CPU tensors that runs the same algorithm as the existing CUDA kernels (one task per 16x16 tile via `at::parallel_for`, a per-pixel loop over the tile's depth-sorted list, per-pixel early stop at T < 1e-4) with a hand-written backward. It is the default for CPU inputs (`RenderOptions::use_cpu_kernels = true`); `false` keeps the LibTorch path as the reference.

Measured on CPU (interleaved A/B, same scene): render -81..-87 %, backward -82..-99 %, render+backward -83..-98 %, full train step -71..-94 % (3.4x-15.6x faster), process peak working set 195 -> 140 MB (-28 %). Outputs match the LibTorch path within its early-stop difference (~1e-4) and gradients are bit-identical across thread counts.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `gaussian_render.cpp`
  - `build_tile_lists` (tile-major, depth-ordered (tile, Gaussian) pairs) is no longer CUDA-only; the CPU kernels use the same `ids`/`ranges` layout as the CUDA kernels.
  - `rasterize_forward_cpu`: per tile, gathers the tile's Gaussians into a contiguous `[count, 10]` buffer (cache-friendly), then per pixel composites front to back with the CUDA kernel's alpha rule (`power > 0` skip, `min(0.99, o * g)`, skip `< 1/255`, stop when T would drop below 1e-4). Writes image/depth/alpha, final T and the last contributing index per pixel.
  - `rasterize_backward_cpu`: walks each pixel's list back to front from the saved last index, recomputing T by division (as the CUDA backward does). Each (tile, Gaussian) pair accumulates into its own row of a zero-initialized `[pairs, 10]` buffer, so threads never write the same memory (no atomics, no locks); one `index_add_` reduces pairs to Gaussians. Result: bit-identical gradients for any thread count (tested).
  - `CudaRasterFunction` became `KernelRasterFunction`, which dispatches to the CUDA or CPU kernels on the tensor's device; the tile size now comes from `meta` (CUDA still always uses 16, the CPU kernels honour `RenderOptions::tile_size`).
- `gaussian_render.hpp`: new `RenderOptions::use_cpu_kernels` (default `true`).
- New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_cpu_raster.cpp` (5 tests, registered in `gaussian_tests`).
- Merged with current main (3524eff); the only conflict was the `gaussian_tests` source list in `CMakeLists.txt` (both test files kept).

## TESTING

New tests (all compare against the LibTorch reference path, `use_cpu_kernels = false`; loss = image + 0.1 depth + alpha with random weights, so every output and every input gradient is checked):

| test | what | max error observed |
|---|---|---|
| `gaussian_cpu_raster_matches_libtorch_sparse` | 2000 small splats, 77x45 px (odd size, partial tiles) | image 1.8e-7, alpha 1.2e-7, depth 7.2e-7; grads <= 6.1e-5 abs (max 123) |
| `gaussian_cpu_raster_matches_libtorch_saturated` | 300 large opaque splats (most pixels stop early) | image 3.1e-4, alpha 4.3e-4, depth 1.5e-3; grads rel. <= 1.4e-2 of max |
| `gaussian_cpu_raster_matches_libtorch_other_tile_size` | tile size 7 | image < 5e-4 |
| `gaussian_cpu_raster_is_deterministic_across_threads` | repeat + `at::set_num_threads(1)` | bit-identical image and all gradients |
| `gaussian_cpu_raster_empty_and_culled_scenes` | 0 splats / all behind camera | background only; d/d(background) exact |

Tolerances: forward 5e-4 (image, alpha) and 2e-3 (depth); gradients `rtol 2e-2, atol 2e-2 * max|grad| + 1e-4`. The difference is not an error of either path but their different early-stop rules: the LibTorch path stops a whole 1024-Gaussian chunk only once every pixel of the tile has T < 1e-4, the kernels stop per pixel (the CUDA kernels have the same ~1e-4 difference to the LibTorch path, see `gaussian_render_cuda_matches_cpu`).

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

## TRADEOFFS

- Default changes: CPU renders now use the fused kernels. Outputs differ from the previous CPU output by up to ~1e-4 (image/alpha) where the per-pixel early stop triggers, exactly like the existing CUDA kernels; `use_cpu_kernels = false` restores the old path bit for bit.

## SUMMARY

`voxelize_sphere` measures accuracy as `100 * (1 - |occupied volume - exact| / exact)`. That is a *signed* sum, so over- and under-estimating boundary leaves cancel each other out. The FIFO refinement then stops at the first lucky cancellation and returns a coarse, visibly wrong sphere with a very high reported accuracy:

* radius 100, targets **99.5 % and 99.9 % both return the same 232 leaves** (reported 99.97 %),
* their occupied set differs from the ball by **24.3 % of its volume** (Monte-Carlo symmetric difference),
* a uniform level-6 grid with center sampling is at 2.2 %.

This PR adds an opt-in **`SphereErrorMetric::Geometric`**. It also bounds the misclassified (symmetric-difference) volume, which cannot cancel. With it the requested target bounds the shape error: at 99.5 % the measured shape error is 0.50 %, against 24.3 % with the default metric. The default (`SignedVolume`) is unchanged and bit-identical, so existing callers, the known leaf counts and the sphere-volume benchmark keep their meaning.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

* `SphereGeometry` (`utils/sphere_geometry.hpp`, shared by CPU and CUDA) gets three helpers:
  * `inside_volume(cell)`: the volume of the cell that lies inside the ball. It is exact along z, with an 8 x 8 midpoint quadrature over (x, y), and never exceeds the cell volume.
  * `misclassified_volume(cell)`: for a boundary cell, the part outside the ball if the leaf is occupied (center inside), else the part inside. It is exactly 0 for cells fully inside or outside, whose occupancy is exact.
  * `geometric_accuracy(misclassified)`.
* `voxelize_sphere` / `voxelize_sphere_cuda` get a new trailing parameter `SphereErrorMetric metric = SphereErrorMetric::SignedVolume`. With `Geometric`, the refinement tracks the misclassified volume incrementally, the same way it already tracks the volume (subtract the parent, add the 8 children). It reports `accuracy = min(volume accuracy, geometric accuracy)`, so the old volume guarantee still holds.
* CUDA: `expand_kernel` also emits the per-parent change of the misclassified volume (only when requested). A cumulative sum gives the first split that reaches the target, the same scheme as the existing volume estimate. Decisions match the CPU path.
* Feature-test macro `MINK_SPHERE_HAS_ERROR_METRIC`. The header documents the cancellation problem on `SignedVolume`.
* Not changed: the occupancy rule (center inside) and the FIFO order. A "fewest leaves" search for the geometric metric would split the boundary cells with the largest misclassified volume first, which is a possible follow-up.

## TESTING

New tests in `tests/adaptive/test_sphere.cpp` (registered in `adaptive_tests`):

| test | checks |
|---|---|
| `sphere_signed_volume_default_is_unchanged` | default == explicit `SignedVolume`, 232 leaves at 99.5/99.9, and that result has a > 20 % Monte-Carlo shape error (documents the problem) |
| `sphere_geometric_metric_bounds_shape_error` | targets 90/95/98/99: achieved >= target, volume accuracy >= target, MC shape error <= 100 - target (+0.15, > 6 sigma), reported error within 5 % + 0.1 of MC, leaf count monotone |
| `sphere_geometric_metric_unreachable_throws` | 99.9 at max_depth 6 throws (the signed metric "reaches" it with 232 leaves); max_voxels limit throws |
| `sphere_geometry_inside_volume_and_misclassified_volume` | fully inside/outside cells are exact; inside volumes of a level sum to the ball volume (2e-3); uniform level-5 misclassified volume == MC symmetric difference (5 %) |
| `sphere_cuda_matches_cpu_geometric_metric` (CUDA) | CPU == CUDA leaves, levels, features, accuracy (1e-9) for 90/95/98/99 |

Commands (Release, `mink-build\adaptive-resample-bounds-cpu`): `adaptive_tests.exe`, `ctest --output-on-failure`.

| state | adaptive_tests CPU | notes |
|---|---|---|
| main 3524eff | 77 tests | counted from the sources; these tests are unchanged |
| this branch 9e58f06 | **81 passed / 0 failed** | +4 CPU tests |
| combined build (this + #17 + #20 + interp fallback, 2c3e406) | all 9 sphere tests pass; gaussian_tests 31/0/4 skipped (CUDA-only) | |

CUDA (sm_75, CUDA 13.4.3): the combined CUDA build is in the build queue. I will post the CUDA results, including `sphere_cuda_matches_cpu_geometric_metric`, as a comment.

## BENCHMARKS

Radius 100, `max_depth` 10. Generated with the analysis mode of the adaptive-vs-uniform benchmark (#17, `adaptive_vs_uniform_bench --sphere`, plus one commit that adds the metric; raw `sphere-cpu-a.jsonl`). MC shape error = Monte-Carlo symmetric difference between the occupied leaves and the ball, from 2M uniform points in the bounding cube (+- 1 standard error). Build times are CPU wall times for one call. They were measured while other jobs loaded the host, so treat them as context only.

| target % | before (`SignedVolume`, default): leaves / reported % / MC shape error % | after (`Geometric`): leaves / reported % / MC shape error % | after: finest level | build ms before / after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 90 | 57 / 92.570 / 37.56 +- 0.05 | 2,157 / 90.049 / **10.05** +- 0.03 | 4 | 5.4 / 2.2 |
| 95 | 64 / 95.493 / 30.00 +- 0.05 | 9,619 / 95.004 / **5.00** +- 0.02 | 5 | 0.1 / 8.8 |
| 98 | 155 / 98.104 / 26.93 +- 0.05 | 74,782 / 98.000 / **1.98** +- 0.01 | 7 | 0.2 / 535 |
| 99 | 204 / 99.223 / 25.34 +- 0.05 | 296,031 / 99.000 / **1.01** +- 0.01 | 8 | 0.2 / 528 |
| 99.5 | 232 / 99.969 / 24.28 +- 0.04 | 1,185,416 / 99.500 / **0.50** +- 0.01 | 9 | 0.2 / 1,737 |
| 99.9 | 232 / 99.969 / 24.28 +- 0.04 | unreachable within max_depth 10 (`runtime_error`) | - | 0.3 / - |

The reported geometric accuracy matches the independent Monte-Carlo measurement to within about 0.05 points at every target. With the default metric, the reported accuracy and the real shape error are unrelated.

CPU/GPU memory: proportional to the leaf count (the default path is unchanged). The geometric metric needs about 10^4-10^6 leaves, against 10^2 for the cancelling metric.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a (geometry utility).

## TRADEOFFS

* Opt-in rather than a new default. The upstream tests pin 57/204 leaves at 90/99 % and `achieved == volume accuracy`, and `benchmarks/` defines the metric as volume accuracy. Under the geometric metric, 99.9 % is not reachable with center-sampled cubes at depth 10, because it needs cells finer than 2r/2^10. Flipping the default is a one-line change if maintainers prefer it.
* The misclassified volume is a quadrature estimate (8 x 8 columns, exact along one axis). The tests bound its deviation from Monte Carlo at 5 %; measured, it is < 1 %.
* The geometric metric costs 64 square roots per boundary child, and its trees are much larger (seconds at 99.5 %).

## REPRODUCTION

```
git checkout 9e58f06            # fix/voxelize-sphere-error, based on main 3524eff
pwsh -File mink-build.ps1 -Src <worktree> -Build <dir> -Cpu -Targets adaptive_tests
<dir>\adaptive_tests.exe
# benchmark table: #17 bench + commit d6998cd, merged with this branch (combined 2c3e406)
adaptive_vs_uniform_bench.exe --sphere --jsonl sphere.jsonl
```

Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0 (cpu build for these numbers). Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors docker/cuda-profile.sh. The host was shared with other jobs (owner's GPU workload, antivirus), so the times are context only. Accuracy numbers are deterministic.

> **Update (head ec3abba, round 4):** the CUDA peak-memory regression described below is fixed by grouping kernel slots in the CUDA `apply_map`. Max reserved is now 184 MB at 20k points (main 128, previously 302) and 908 MB at 200k / C 32->64 (main 808, previously 1876). Max allocated is back at main's level. 200k is also faster (fwd+bwd x1.13-1.14). Follow-up comments have the order-alternated A/B results, the fresh-main A/B, the failed batched-GEMM experiment and the suites. The original numbers below are kept unchanged.

## SUMMARY

Adaptive sparse convolution on CUDA gets **3.1-4.5x faster forward and 2.5-4.0x faster forward+backward** when the kernel map is cached (the steady state of a training loop). Two changes:

1. **Per-entry device cache.** Each `KernelMapCache` entry keeps its kernel map's index and weight arrays on every device/dtype it has been applied with (`KernelMapDeviceCache`). Before this, every `adaptive_convolution` / `adaptive_convolution_transpose` call re-uploaded `in_index`, `out_index` and the per-pair weights: 3 host-to-device copies of P elements per call.
2. **Batched CUDA `apply_map`.** On CUDA, one `index_select` gather, one per-pair weight multiply and one `index_add_` scatter cover all 27 kernel slots. Only the GEMM still runs per slot, on `split_with_sizes` row blocks. Launches per call drop from ~4 per slot to ~1 per slot + 4.

The CPU path keeps the per-slot formulation, so CPU numerics stay bit-identical to main (see TRADEOFFS: batching was slower on the CPU). Output topology, gradients and the public API are unchanged.

Cost: peak CUDA memory goes up, because the full gather and product buffers are materialized. In the 20k-point benchmark, max allocated rises 116 -> 161 MB and max reserved 128 -> 302 MB.

Benchmarks ran while the owner's GPU services shared the GPU (details under BENCHMARKS). The numbers are interleaved A/B medians, and several follow-up rows are still pending. They will come in a PR comment.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `kernel_map.hpp/.cpp`:
  - `KernelMapDeviceCache::get(map, device, dtype, with_weight)` is mutex-protected. It keeps one slot per device and one weight copy per dtype.
  - Weights are converted in the same order as before (`.to(device).to(dtype)`), so per-pair values are identical.
  - `KernelMapEntry::device` is a `shared_ptr`, so every copy of a cache entry shares it. `KernelMapCache::clear()` or eviction frees the device memory.
- `ops.cpp::apply_map(x, weight, entry, transpose, n_out, weighted)`:
  - CUDA: `xs = x.index_select(0, from)` over all P pairs, then `xs *= w` if weighted, then `split_with_sizes(slot sizes)`, then `block_k.matmul(W_k)` per non-empty slot, then `cat`, then one `y.index_add_(0, to, ...)`.
  - The pairs are sorted by slot, so the scatter sees the same rows in the same order as the per-slot loop.
  - `split_with_sizes` / `unbind` are used instead of per-slot `slice` / `select` views. With views, autograd allocated one full-size zero gradient per slot in backward (the failed v1, see TRADEOFFS).
  - CPU: the per-slot loop as on main, now reading the cached arrays.
- Empty maps (no pairs) still return zeros that stay connected to `x` and `weight`, so `backward()` gives zero gradients (the contract from the empty-batch fix).
- Determinism: CUDA `index_add_` uses atomics on main too, so float32 results can differ in the last bits between runs. `docs/adaptive.md` now says so, and points to `torch::globalContext().setDeterministicAlgorithms(true, false)` for bit-reproducible outputs (tested).

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_device_kmap.cpp`, 5 tests, compiled into the existing `adaptive_tests` target (so CTest runs them):
- `device_kmap_cpu_matches_per_slot_reference` / `device_kmap_cuda_matches_per_slot_reference`: forward output and feature/weight gradients of `adaptive_convolution`, plus the transposed convolution, against the original per-slot formulation.
  - Covers all 3 modes x output shift {0, -1}.
  - Tolerances: float64 1e-12; float32 1e-5 (CPU) / 1e-4 (CUDA).
- `device_kmap_cache_uploads_once_per_device_and_dtype`: entry copies share the cache; the same device/dtype returns the same storage; a new dtype gets its own copy; CPU results repeat exactly.
- `device_kmap_empty_map_gives_zeros`: empty input, then backward gives zero weight gradients and no error.
- `device_kmap_cuda_deterministic_mode_is_bit_reproducible`: bit-identical with deterministic algorithms on; within 1e-4 otherwise (1.57e-5 observed, 27 slots x 8 channels).

| suite | build | main 3524eff (before) | this branch (after) |
|---|---|---|---|
| adaptive_tests | CPU (LibTorch cpu) | pending (queued) | **82 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped** (50b2f6b; CUDA-only tests return early on CPU) |
| gaussian_tests | CPU | pending (queued) | **31 / 0 / 4 skipped** (CUDA-only) (50b2f6b) |
| adaptive_tests | CUDA sm_75 | pending (queued) | **84 / 0 / 0** (24cafb4: same CUDA code as 50b2f6b; 50b2f6b changes only the CPU branch of `apply_map`) |
| gaussian_tests | CUDA | pending (queued) | **37 / 0 / 0** (24cafb4) |
| ctest | CPU / CUDA | pending | pending (full build + `ctest -V` queued) |

Main has the same test files minus `test_device_kmap.cpp`, so the expected "before" count is the "after" count minus 5. The measured main runs and ctest are queued and will be posted as a comment.

Commands (from the build dir): `.\adaptive_tests.exe`, `.\gaussian_tests.exe`, `ctest --test-dir . -V`.

## BENCHMARKS

Tool: `adaptive_kmap_bench` (already on main) with `--conv cuda|cpu`. It times `adaptive_convolution` with the kernel map already built and cached.
- Workload: half the points uniform in [0,256)^3, half in [0,16)^3, refined to depth 4 inside [0,16)^3.
- 20k points give 41,376 leaves and 905,482 pairs.
- `fwd` = forward under NoGrad, synchronized. `fwdbwd` = forward + backward w.r.t. features and weight. `cuda` = forward between CUDA events. `first` = first call after the map build: a single sample, uploads included.

Method:
- A and B binaries come from the same build dir and flags.
- Runs are interleaved A B A B ... (5 rounds) under the exclusive bench lock (GPU + no concurrent compiles).
- Each cell: median of the per-process medians [min-max over all timed reps]. Each process does 3 warm-ups and 10 timed reps.
- "before" = upstream f93b7bc + the bench file (`219d41b`). Its convolution path (`apply_map`, kernel-map cache, `adaptive_convolution`) is byte-identical to main 3524eff: main only changed `interpolate` and kernel-map *construction* in `ops.cpp` / `kernel_map.cpp` since then, and construction is untimed here.
- "after" = `149f07e`. Its CUDA path is identical to the head 50b2f6b; later commits only merged main and changed the CPU branch.
- A rerun against a fresh main 3524eff binary is queued.

**Host contention:** the GPU was not idle. The owner's Samaritan services were running: a Whisper worker at ~99 % SM in `nvidia-smi pmon` most samples, and an ollama server, together holding ~7.2-7.7 of 8 GB VRAM. Defender and a Python service also loaded the CPU. Both arms see the same contention because the runs are interleaved, so the medians are comparable. Absolute times are pessimistic, and the max values are noisy.

### CUDA, 20k points, C_in 8 -> C_out 16, float32 (`--conv cuda --depth 4 --channels 8 --cout 16 --modes center,volume --warmup 3 --reps 10`)

| metric | before | after (this PR) | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| CenterSampled fwd (ms) | 5.58 [4.30-7.51] | 1.83 [1.51-3.56] | **-67.2 % (x3.05)** |

| VolumeWeighted fwd+bwd (ms) | 22.05 [12.39-51.55] | 5.46 [4.23-7.88] | **-75.2 % (x4.04)** |
| VolumeWeighted first call (ms, 1 sample) | 33.58 | 27.59 | -17.8 % |
| CUDA max allocated (MB) | 116.1 | 160.7 | **+38.4 % (regression)** |

| CPU peak working set (MB) | 620.0 | 605.9 | -2.3 % |
| throughput, CenterSampled fwd+bwd steps/s (1000 / median ms) | 67.8 | 172.4 | +154 % |

### Other metrics

| metric | status |
|---|---|
| Kernel-map build time (`kmap_*_cold/warm`) | Unchanged code: map construction is untouched. An A/B against main is queued to confirm. |
| OverlapWeighted CUDA conv (2k points) | pending: the earlier run against the old upstream baseline was invalid (the baseline's pre-#15 overlap scan plus GPU starvation made it run > 15 min); rerun vs main queued |

| Kernel time | n/a: no Nsight on the test host. The `cuda` rows are CUDA-event times of the forward. |

Raw outputs (A/B JSON + per-process stdout) are in the lab results folder: `results/adaptive-perf/av5v2/cuda_n20k_c8x16.{json,raw.txt,txt}`.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a. This is a pure execution change: same pairs, same per-pair weights, same per-slot GEMMs. Outputs match the per-slot reference to 1e-12 in float64, and float32 differs only by atomic accumulation order, as on main. Model quality cannot change, so no training run was done.

## TRADEOFFS

- **Memory regression on CUDA.** Gathering all P rows at once materializes [P, C_in] and [P, C_out] buffers instead of one slot's worth. With the caching allocator, max reserved grows 128 -> 302 MB at 20k points / 0.9M pairs. Per-convolution memory scales with the pair count, about P x (C_in + C_out) x 4 bytes, plus the cached int64 index arrays (16 B per pair, per device) that live as long as the cache entry. `KernelMapCache::clear()` / `set_capacity()` bound the cached part.
- **First call** after a map build includes the one-time upload. It is +12 % for CenterSampled (one noisy sample) and -18 % for VolumeWeighted. Every later call skips the uploads.
- **Failed attempt, v1 (acc7580): per-slot `slice` / `select` views of one big gather.**
  - Forward was x2.7-3.3, but forward+backward only x1.13-1.40 (CenterSampled fwd+bwd 13.96 -> 12.33 ms).
  - CUDA reserved went 148 -> 422 MB, because every `SliceBackward` / `SelectBackward` allocates a full-size zero gradient per kernel slot.
  - The 200k-point run of v1 failed.
  - Fixed in v2 (149f07e) with `split_with_sizes` / `unbind` (one concatenation in backward): fwd+bwd x2.5-4.0.
- **Reverted on the CPU (50b2f6b).**
  - The batched path measured slower on the CPU in an interleaved A/B: OverlapWeighted fwd 16.6 -> 50.1 ms (x0.33), fwd+bwd 111 -> 190 ms, and +110-125 MB peak working set (large fresh [P, C] allocations).
  - That run was noisy: CenterSampled fwd range 17-1388 ms, under heavy host CPU load.
  - The CPU therefore keeps the per-slot loop. Only the device cache is shared, and on the CPU `.to(kCPU)` was already a no-op.
- **Not addressed here:** the GEMMs still run per slot, so CUDA launches still scale with the kernel volume. A batched-GEMM follow-up is being measured separately.
- Results are not bitwise reproducible on CUDA in float32 (atomics), which is unchanged from main.

## SUMMARY

Numerical robustness of the Gaussian projection and value types:

1. **Frustum clamp measured from the principal point.** The Jacobian clamp was symmetric around the image center (`+-1.3 * 0.5 W / fx`), which is wrong when `cx != W/2` (cropped or off-center intrinsics): a 64-px crop of a 128-px image (same intrinsics, `cx = 64`) rendered differently from the corresponding half of the full image (max 0.0135 image / 0.028 alpha difference). Limits are now `(cx + 0.15 W)/fx` to the left and `(W - cx + 0.15 W)/fx` to the right (as in gsplat); identical to the old clamp for a centered principal point. Crop and full image now agree exactly (0 difference).
2. **Stable 2D covariance determinant.** `det = a*c - b*b` cancels catastrophically in float32 for long thin splats; it is now `|m1 x m2|^2 + 0.3 (|m1|^2 + |m2|^2) + 0.09` (Lagrange identity on the rows of the 2x3 projected factor), a sum of squares. A 45-degree needle (2000 px x 0.01 px) was off by 0.0105 against float64; now 6.8e-4. The eigenvalue discriminant `mid^2 - det` is computed as `((a - c)/2)^2 + b^2`.
3. **Stable depth sort.** `argsort(stable=true)`: splats at exactly equal depth composite in index order on every device/sort implementation.
4. **`Gaussian3D::mahalanobis_squared`** evaluates `sum_k ((R^T d)_k / s_k)^2` instead of `d^T Sigma^-1 d` through the explicit inverse (entries ~1/s_min^2): float `{2, 0.5, 1e-3}` gave 2.75 instead of 2.89, float64 lost 1.3e-4 relative at a thin axis of 1e-5.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `gaussian_render.cpp`: clamp limits from `camera.cx/cy`; determinant via `at::linalg_cross` of the two rows of `J W R S` (differentiable, same value in exact arithmetic, so gradients are mathematically unchanged); discriminant rewrite in the culling block; stable argsort.
- `gaussian3d.hpp`: rotate-then-scale Mahalanobis distance (also used by `density`).
- New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_projection.cpp` and the float64 brute-force reference `tests/gaussian/gaussian_reference.hpp` (shared verbatim with the tile-bounds PR; uses the principal-point-aware clamp, identical to main's for centered cameras).

## TESTING

| test (CPU / CUDA kernels / LibTorch-on-CUDA) | main | this PR | tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64-px crop vs left half of 128-px image | 0.0135 image, 0.0279 alpha | 0 | 1e-5 |
| off-center camera (cx = W) vs float64 reference | 0.043 image, 0.071 alpha | 1.6-1.7e-7 | 5e-4 |
| 45-degree needle (sigma 2000 px x 0.008 px, o = 0.3) vs float64 | 0.0105 image, 0.0116 alpha | 6.2-6.8e-4 | 3e-3 |
| 600 splats at bit-identical depth vs reference (index order) | 3.8e-7 (main's sort happened to be stable here) | 3.5-3.8e-7 | 5e-4 |
| float Gaussian3D Mahalanobis, scale ratio up to 2e4, vs float64 at the same point | 0.250122 vs 0.25 (fail) | pass | ~1e-5 rel + rounding of R^T d |
| float64 Gaussian3D Mahalanobis, thin axis 1e-4 .. 1e-6 | 2.89038 vs 2.89 | pass (1e-9) | 1e-9 |

The needle's remaining 6.8e-4 is float32 rounding of a, b, c (~0.1 at 2e6 px^2), which only affects the long axis where the power is < 0.01 inside the image; it would need a different conic representation to remove.

| suite | before (main) | after |
|---|---|---|
| gaussian_tests CPU (PR #5 CMake fix) | 31 passed, 2 skipped | 36 passed, 1 failed, 2 skipped (previous revision; see below) |
| gaussian_tests CUDA | 35 passed | 40 passed, 1 failed (previous revision; see below) |
The one failure in that run was the new test `gaussian3d_double_mahalanobis_thin_axes_are_exact` itself, which used a thin axis of 1e-8, below `Gaussian3D::kMinimumScale` (1e-6), so the value type rejected it. The final revision tests 1e-4, 1e-5 and 1e-6; a re-run of the final revision on CPU and CUDA is queued and will be posted as a comment. All other new and existing tests passed. The same library change also passed in a combined build with all other gaussian branches (CPU 60/0/9 skipped, CUDA 71/0/0).

## BENCHMARKS

n/a: correctness fix. The determinant adds one batched cross product to the ~100 LibTorch projection ops; it was not benchmarked in isolation.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a. Training on centered cameras is unaffected (identical clamp); cropped/off-center cameras now get the correct projection Jacobian near the borders.

## TRADEOFFS

- For `cx != W/2` the clamp changes rendered output near the image border for splats beyond the old symmetric limit; that is the bug fix, but it changes results of existing off-center renders.
- Textual conflict with `perf/gaussian-tile-bounds` (radius block); resolution keeps the tile-bounds code (the eigenvalue is not needed there) plus the stable sort and determinant.

## REPRODUCTION

- Branch `fix/gaussian-projection-stability` (base f93b7bc). "main" numbers: the same test file built against main's renderer (local probe build, not part of the PR).
- `gaussian_tests.exe gaussian_projection` and `gaussian_tests.exe gaussian3d_`.

body:
## SUMMARY
Adds a bridge between 3D Gaussian splats (`GaussianTensor`) and adaptive mixed-resolution sparse voxels (`adaptive::AdaptiveSparseTensor`). Until now there was no Gaussian-to-voxel bridge (gaussian/README.md: "There is not yet a Gaussian-to-sparse-voxel bridge or adaptive spatial index"). New header `MinkowskiEngine/gaussian/gaussian_adaptive.hpp`:

- `gaussians_to_adaptive(gaussians, config, options, map*)` voxelizes Gaussians into an adaptive tensor. Each Gaussian gets a level from its extent. Mass and colour are opacity-weighted and differentiable with respect to the Gaussian parameters.
- `adaptive_to_gaussians(tensor, options)` creates one Gaussian per leaf. It is differentiable with respect to the leaf features.
- `refine_by_gaussian_density(tensor, gaussians, max_per_leaf, max_level)` splits leaves that contain too many Gaussian means.
- `find_leaves(tensor, points)` uses the adaptive tree as a spatial index (point -> leaf row).
- `adaptive_config_for(gaussians, max_depth)` builds a grid from the Gaussians' scale quantile and bounding box.

The new code is in new files plus one CMake registration and a README update. No existing API changes.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS
**Level choice.** Gaussian *i* with largest axis scale s_i targets `l_i = clamp(round(log2(max_d base[d] / (cell_per_sigma * s_i))), min_level, max_level)`. Its cell edge is about `cell_per_sigma * s_i`, so small Gaussians get fine cells and large ones coarse cells. s = 0 maps to the finest allowed level, and s larger than the coarsest cell maps to level 0.

**Splat / topology.** There are two splat modes:
- `Center` puts the whole Gaussian in the level-l_i cell containing its mean.
- `BoxIntegral` spreads it over the level-l_i cells within `support_sigma` axis standard deviations. Weights are the per-axis normal integrals with std sqrt(Sigma_dd) from the rotated covariance (axis-aligned approximation), renormalized over the truncated window. The window is clipped to `max_cells_per_axis` for huge splats.

A deposit cell that contains a finer deposit is subdivided: its weight is pushed to the 2^3 children in proportion to the Gaussian's integral over each child, recursively. The result has no overlapping leaves (`has_overlapping_leaves() == false`), fine leaves where small Gaussians are, and coarse leaves elsewhere. Each Gaussian's weights sum to 1, so total mass is conserved exactly.

`min_weight` (default 1e-15) drops far-tail entries and renormalizes, so mass is still conserved. Without it, entries of about 1e-40 produced float32-denormal leaf masses whose mean attributes were rounding noise and differed between CPU and CUDA (found by the CPU-vs-CUDA test).

**Features** `[mass, r, g, b, f_0..]`:
- `mass_j = sum_i w_ij * m_i`, where `m_i` = opacity, or opacity * (2 pi)^{3/2} * prod(scales) with `weight_by_volume`.
- Colours and features are mass-weighted means (or sums with `mean_attributes = false`).

They are built with `index_select` / `index_add` on the Gaussians' device and dtype, so gradients reach opacities, colours, features and (with `weight_by_volume`) scales. Topology and weights are piecewise constant in positions, rotations and scales, so those get no gradient (documented).

**Inverse.** `adaptive_to_gaussians` places an axis-aligned Gaussian at each leaf centre with sigma = `sigma_per_cell` * leaf size (0.5 inverts `cell_per_sigma` = 2, so the topology is a fixed point of the round trip). Opacity is `-expm1(-mass)`. Plain `1 - exp(-m)` rounds to 0 for m < 1e-17, which silently zeroed far-tail leaves; the round-trip test caught this.

**Robustness.**
- Non-finite or negative scales, non-finite positions, zero quaternions, non-3-D configs and invalid options throw `std::invalid_argument`.
- Coordinates must stay below 2^52 finest cells (exact in double, same rule as the adaptive range checks); larger ones throw instead of aliasing.
- Runaway BoxIntegral splats throw `std::length_error` (`max_entries`).

Levels, keys and weights are computed on the host in double (`at::parallel_for`); aggregation runs on the input device.

## TESTING
New file `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_adaptive.cpp`, registered in `gaussian_tests` (CTest), with 15 tests:
- dense **brute-force reference** (independent erf integrals over leaf/window boxes from `covariances()`; checks every Gaussian x leaf weight, mass and colour for both splats, with and without `min_weight`)
- **finite-difference gradcheck** (double; opacities, colours, features; both splats; with/without `weight_by_volume`; plus `adaptive_to_gaussians` backward)
- mass conservation and extensive attributes
- level assignment
- small-inside-large subdivision
- round trip (topology fixed point)
- `refine_by_gaussian_density` against brute-force counts
- empty and single-Gaussian inputs
- degenerate covariances: zero, 1e-30, 1e30, needle, flat disc, rotated
- extreme coordinates (+-1e9, beyond 2^52)
- `find_leaves` against brute-force box tests
- option validation and `min_weight`
- adaptive conv + pool on the bridge output with gradients reaching opacities

The CPU and CUDA reruns on the merged head are queued on the shared build slots; their results will be posted as a PR comment.

Development failures, kept for the record: the first CPU run had 3 failures, all fixed.

- Two test expectations were wrong: colour tolerance on ~1e-20-mass leaves, and the clipped splat being subdivided.

The first CUDA run showed float32 CPU-vs-CUDA attribute differences of up to 2.04 on denormal-mass leaves. That led to `min_weight`.

## BENCHMARKS
This is a new feature, so there is no "before" (n/a). Conversion cost against N comes from `benchmarks/gaussian_adaptive_bench.cpp` (new target `gaussian_adaptive_bench`):
- scene: N Gaussians uniform in [0,64)^3, log-uniform scales 0.02-2, random rotations, float32, seed 1234; base 64, depth 8

> **Stacked on #15** (`perf/adaptive-overlap-descent`): this branch contains #15's two commits plus two commits of its own (`perf(adaptive): parallel kernel-map build, node-table find_containing, hashed output topology` and `perf(adaptive): parallel interpolate() ...`). Review only those two; once #15 merges, the diff shrinks to them. All numbers below compare against #15 (A) to isolate this change. For CenterSampled/VolumeWeighted, #15 measured the same as upstream (within noise; see #15).

## SUMMARY

Adaptive kernel-map construction and `interpolate()` ran on one thread with an `std::unordered_map` probe per present level. This PR:
1. builds kernel maps on several threads, in blocks of outputs concatenated in order, so maps are **bit-identical and in the same order** for any thread count;
2. moves `Topology::find` / `find_containing` onto #15's flat open-addressing node table, with an early exit: a cell that is neither a leaf nor an ancestor of one ends the search;
3. replaces `derive_output_topology`'s `std::set` plus per-level ancestor probes with sort/unique and a hash set, checking only levels that hold keys, in parallel;
4. parallelizes `interpolate()` the same way (block-ordered, so the result is bit-identical).

Kernel-map build is **5-8x faster** (CenterSampled/VolumeWeighted) and **3.6-4.7x faster** (OverlapWeighted). Strided maps (shift -1) are 3-5x faster. Multilinear interpolation is **1.9-3.5x** faster and Nearest 1.4-5x.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `adaptive_topology.{hpp,cpp}`: `parallel_block_count(n, work)` + `run_parallel_blocks(n, blocks, f)`, built on the existing `std::thread` runner (no OpenMP, same reason as the existing code). The thread count follows the estimated work (`n_out * K^D`), not n, so small maps stay single-threaded. `find()` uses the node table (one flat-table probe instead of an `unordered_map` lookup), so the `unordered_map` index is no longer built for kernel maps. `find_containing` probes from the coarsest present level; `kInternal` means "descend", and `kEmpty` stops early. The proof that this is equivalent: nested cells. `(p - o) / s_l` scales exactly by 2 per level, so `floor` at level l+1 >> 1 equals `floor` at level l.
- `kernel_map.cpp` `build_pairs`: each block keeps per-slot lists. The final arrays are allocated once, and the blocks are copied slot by slot in block order, which is exactly the serial (slot, output, input) order. The node table is built before the workers start.
- `kernel_map.cpp` `derive_output_topology`: coarsen (parallel), sort, unique; then flag keys that have an ancestor among the present levels with a hash set (parallel), and compact in order. The output is identical to the `std::set` version (tested against it).
- `ops.cpp` `interpolate()`: blocks of points on worker threads. The (point, leaf, weight) lists are concatenated in block order, so `index_add_` sees the same sequence as before.

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_parallel_kmap.cpp` (in `adaptive_tests`):
- `parallel_kmap_matches_serial_oracle`: random trees D = 2/3/4 (~1.5-5K leaves, large enough for several threads), all 3 modes x shifts 0/-1/-2. The test requires exact equality of the output topology against the original `std::set` derivation, and of `kernel_offsets`, in/out/kernel indices and weights against a serial re-implementation of the original `build_pairs` (exact-key level probing, grid-scan overlap). A second build must be bit-identical.
- `find_containing_matches_level_probe_oracle`: D = 2/3/4, 20,000 points each, including points on leaf corners, at 1e30, inf and NaN, against the original level probe. `find()` is checked on every leaf key and on absent parent keys.
- `parallel_interpolate_matches_serial_oracle`: 60,000 points (multi-threaded), Nearest and Multilinear, `torch::equal` against a serial oracle.

| suite (CPU) | upstream | #15 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| adaptive_tests | 70/70 | 74/74 | 77 passed, 0 failed |
| gaussian_tests | 31 + 2 skipped | same | 31 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped |
| CUDA suites | 72/72, 35/35 | 76/76, 35/35 | pending on the shared queue (a comment will follow) |

## BENCHMARKS

`adaptive_kmap_bench`, CPU build, interleaved A/B (`ab.py`, A = #15, B = this PR), 3 rounds x (2 warm-up + 5 timed) per process, exclusive bench lock. The tables give the median of run medians and [min-max] of all timed repeats. Pair counts are identical in every row (checked by the driver). 12 hardware threads.

Kernel-map build, depth 4, n = 20000 (41,376 leaves), measured on the final commit:

| CenterSampled (905,482 pairs) | 241.8 / 215.3 ms | 37.4 / 32.7 ms | x6.5 / x6.6 |
| VolumeWeighted | 259.4 / 236.3 ms | 43.8 / 36.8 ms | x5.9 / x6.4 |

| case | metric | #15 | this PR | change |

| depth 4, shift -1 | CenterSampled cold / warm (163,810 pairs) | 77.2 / 68.2 ms | 25.5 / 14.0 ms | x3.0 / x4.9 |
| depth 4, shift -1 | OverlapWeighted cold / warm (939,347 pairs) | 276.5 / 262.4 ms | 59.3 / 64.5 ms | x4.7 / x4.1 |
| depth 6, region 4, n = 200 (32,882 leaves) | CenterSampled cold / warm | 185.4 / 202.5 ms | 37.8 / 25.4 ms | x4.9 / x8.0 |
| same | VolumeWeighted cold / warm | 228.4 / 228.5 ms | 31.2 / 26.8 ms | x7.3 / x8.5 |
| same | OverlapWeighted cold / warm (1,316,437 pairs) | 671.1 / 665.5 ms | 158.1 / 170.3 ms | x4.2 / x3.9 |
| n = 200000, depth 4 (64,001 leaves) | CenterSampled cold / warm (1,613,781 pairs) | 279.3 / 293.1 ms | 56.7 / 47.7 ms | x4.9 / x6.2 |
| same | OverlapWeighted cold / warm (1,863,576 pairs) | 843.3 / 844.5 ms | 184.4 / 192.7 ms | x4.6 / x4.4 |

Interpolation (final commit):

|---|---|---|
| depth 4, 20,000 points | 27.9 -> 10.9 ms (x2.6) | 4.3 -> 2.9 ms (x1.5) |
| depth 6, region 4, 20,000 points | 272.8 -> 147.7 ms (x1.9) | 18.4 -> 3.5 ms (x5.2) |
| n = 200000, 200,000 points | 521.4 -> 148.6 ms (x3.5) | 50.8 -> 35.4 ms (x1.4) |

Peak working set (whole process):

| run | #15 | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| depth 4, kmap all modes | 220.9 MB | 179.1 MB (-42 MB: no `unordered_map` index) |
| depth 4, interpolation | 188.5 MB | 160.4 MB |
| depth 6, kmap + interpolation | 341.9 MB | 368.0 MB (+26 MB: per-block lists before concatenation) |
| n = 200000, interpolation | 411.9 MB | 447.1 MB (+35 MB) |

GPU memory / kernel time: n/a. Host-only code; in CUDA builds the map is also built on the host.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a. Kernel maps, output topologies and interpolation results are bit-identical, so training is numerically unchanged.

## TRADEOFFS

- The peak working set rises 26-35 MB on the larger runs: the per-block pair lists coexist with the final arrays during concatenation. It falls by about 40 MB where the old `unordered_map` index dominated. A two-pass build (count, then fill in place) would remove the duplication at the cost of doing the work twice. I did not pursue it.
- Threads are plain `std::thread`s spawned per call (as in the existing `parallel_blocks`). That overhead (about 0.1 ms) is why small maps stay serial.
- OverlapWeighted scales less (x3.6-4.7) than the point-lookup modes: its hit lists vary in length and the descent is memory-bound.
- Speedups depend on the core count (6C/12T here).

## REPRODUCTION

- Stacked on #15; base upstream f93b7bc. Tests: `adaptive_tests.exe`, `gaussian_tests.exe`.
- A/B examples: `ab.py --rounds 3 --a pr15=... --b pr=... -- --depth 4 --modes center,volume,overlap --interp 0 --warmup 2 --reps 5`; `-- --depth 4 --shift -1 --modes center,overlap --interp 0 ...`; `-- --n 200 --depth 6 --region 4 --modes center,volume,overlap --interp 20000 ...`; `-- --n 200000 --depth 4 --modes center --phases none --interp 200000 ...`
- Build: CMake 4.2.3 + Ninja, Release, CPU_ONLY with LibTorch 2.15.0+cpu (PR #5's CMake fix injected at configure time).
- Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors docker/cuda-profile.sh.

## SUMMARY

CUDA rasterizer backward (`raster_backward_kernel`): skip the per-Gaussian warp reduction when no lane of the warp is hit, and keep the batch's Gaussian ids in shared memory. Backward is 19 % (512 px) to 41 % (1024 px) faster on the 139k-splat test scene; the train step 16-22 % faster. Gradients are unchanged up to the run-to-run nondeterminism of the float atomics.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

Before, every one of the 8 warps of a tile block ran, for every Gaussian of the tile list, 10 x 5 `__shfl_down_sync` reductions plus a global read of `ids[begin + base + j]` by lane 0, even when all 32 pixels of the warp had alpha below 1/255 (most pairs: the tile list is a superset of each warp's footprint, and pixels past their `last_index` contribute nothing).

- `if (!__any_sync(0xffffffff, alpha >= 0)) continue;` right after evaluating alpha. The branch is warp-uniform (the loop bounds are block-uniform and all 256 threads stay in the loop), so the full-mask shuffles remain valid. When it is taken every `v[k]` would have been 0 and no atomic would have been issued (`v[k] != 0` guard), so the result is unchanged; the per-pixel state (`T`, `acc`, `last_alpha`) is only updated for hit pixels anyway.
- `__shared__ int32_t batch_ids[256]` filled together with the attribute batch; lane 0 reads the destination row from shared memory.

## TESTING

New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_cuda_backward.cpp` (CUDA-only):
- sparse: 3,000 small splats on a 77x45 image (partial tiles on both axes) - most (warp, Gaussian) pairs are skipped; max gradient error vs the LibTorch path 2.7e-5 at max|grad| 98 (positions/scales);
- saturated: 400 large overlapping splats on 50x66 - all lanes hit, pixels stop early at different `last_index`; within the existing kernel-vs-reference tolerance (2e-2 max|grad| + 1e-4).
Both use image + depth + alpha in the loss and check all six inputs.

| suite | before (main) | after |
|---|---|---|
| gaussian_tests CUDA | 35 passed, 0 failed | 37 passed, 0 failed |
| gaussian_tests CPU (PR #5 CMake fix) | 31 passed, 2 skipped | 31 passed, 4 skipped (2 new CUDA-only) |

Gradient equality (one deterministic backward per config, `gaussian_render_bench --dump-grads / --compare-grads`, max over the six raw model parameters of max|diff| / max|grad|):

| config | main vs main (second run) | this PR vs main |
|---|---|---|
| 20k splats, 512 px | 3.3e-6 | 8.0e-6 |
| 20k splats, 1024 px | 8.8e-6 | 9.4e-6 |
| 139k splats, 512 px | 8.3e-6 | 7.5e-6 |
| 139k splats, 1024 px | 8.2e-6 | 2.0e-5 |

Not bit-identical, but neither is main against itself: the float `atomicAdd` order varies between runs. The differences are of the same size.

## BENCHMARKS

`gaussian_render_bench` (PR `perf/gaussian-render-bench`), test.ply, RTX 2080 SUPER, CUDA kernels, one bench lock, binaries interleaved main/PR x 3 processes, 2 warm-ups + 5 timed iterations each (15 samples), median (min-max), CUDA synchronized around each phase. Backward = `loss.backward()` of image + depth + alpha weighted sums (includes the LibTorch projection backward); train = `GaussianTrainer::step`.

| config | metric | main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 139,410 splats, 512 px | backward ms | 22.02 (20.60-26.14) | 17.80 (14.53-20.82) | -19.2 % |
| | fwd+bwd ms | 35.88 (31.42-46.01) | 31.63 (24.10-37.20) | -11.8 % |
| | train step ms | 35.95 (32.76-60.86) | 30.04 (25.55-34.57) | -16.4 % |
| 139,410 splats, 1024 px | backward ms | 35.45 (33.58-36.91) | 20.93 (19.74-23.98) | -41.0 % |
| | fwd+bwd ms | 53.79 (48.86-60.67) | 38.04 (35.10-42.90) | -29.3 % |
| | train step ms | 60.85 (59.44-64.96) | 47.58 (45.01-50.02) | -21.8 % |
| 20,000 splats, 512 px | backward ms | 16.87 (10.53-24.04) | 13.01 (9.39-21.75) | -23 % (noisy) |

## SUMMARY

Opacity-aware, anisotropic tile bounds for the rasterizer (CPU and CUDA paths share them). A Gaussian is assigned to the tiles of the axis-aligned box of the ellipse where its alpha actually reaches the 1/255 cut-off, instead of a square box of 3 sigma of the major axis. This

- removes 47-56 % of the (tile, Gaussian) pairs on the 139k-splat test scene, making CUDA render 25-33 % and the train step 19-26 % faster, with 26-43 % less peak VRAM in the forward pass;
- fixes visible alpha that the 3-sigma box dropped: an opaque splat (o > 0.35) still has alpha 0.011*o > 1/255 at 3 sigma, so whole tiles of its footprint were missing (up to 0.0056 image error on a needle splat, now 6e-6 against a brute-force reference). The image no longer depends on the tile size.

Also adds `RenderOutput::tile_pairs` and an int32-range check for the CUDA tile lists.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `gaussian_render.cpp`: alpha at Mahalanobis distance m is `o exp(-m^2/2)`, dropped below 1/255, so nothing beyond `m^2 = 2 ln(255 o)` contributes (3.33 sigma for o = 1, 1.8 sigma for o = 0.02). Half-extents `rx = ceil(m sqrt(a))`, `ry = ceil(m sqrt(c))` (a, c = diagonal of the dilated 2D covariance) bound that ellipse exactly; a slack of 0.01 on m^2 keeps pixels whose alpha rounds to exactly 1/255. Culling against the image uses the same box. `radii` = max(rx, ry).
- `build_tile_lists`: `TORCH_CHECK` that pairs and Gaussians fit in int32 (the CUDA kernels index with int32) instead of silently overflowing.
- `RenderOutput::tile_pairs` ([] int64, read with `.item()` only when needed).
- docs/rendering.md: output table (`visible` means "passed culling", `radii` semantics, `tile_pairs`) and the footprint rule.

## TESTING

New `tests/gaussian/test_gaussian_tile_bounds.cpp` + `tests/gaussian/gaussian_reference.hpp` (float64 brute-force reference: every Gaussian composited at every pixel, no tiles, no culling box, no early stop; pixels within float rounding of the 1/255 cut-off are excluded, < 0.04 %):

| test | result on this branch | same check on main |
|---|---|---|
| random opaque scenes (240 splats, 61x47 px, tiles 16 / 7 / 64) vs brute force, CPU | max image err 8.6e-7 | 8.6e-7 (small splats: tile rounding hides the clipping) |
| same on CUDA kernels and LibTorch-on-CUDA | 8.6e-7 | 8.3e-7 |
| larger splats (seed 3, footprints of several tiles) | 4.3e-7 | not run on main |
| needle (0.4 x 0.004, o = 0.9) vs brute force | 6.4e-6, 14 tile pairs (one row) | 5.6e-3 (FAIL); pairs not measured (3-sigma square box estimate: 12 x 12 tiles) |
| radius of o = 0.99 vs o = 0.02 at equal geometry | 27 / 15 px | upstream radius below 3.33 sigma (FAIL) |
| tile_pairs consistency (1 tile = visible count, CPU vs CUDA within 1 %) | pass | n/a |

Tolerance: 5e-4 image/alpha, 2e-3 depth (float32 plus the T < 1e-4 early stop).

| suite | before (main) | after |

| gaussian_tests CPU (PR #5 CMake fix) | 31 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped | 35 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped |

The same change also passes the gradcheck suite of PR #14 and all other gaussian tests in an integration build with the other open gaussian branches (CPU 60/0/9 skipped, CUDA 71/0/0).

## BENCHMARKS

`gaussian_render_bench` (PR `perf/gaussian-render-bench`, same camera as `gaussian_ply_bench`), test.ply, RTX 2080 SUPER, CUDA kernels. One bench lock, binaries interleaved base/branch x 3 processes, each 2 warm-ups + 5 timed iterations (15 samples per cell); median (min-max). Pairs for main are computed from its square 3-sigma box (`radii`, 16-px tiles). ## SUMMARY

Adds opt-in `drop_empty` refinement (AV9). `refine`, `refine_by_density`, `refine_by_variance` and `refine_if`
take a trailing `bool drop_empty = false`. When set, a refined leaf is replaced only by the children that contain at
least one source point, instead of all `2^D` children.

On the five datasets of the adaptive vs uniform benchmark (#17):
* ROI refinement creates **82-98 % fewer leaves**, and kernel-map build, forward and forward+backward are **9-270x
  faster**. At depth 5: 1,032,755 -> 20,437 leaves, kmap 6.27 s -> 0.11 s, forward 1.52 s -> 5.6 ms.
* Held-out error barely changes for ROI refinement (nRMSE +0.1 to +7.4 %).
* Density and variance refinement also shrink (0-69 %), but they lose held-out coverage and accuracy. Details under
  TRADEOFFS.

The default behaviour is unchanged: same keys, features, kernel maps and errors on every benchmark case.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

* `refine_step` takes an optional per-leaf child bitmask (bit i is the i-th child of `child_keys`). `Split`
  divides by the number of kept children, so sums are still conserved.
* `occupied_children`: for every source point inside a selected leaf, it locates the point at `level + 1`, checks
  that the child's parent is the leaf, and sets the child bit. A point that cannot be placed conservatively keeps all
  children. Selected leaves that contain no point are deselected (left unrefined), which also guarantees the refine
  loops terminate.
* Shared driver `refine_selected` (a private member). `refine_by_density` and `refine_by_variance` reuse their
  existing point-to-leaf assignment, so the extra cost there is one O(P) pass. `refine` and `refine_if` pay one
  `assign_points` per step, and only when `drop_empty` is set.
* `drop_empty` without source points (`from_voxels`) throws `std::invalid_argument`. The default path does not
  need source points.
* Invariant (tested): on a `from_points` tensor, `refine` / `refine_by_density` / `refine_by_variance` (with
  non-negative thresholds) and `drop_empty` give exactly the default result with its point-free leaves removed: same
  keys, same features. Every remaining leaf contains a source point, and no leaves overlap.
* Feature-test macro `MINK_ADAPTIVE_HAS_DROP_EMPTY`. The benchmark in #17 uses it to add `+drop` variants.
* The API change is source-compatible (trailing defaulted parameter). It is not ABI-compatible for code compiled
  against the old header.

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_drop_empty.cpp` (10 tests, in `adaptive_tests`):
* only occupied children are created;
* equality with the filtered default result for region / density (k = 0, 4, 16, 64) / variance;
* `refine_if` never creates point-free leaves;
* `Split` conserves sums;
* negative coordinates and D = 2;
* gradients reach the parent once per kept child;
* source points are required;
* the default is unchanged.

dirs.

body:
> **Stacked on #15** (`perf/adaptive-overlap-descent`): this branch contains #15's two commits plus one commit of its own (`feat(adaptive): opt-in CenterAveraged convolution mode`). Review only the last commit; once #15 merges, the diff shrinks to it. The new mode uses #15's `for_each_overlap` descent, and would be very slow without it.

## SUMMARY

With `CenterSampled` (the default), a kernel tap of a coarse output leaf is the centre `c + offset * s_out`. That point is a vertex shared by the 2^D finer leaves under it, and `find_containing` returns only the one whose lower corner sits there (`2c+1`). So:
- coarse leaves next to a refined region see one child per tap;
- with `output_level_shift = -1` over a refined region, only one of the 2^D children under each output reaches it. 7/8 of those input leaves get **zero gradient** (`VolumeWeighted` has the same pairs, scaled).

This PR adds an **opt-in** mode, `AdaptiveConvMode::CenterAveraged`. It behaves like `CenterSampled` while the leaf containing the tap point is at the output leaf's level or coarser (weight 1). When the tap cell is split into finer leaves (or no leaf at that level or coarser contains the point), the tap reads the average of the leaves inside the tap cell, weighted by overlap volume over total overlap volume. Defaults and all existing modes are unchanged.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- `kernel_map.hpp`: new enum value `CenterAveraged`, appended last so existing values and cache keys are unchanged, with documentation.
- `kernel_map.cpp` `build_pairs`: for `CenterAveraged`, if `find_containing(t)` is -1 or finer than the output leaf, collect the leaves overlapping `[t - s_out/2, t + s_out/2)` with `for_each_overlap`. Each gets weight `ov / sum(ov)`, so the weights of a tap sum to 1. Otherwise the pair is the same as `CenterSampled`'s. `ops.cpp` already treats every non-`CenterSampled` mode as weighted, so it needs no change.
- On uniform grids (and for fine outputs over coarse inputs) no tap cell is split. The maps then equal `CenterSampled` exactly (tested).
- `docs/adaptive.md`: mode table row and an explanation of the coarse-to-fine tap behaviour.
- The benchmark gains a mode name, `averaged`.

## TESTING

New `tests/adaptive/test_center_averaged.cpp`, in `adaptive_tests`:
- `center_averaged_weights_partition_each_split_tap`: for shifts 0/-1/-2, every (slot, output) tap's weights sum to 1 (1e-12), single-leaf taps have weight exactly 1, and every tap `CenterSampled` reads is also read.
- `center_averaged_shift_minus_one_reaches_every_input_leaf`: K = 1 and 3, `output_level_shift = -1`. With `CenterAveraged`, every input leaf gets a non-zero feature gradient. With the default mode some do not, which documents the existing behaviour.
- `center_averaged_gradients_match_finite_differences`: forward (features and weight) and transposed convolution, shift 0 and -1, double, central differences (eps 1e-6, rtol 1e-5, atol 1e-6).
- `center_averaged_equals_center_sampled_without_split_taps`: a uniform grid with holes (K = 3, 5) gives identical maps and outputs, and fine outputs over coarse inputs give weight 1.

| suite | upstream main f93b7bc | #15 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| adaptive_tests (CPU) | 70/70 | 74/74 | 78 passed, 0 failed |
| gaussian_tests (CPU) | 31 passed, 2 skipped | same | 31 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped |
| CUDA suites | 72/72, 35/35 | running | running (a comment will follow) |

## BENCHMARKS

`adaptive_kmap_bench`, depth 4, n = 20000 (41,376 leaves), CPU build, exclusive bench lock. Kernel-map build, warm (lazy indices built).

Default modes, interleaved A/B against #15 (3 rounds x (2 warm-up + 5 timed)): the code path is unchanged, and all differences are run-to-run noise. Ranges overlap, and both directions appear in the same run.

| mode | #15 | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| CenterSampled cold / warm | 213.2 / 229.9 ms | 207.0 / 209.5 ms | -2.9 % / -8.9 % |
| VolumeWeighted cold / warm | 251.9 / 221.6 ms | 219.1 / 262.0 ms | -13.0 % / +18.2 % |
| OverlapWeighted cold / warm | 558.1 / 600.3 ms | 635.0 / 620.4 ms | +13.8 % / +3.3 % |
| peak working set | 220.3 MB | 219.5 MB | |

Cost of the new mode (same binary, 3 runs x (2 warm-up + 5 timed); median of the run medians, [min-max of all timed repeats]):

| shift | mode | pairs | kmap warm |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | CenterSampled | 905,482 | 203.4 ms [186.8-259.8] |
| 0 | CenterAveraged | 999,667 | 293.8 ms [252.1-332.2] |
| 0 | OverlapWeighted | 999,667 | 627.3 ms [540.0-768.1] |
| -1 | CenterSampled | 163,810 | 74.1 ms [54.9-104.8] |
| -1 | CenterAveraged | 939,347 | 270.6 ms [233.5-367.0] |
| -1 | OverlapWeighted | 939,347 | 276.1 ms [236.5-368.2] |

With shift -1, `CenterAveraged` reads 5.7x more input pairs than `CenterSampled`: all children instead of one per tap. The convolution cost scales with pairs. GPU memory / kernel time: n/a (host map build; the feature path is unchanged).

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

No training run. The functional effect is shown by the tests: with `output_level_shift = -1`, every input leaf under a coarsened output contributes and receives gradient, where the default mode reaches 1 of 2^D. On the benchmark workload, the strided map reads 939,347 pairs instead of 163,810.

## TRADEOFFS

- Opt-in, so existing models are unaffected. Making it the default would change outputs for any mixed-level or strided use, which is why I did not do that.
- About 1.45x the map-build time of `CenterSampled` at shift 0, and about 3.7x at shift -1 (because of the extra pairs). Convolution time grows with the pair count.
- It averages over occupied leaves only. Empty parts of a split tap cell do not dilute the average (consistent with `Reduction::Mean`). A volume-normalised variant (divide by the cell volume) would need a separate flag.
- `Multilinear` interpolation and the separate jump at level boundaries are untouched.

## REPRODUCTION

- Base: upstream f93b7bc; stacked on #15. Commands: `adaptive_tests.exe`, `gaussian_tests.exe`. Bench: `adaptive_kmap_bench --depth 4 --shift <0|-1> --modes center,averaged,overlap --interp 0 --phases warm --warmup 2 --reps 5`. A/B: `ab.py --rounds 3 --a pr15=... --b pr=... -- --depth 4 --modes center,volume,overlap --interp 0 --warmup 2 --reps 5`
- Build: CMake 4.2.3 + Ninja, Release, CPU_ONLY with LibTorch 2.15.0+cpu (PR #5's CMake fix injected at configure time). CUDA build: CUDA 13.4.3 + LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134, sm_75.
- Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88, Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors docker/cuda-profile.sh.

## SUMMARY

Coordinate-map insertion, strided maps and kernel maps on CUDA run thrust algorithms (`sort_by_key`, `reduce_by_key`, `inclusive_scan`, `remove_if`, `unique`, `sort`, ...) with the `thrust::device` policy. That policy allocates each algorithm's temporary storage with `cudaMalloc` and releases it with `cudaFree`, which synchronizes the whole device. This PR passes an execution policy that takes those temporaries from PyTorch's CUDA caching allocator instead.

Measured on an RTX 2080 SUPER: a training-style step (new `SparseTensor` from coordinates + `MinkowskiConvolution` forward + backward) is **16-18 % faster** at 100k points (forward including map construction 27-34 % faster), 4.4 % at 400k points / 64 channels. Cached-map convolution is unaffected.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

- New `MinkowskiEngine/src/thrust_policy.cuh`: `detail::thrust_policy()` returns `thrust::cuda::par(allocator).on(0)` where the allocator calls `c10::cuda::CUDACachingAllocator::raw_alloc_with_stream(n, 0)` / `raw_delete`.
  - Same stream as before (legacy default stream, which `thrust::device` uses), and `par` is synchronous like `thrust::device`, so ordering and host-side semantics do not change.
  - Blocks are allocated for stream 0, so a block released by one algorithm is only reused by later work on that stream (stream-ordered reuse).
- `src/coordinate_map_gpu.cu` (21 call sites) and `src/kernel_map.cuh` (`decompose`: `sort_by_key`, `reduce_by_key`): `thrust::device` -> `::minkowski::detail::thrust_policy()`. No algorithm changes.
- Not changed here: the pooling, broadcast and spmm kernels also use `thrust::device` / `cudaMalloc` (and `cudaMallocManaged` in spmm); they are not on the per-step map construction path measured here.

## TESTING

| Suite | Build | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| core_tests (incl. CPU vs CUDA conv/pool agreement, CUDA quantization) | CUDA * | 44 passed, 0 failed | 44 passed, 0 failed |
| adaptive_tests | CUDA * | 72 passed, 0 failed | 72 passed, 0 failed |
| gaussian_tests | CUDA * | 35 passed, 0 failed | 35 passed, 0 failed |

\* Built and tested on one combined branch (this PR on top of #10, #12, #13, #16) because only one CUDA build dir per agent fits the shared machine. `core_tests` comes from #10; its `cpu_cuda_*` tests compare CUDA convolution/pooling (whose kernel maps go through the changed code) against the CPU path and a dense reference. This PR itself only changes the three CUDA files above, which are identical on `main` and on that branch. CPU_ONLY builds do not compile these files.

## BENCHMARKS

`core_conv_bench` from #10 (with its `--rebuild` flag: every iteration builds a new `SparseTensor` from the same coordinates, i.e. coordinate-map insertion + kernel map + conv forward/backward, like a training step on a new batch). A = combined branch without this PR, B = with it. Interleaved A B A B for 5 rounds under an exclusive GPU + machine lock, 2 warm-ups + 5 timed iterations per round (n = 25 per side), `torch::cuda::synchronize()` before each timer read. Raw: `results/core-engine/c7_bench/`.

| Config (fp32, kernel 3) | Metric | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 x 50k pts, 32 -> 32, stride 1, `--rebuild` | step median (min-max) | 7.11 ms (5.75-8.99) | 5.83 ms (4.65-6.88) | **-17.9 %** |
| | forward incl. map construction | 4.42 ms | 2.92 ms | **-33.9 %** |
| | backward | 2.35 ms | 2.26 ms | -3.8 % |
| | CUDA peak allocated / reserved | 108 / 132 MiB | 108 / 156 MiB | 0 % / +18 % |
| 2 x 50k pts, 32 -> 32, stride 2, `--rebuild` | step median (min-max) | 5.79 ms (4.90-9.43) | 4.85 ms (4.27-6.74) | **-16.3 %** |
| | forward incl. map construction | 3.73 ms | 2.72 ms | -27.1 % |
| | CUDA peak allocated / reserved | 111 / 132 MiB | 111 / 132 MiB | 0 % |
| 2 x 200k pts, 64 -> 64, stride 1, `--rebuild` | step median (min-max) | 41.83 ms (39.89-47.77) | 40.00 ms (38.44-45.88) | -4.4 % |
| | forward incl. map construction | 21.74 ms | 19.85 ms | -8.7 % |
| | CUDA peak allocated / reserved | 975 / 1042 MiB | 975 / 1040 MiB | 0 % |
| 2 x 50k pts, 32 -> 32, cached map (no rebuild) | step median (min-max) | 2.53 ms (2.37-3.73) | 2.64 ms (2.35-3.26) | +4.6 % (noise: no changed code runs here, stdev 0.30-0.38 ms) |

- CPU peak working set: unchanged within noise (CUDA path only).
- Kernel time: not measured separately (no Nsight tools on the host); the gain is host/driver time from avoided `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` pairs and their implicit device synchronizations.

## MACHINE LEARNING RESULTS

n/a (no numerical change: same algorithms, same stream, same order). For training, per-step map construction is the part that improves; at 100k points per batch it is about 1.3 ms of a 7 ms single-layer step.

## TRADEOFFS

- Temporaries now stay in PyTorch's cache after use: peak reserved memory can be higher (+24 MiB in one config above); `torch::cuda::empty_cache()`-style calls release them as with any cached tensor memory.
- Larger inputs gain less (the step becomes compute-bound: -4.4 % at 400k points / 64 channels).
- Other `thrust::device` / `cudaMalloc` / `cudaMallocManaged` sites (pooling, broadcast, spmm/interpolation) and the stream-0 copy/accumulate kernels with their stream synchronizations are left for a follow-up; they are not on the measured path.

## REPRODUCTION

- Benchmark: `core_conv_bench --device cuda --points 50000 --extent 96 --batches 2 --cin 32 --cout 32 --stride 1 --warmup 2 --repeats 5 --seed 0 --rebuild` (also `--stride 2 --seed 4`, and `--points 200000 --extent 128 --cin 64 --cout 64 --seed 3`).
- Hardware: Ryzen 5 5600X 6C/12T, 16 GB RAM, RTX 2080 SUPER 8 GB sm_75, driver 610.88 (WDDM), Windows 11, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 13.4.3, LibTorch 2.15.0+cu134. Docker was not available on the test host; the native toolchain mirrors `docker/cuda-profile.sh` (same CUDA 13.x / LibTorch 2.15.0 pins). `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` are comparatively expensive under WDDM; the gain on Linux may be smaller.

## SUMMARY

Adds `adaptive_vs_uniform_bench` (registered in CMake, smoke run in CTest) plus a stdlib-only driver
`tests/adaptive/run_adaptive_vs_uniform.py`. The existing `adaptive_bench` compares adaptive leaves with the
**dense** refinement of the occupied cells (`uniform_voxels_est`), which flatters adaptive. This benchmark compares
adaptive trees with **sparse** uniform voxelizations at the coarsest level, the finest level, and at a voxel size whose
occupied count matches `refine_by_density(16)`, on five deterministic datasets, CPU and CUDA, and reports accuracy next
to cost. No library code changes.

Findings (details and raw numbers below):

* **Adaptive wins on accuracy per voxel for clustered data.** Clustered set: `refine_by_density(64)` with 12,351
  leaves has a lower held-out error (nRMSE 0.492) than sparse uniform with 2.2x the voxels (26,652, nRMSE 0.517). At an
  equal voxel count, `refine_by_density(16)` has 14 % lower nearest error (0.447 vs 0.517), 30 % lower multilinear
  error (0.175 vs 0.251) and 0.923 vs 0.802 coverage.
* **It loses at equal voxel count when density is roughly uniform.** Sphere shell: matched uniform 0.398 vs adaptive
  0.418. Uniform random: the density criteria never refine, and variance refinement spends 8x the voxels for a 1 % gain.
  For the Gaussian-PLY colours and the scan intensities the error is flat across all methods, so the cheapest method
  wins.
* **Each leaf costs more.** Refinement creates all `2^D` children, so refined regions are tiled with empty siblings.
  An adaptive leaf has 21-26 kernel-map neighbours, against 6-15 for a sparse uniform voxel. At equal voxel count on
  CPU, kernel-map build is about 2.1x and forward about 2.3x the uniform cost (clustered: 174 vs 83 ms, 14.7 vs 6.3 ms).
* **ROI refinement explodes.** Refining a 32^3 box to depth 4 gives 128-154K leaves, mostly empty, with accuracy
  unchanged outside the box. At depth 5 it gives 1.03M leaves, 4.95 GB peak RAM and a 1.3 s CPU forward. The proposed
  `drop_empty` feature (separate PR) targets this.
* **On CUDA the adaptive engine is launch-bound.** On the same uniform voxel sets, MinkowskiEngine conv is 7.5-13x
  faster per forward (0.3-0.6 ms vs 3.5-5 ms) and 5-18x faster per forward+backward. Its kernel map takes about 1-3 ms,
  against 23-1,580 ms for the host-built adaptive map. The adaptive CUDA forward has a floor of about 3.5-4 ms however
  few leaves there are (897 leaves: 3.8 ms), because it launches per kernel slot and re-uploads the map on every call.
  Voxel savings therefore cannot make it beat MinkowskiEngine on GPU until that overhead is removed.
* **Crossover today:** adaptive pays off on CPU, for clustered or multi-density data, with ``refine_by_density``
  k >= 16, and without large ROI refinements. Uniform sparse wins on GPU, on uniform-density data, and whenever the
  field is not resolvable at the finer levels.
* **`voxelize_sphere` reports signed-error accuracy.** It stops at the first split where the signed volume error
  cancels. Targets 99.5 % and 99.9 % both return 232 leaves (50 m and 25 m boundary cells) with a reported 99.97 %, but
  the geometric symmetric-difference error is **24.3 %**. A uniform level-6 grid is at 2.2 %. Inside one level the
  signed error changes sign 3 times. See the sphere table.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS

* Datasets: all in [0,256)^3. Train/test split is every 10th point held out (90k/10k).
  `uniform`, `clustered` (12 Gaussian clusters, sigma 2/4/8, 90 %, plus 10 % background) and `shell` (r = 100,
  radial sigma 0.5) carry a 4-channel multi-scale sine field (wavelengths 64/32/16/8).
  `ply` uses the `tests/data/test.ply` Gaussian centres (139,410; 0.5-99.5 % quantile box) with RGB from SH DC.
  `scan` uses 21 frames of `tests/data/voxels` (105k occupied 1 m voxels, jittered inside the voxel) with
  intensity values; its ROI is the first target.
  Seeds are fixed (`--seed`, torch CPU generator).
* Methods:
  * `u_coarse` / `u_fine`: `from_points` at the base / finest voxel size.
  * `u_matched`: bisection on the voxel size to match the `a_dens16` count. Its `build_ms` includes the 40-step
    search.
  * `a_roi`: refine a 4x4x4 base-cell box to `max_depth`.
  * `a_densK`: `refine_by_density(K)`.
  * `a_var`: `refine_by_variance(0.05 x global feature variance)`.
  * Every adaptive tree is re-voxelized from the points afterwards. Point-free leaves keep their replicated parent
    value, which is the fairest fill for keep-empty refinement.
* Metrics:
  * `voxels`, level histogram, feature and coordinate bytes, kernel-map pairs, and pairs per leaf.
  * `kmap cold`: `build_adaptive_kernel_map` on a fresh topology with an empty cache.
  * Adaptive `fwd` and `fwd+bwd`: one 3x3x3 `CenterSampled` conv, 16 to 16 channels, float32, cached map.
  * MinkowskiEngine `MinkowskiConvolution(16,16,3)` on the same uniform coordinates. `first` means a new coordinate
    manager; `kmap est` = cold - insert - warm.
  * `first conv`: the first conv in a fresh process.
  * Held-out `Nearest` nRMSE (RMSE / std of the test values; uncovered points predict 0), coverage, and
    `Multilinear` RMSE on 2,000 test points.
  * Peak RAM is the process `PeakWorkingSetSize`, one process per case. Peak VRAM is the caching-allocator
    `allocated_bytes` peak, reset per case.
* `--sphere` compares four quantities: `voxelize_sphere`'s reported accuracy, the signed volume error, a 2M-point
  Monte Carlo symmetric-difference error, and per-level sparse uniform solid spheres. It also replays the FIFO split
  order and counts sign changes of the signed error per level.

## TESTING

* New CTest entry `adaptive_vs_uniform_bench_smoke`: tiny sizes, one repetition, all method types.
* Commands, run in the build dir:
  * `adaptive_tests.exe`
  * `gaussian_tests.exe`
  * `ctest --output-on-failure`
